2.big: The church, Jewish and Gentile together, is now the temple where God lives by his Spirit.
2.diff: Most scholars read 'prophets' here as New Testament prophets alongside the apostles, both of whom had a foundational role. Whether prophecy continues in the same sense today is part of the wider debate about spiritual gifts.

3.ctx: Paul begins a prayer, breaks off to explain his ministry, and resumes the prayer in verse 14.
3.mean: Paul describes himself as a prisoner for the sake of the Gentiles, and explains the 'mystery' revealed to him: that Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and partakers of the promise in Christ. In the New Testament a mystery is not a puzzle but something previously hidden and now made known. Through the church, God's manifold wisdom is now displayed even to the heavenly powers.
3.big: God's long-hidden plan was to unite Jews and Gentiles in one body, and the church itself displays his wisdom.

3.ctx: Paul resumes the prayer he began in 3:1 and broke off to explain his ministry. Jews usually prayed standing; kneeling signals unusual earnestness.
3.mean: Paul says he kneels before the Father and prays that they would be strengthened with power through his Spirit, that Christ may dwell in their hearts through faith, and that, rooted in love, they may grasp the breadth, length, height and depth of the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge. He closes with a doxology to the one able to do far more than all we ask or imagine.
3.big: Paul prays that believers would know by experience a love too great to be fully understood.

4.ctx: The turning point of the letter: chapters 1–3 describe what God has done; chapters 4–6 describe how to live in response. 'Therefore' marks the shift.
4.mean: Paul urges them to walk worthy of their calling, with humility, gentleness and patience, eager to keep the unity of the Spirit. There is one body, one Spirit, one hope, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all. Christ has given gifts — apostles, prophets, evangelists, shepherds and teachers — to equip the saints for the work of ministry and build up the body until all reach maturity, speaking the truth in love.
4.big: Christ gives leaders to equip every believer, so that the whole body grows up into him.
4.diff: Verse 8 quotes Psalm 68:18 with 'gave gifts' where the Hebrew has 'received gifts', a difference scholars explain in several ways. Verse 9's 'descended into the lower regions' is read by some as the incarnation, by others as Christ's descent to the realm of the dead. Whether apostles and prophets continue today is debated among evangelicals.

4.ctx: Ephesus was a centre of pagan worship, notably the great temple of Artemis.
4.mean: Paul says they must no longer walk as the Gentiles do, in the futility of their minds, darkened in understanding and hardened in heart. They were taught to put off the old self, be renewed in the spirit of their minds, and put on the new self, created after the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness. He then gives concrete examples: speak truth, do not let anger lead to sin, do not steal but work and share, speak only what builds up, do not grieve the Holy Spirit, and forgive as God in Christ forgave you.
4.big: The new life in Christ is put on in the ordinary details of speech, work and forgiveness.

5.ctx: Continuing the practical instruction begun in 4:17. Sexual immorality was widely accepted in Greco-Roman society and bound up with some pagan worship, so Paul's standard would have marked the church out sharply.
5.mean: Paul says to be imitators of God as beloved children and to walk in love, as Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering. Sexual immorality, impurity and greed must not even be named among them, nor crude talk; instead, thanksgiving. No one who is sexually immoral, impure or covetous has an inheritance in the kingdom.
5.big: Believers are to imitate God's self-giving love and reject everything that contradicts it.

5.ctx: The contrast between darkness and light runs through the passage.
5.mean: Paul says they were once darkness but now are light in the Lord, and should walk as children of light, exposing the unfruitful works of darkness. Look carefully how you walk, making the best use of the time. Do not get drunk with wine, but be filled with the Spirit, addressing one another in psalms, hymns and spiritual songs, giving thanks always, and submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ.
5.big: Being filled with the Spirit shows itself in worship, thanksgiving and mutual submission.
5.diff: Christians differ over what 'filled with the Spirit' involves — whether a repeated experience, an ongoing state, or both. Paul's own description here is corporate and practical: singing, thanksgiving and submission to one another.

5.ctx: The 'household code' begins, a common form in ancient moral writing that addressed husbands and wives, parents and children, masters and slaves.
5.mean: Paul says wives should submit to their husbands as to the Lord, for the husband is the head of the wife as Christ is head of the church. Husbands should love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her. He quotes Genesis 2:24 and says this mystery refers to Christ and the church. Verse 21 — submitting to one another — introduces the whole section.
5.big: Christian marriage is meant to picture the relationship between Christ and his church.
5.diff: This passage is central to the complementarian and egalitarian debate. Complementarians, including most Reformed churches, read it as teaching a husband's loving headship and a wife's willing submission, both modelled on Christ. Egalitarians emphasise verse 21's mutual submission and read 'head' as 'source' rather than 'authority'. All agree that Paul's demand on husbands — to love as Christ loved, giving himself up — rules out any selfish or harsh use of headship.

6.ctx: The household code continues from 5:21. In Roman law a father held near-absolute power over his children, so Paul's instruction to fathers not to provoke them was a real restraint.
6.mean: Paul tells children to obey their parents in the Lord, quoting the fifth commandment with its promise. Fathers are not to provoke their children to anger, but to bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.
6.big: The gospel reshapes family life in both directions: honour from children, patience from fathers.

6.ctx: Slavery in the Roman world was widespread and not based on race; slaves could be household managers or labourers.
6.mean: Paul tells slaves to obey their earthly masters with sincerity, as serving Christ, knowing that the Lord will reward everyone for the good they do, slave or free. Masters are to do the same, stop threatening, and remember that both they and their slaves have the same Master in heaven, who shows no partiality.
6.big: Master and slave stand as equals before the same Lord, which begins to undermine the institution itself.
6.diff: Paul regulates rather than abolishes slavery here, which troubles modern readers. Christians have long noted that the principles he states — equal accountability to one Master, no partiality — are the ones later Christians drew on to end the slave trade.

6.ctx: The closing section of the letter. Roman soldiers would have been a familiar sight to a prisoner.
6.mean: Paul says to be strong in the Lord and put on the whole armour of God, because the struggle is not against flesh and blood but against spiritual forces of evil. He lists the belt of truth, breastplate of righteousness, shoes of the gospel of peace, shield of faith, helmet of salvation and sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God. Much of the imagery comes from Isaiah, where it describes God's own armour. He ends by asking for prayer that he may speak boldly.
6.big: Believers face a real spiritual battle, and stand in it with God's own armour and with prayer.

6.ctx: Tychicus, a trusted companion from the province of Asia, carries the letter (compare Colossians 4:7).
6.mean: Paul says Tychicus will tell them how he is and encourage them. He closes with peace, love and faith from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, and grace to all who love the Lord with undying love.
6.big: The letter ends as it began, with grace and peace from the Father and the Son.

1.ctx: Philippi was a Roman colony in Macedonia, the first place Paul planted a church in Europe (Acts 16). He writes from prison, probably in Rome in the early 60s, to a church that had supported him financially.
1.mean: Paul and Timothy greet the saints in Christ Jesus at Philippi, with the overseers and deacons. The letter is warm and personal throughout.
1.big: Paul writes as a servant of Christ Jesus to a church he loves.
1.diff: The letter's place of writing is debated — Rome, Ephesus and Caesarea have all been proposed. Rome is the traditional view. Nothing in its teaching depends on the answer.

1.ctx: A thanksgiving, as in most of Paul's letters. The Philippians had supported Paul financially from the start (4:15–16), which is the 'partnership in the gospel' he has in mind.
1.mean: Paul says he thanks God every time he remembers them because of their partnership in the gospel from the first day. He is sure that he who began a good work in them will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ. He prays that their love may abound in knowledge and discernment, so that they may be pure and blameless, filled with the fruit of righteousness.
1.big: God finishes what he starts in his people.
1.diff: Reformed theology has often cited verse 6 in support of the perseverance of the saints — that God will keep those he has saved. Others read it primarily as Paul's confidence about this particular church. The verse's focus is on God's faithfulness rather than human endurance.

1.ctx: Paul is under guard, probably chained to a soldier in rented quarters, awaiting trial.
1.mean: Paul says his imprisonment has actually advanced the gospel: the whole imperial guard knows he is in chains for Christ, and most believers have become bolder. Some preach Christ from rivalry, others from goodwill. Paul's response is that in every way Christ is proclaimed, and in that he rejoices.
1.big: Paul measures his circumstances by what they do for the gospel, not what they do for him.

1.ctx: Paul is awaiting a verdict that could mean release or execution. He writes knowing either outcome is possible, and weighs them openly.
1.mean: Paul says that to live is Christ and to die is gain. He is torn between departing to be with Christ, which is far better, and remaining in the flesh, which is more necessary for them. He is convinced he will remain for their progress and joy in the faith.
1.big: For Paul, Christ is the meaning of life and the gain of death.
1.diff: Verse 23, 'to depart and be with Christ', is one of the main texts Christians cite for believers being with Christ immediately after death, before the final resurrection.

1.ctx: 'Live worthy' uses a word connected with citizenship — pointed in a Roman colony proud of its status.
1.mean: Paul says to conduct themselves in a manner worthy of the gospel, standing firm in one spirit, striving side by side for the faith, not frightened by opponents. It has been granted to them not only to believe in Christ but also to suffer for his sake.
1.big: Suffering for Christ is presented as a gift alongside faith, not a sign that something has gone wrong.

2.ctx: Paul appeals for unity, apparently because of tension in the church (see 4:2).
2.mean: Paul says that if there is any encouragement in Christ, comfort from love, or participation in the Spirit, they should complete his joy by being of the same mind. Do nothing from selfish ambition or conceit, but in humility count others more significant than yourselves, looking to their interests as well as your own.
2.big: Unity in the church depends on humility that puts others first.

2.ctx: Many scholars think verses 6–11 are an early Christian hymn, which Paul quotes or composed. It is one of the most important passages about Christ in the New Testament.
2.mean: Paul says to have the mind of Christ, who, though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself by taking the form of a servant, being born in human likeness. He humbled himself by becoming obedient to death, even death on a cross. Therefore God highly exalted him and gave him the name above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord. Paul applies Isaiah 45:23 — where the LORD swears that every knee will bow to him — to Jesus. The passage holds together Christ's full deity and his full humanity, which the church has expressed as the two natures in one person (see the note on Mark 4:35).
2.big: The eternal Son took the lowest place, and God has given him the highest — and that pattern is the one believers are to follow.
2.diff: What 'emptied himself' means has been debated. The historic understanding is that the Son did not give up his divine nature but took on human nature and the status of a servant — adding rather than subtracting. Some modern 'kenotic' theories propose that he set aside certain divine attributes; most Reformed and evangelical theologians reject this, since the text says he was 'in the form of God' and the emptying consists in 'taking the form of a servant'.

2.ctx: 'Therefore' ties this to the example of Christ just described.
2.mean: Paul says to work out their own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in them, both to will and to work for his good pleasure. Do everything without grumbling, so that they may shine as lights in a crooked generation, holding fast to the word of life. Even if Paul is poured out as a drink offering, he rejoices.
2.big: Believers work hard at living out their salvation precisely because God is already at work within them.
2.diff: Verses 12–13 are a classic text on how God's work and human effort relate. Reformed theology stresses that God's working is prior and effective, and human effort its result; other traditions place more weight on cooperation. All agree Paul is not telling them to earn salvation, which he denies in 3:9.

2.ctx: Two companions whose examples illustrate the self-giving Paul has described.
2.mean: Paul hopes to send Timothy, who is genuinely concerned for their welfare and has served with Paul like a son with a father. He sends back Epaphroditus, their messenger, who nearly died in the work of Christ, and asks them to honour such men.
2.big: The mind of Christ is seen in ordinary people who put others' needs above their own.

3.ctx: Paul warns against teachers insisting on circumcision, as in Galatians. The abrupt change of tone leads some scholars to think the letter combines more than one of Paul's letters, though many see a single letter.
3.mean: Paul says to watch out for the 'dogs' and 'mutilators of the flesh'. He could boast more than anyone in his Jewish credentials — circumcised on the eighth day, a Hebrew of Hebrews, a Pharisee, blameless under the law. But whatever gain he had he now counts as loss, even as rubbish, compared to knowing Christ Jesus and being found in him, not having a righteousness of his own from the law, but the righteousness from God that depends on faith.
3.big: The best religious record in the world is worthless compared with the righteousness God gives through faith in Christ.
3.diff: As in Galatians 2:16, 'faith in Christ' in verse 9 can also be translated 'the faithfulness of Christ'. Reformed theology reads verse 9 as a clear statement of imputed righteousness — a righteousness from God credited to the believer. Some New Perspective scholars emphasise Paul's ethnic credentials as the 'righteousness of my own'. Both agree Paul rejects any righteousness grounded in the law.

3.ctx: Having renounced his own righteousness, Paul guards against the opposite error of thinking he has arrived.
3.mean: Paul says he has not already obtained this or been made perfect, but presses on to make it his own, because Christ Jesus has made him his own. Forgetting what lies behind and straining forward, he presses on toward the goal for the prize of the upward call of God in Christ Jesus.
3.big: The Christian life is lived between being grasped by Christ and finally grasping him.

3.ctx: Philippi was a Roman colony whose citizens held Roman citizenship though they had never seen Rome.
3.mean: Paul says to imitate him and those who walk as he does, because many walk as enemies of the cross, whose god is their belly and whose minds are set on earthly things. But our citizenship is in heaven, from which we await a Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform our lowly body to be like his glorious body.
3.big: Believers are citizens of heaven now, awaiting a Saviour who will transform even their bodies.

4.ctx: Two women in the church, Euodia and Syntyche, who had worked alongside Paul, were in disagreement.
4.mean: Paul urges them to agree in the Lord and asks a companion to help them. He then says to rejoice in the Lord always, let their gentleness be known to all, and not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let their requests be made known to God. The peace of God, which surpasses understanding, will guard their hearts and minds in Christ Jesus. Whatever is true, honourable, just, pure, lovely and commendable — think about these things.
4.big: The answer to anxiety is thankful prayer, and God's promise in response is his peace.

4.ctx: The Philippians had sent Paul a gift through Epaphroditus (2:25), and prisoners in the Roman system depended on friends for food and necessities.
4.mean: Paul thanks them, while saying he has learned to be content in whatever situation — in plenty and in hunger. He can do all things through him who strengthens him. He rejoices in their gift not for his own sake but for the fruit it credits to them, calling it a fragrant offering pleasing to God. And his God will supply every need of theirs according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus.
4.big: Contentment comes from Christ's strength, not from circumstances.
4.diff: Verse 13 is often quoted as a promise of success in any endeavour. In context it is about enduring every circumstance — plenty or want — through Christ's strength.

4.ctx: The closing greetings. 'Caesar's household' meant the large imperial staff of slaves and freedmen, not necessarily the emperor's family.
4.mean: Paul greets every saint in Christ Jesus, passes on greetings from those with him — especially those of Caesar's household — and closes with the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ.
4.big: The gospel has reached even into the emperor's household.

1.ctx: Colossae was a small town in the Lycus valley of Asia Minor, near Laodicea and Hierapolis. Paul had not visited it; the church was founded by Epaphras (1:7). Paul writes from prison, most likely in Rome.
1.mean: Paul and Timothy greet the saints and faithful brothers in Christ at Colossae with grace and peace from God the Father.
1.big: Paul writes to a church he has never met, as one family in Christ.
1.diff: As with Ephesians, some scholars question whether Paul wrote Colossians, noting differences of style. The letter claims Paul as author, and many scholars, including most evangelicals, accept it; its close links with Philemon support that.

1.ctx: A thanksgiving and prayer, as usual in Paul's letters, for a church he knows only through Epaphras.
1.mean: Paul says he thanks God for their faith in Christ and love for all the saints, springing from the hope laid up for them in heaven, which they heard in the gospel now bearing fruit in the whole world. He prays that they may be filled with the knowledge of God's will, walk worthy of the Lord, and give thanks to the Father who has transferred them from the domain of darkness to the kingdom of his beloved Son, in whom they have redemption, the forgiveness of sins.
1.big: Believers have already been rescued from darkness and brought into the kingdom of God's Son.

1.ctx: Many scholars think verses 15–20 are an early Christian hymn. It is one of the highest statements about Christ in the New Testament, and a key passage in discussions with Jehovah's Witnesses.
1.mean: Paul says the Son is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn over all creation, because by him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible — all things were created through him and for him. He is before all things, and in him all things hold together. He is the head of the body, the church; the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, so that in everything he might be preeminent. In him all the fullness of God was pleased to dwell, and through him God reconciled all things to himself, making peace by the blood of his cross.
1.big: The one who made and sustains all things is the same one who reconciled all things through his cross.
1.diff: 'Firstborn' has been read by some groups, including Jehovah's Witnesses, to mean Christ was the first thing created. The historic Christian reading is that 'firstborn' means rank and supremacy, as in Psalm 89:27 where David, the youngest son, is called firstborn — and verse 16 says all things were created through him, which would include any created thing. The New World Translation's insertion of 'other' ('all other things') is not in the Greek.

1.ctx: Paul turns to his own ministry, written from prison for a church that had not seen him.
1.mean: Paul says he rejoices in his sufferings for their sake, and in his flesh fills up what is lacking in Christ's afflictions for the sake of his body, the church. God made known to him the mystery hidden for ages: Christ in you, the hope of glory. Him we proclaim, warning and teaching everyone with all wisdom, that we may present everyone mature in Christ.
1.big: The heart of the gospel mystery is Christ living in his people and their future glory with him.
1.diff: Verse 24 does not mean Christ's saving suffering was incomplete, which Paul denies elsewhere. Most interpreters read it as the sufferings the church, Christ's body, must still endure in spreading the gospel, which Paul shares.

2.ctx: Paul addresses the particular danger facing the Colossians: teaching that added philosophy, special knowledge, rituals and angel-worship to Christ.
2.mean: Paul says he struggles for them and for those at Laodicea, that they may reach all the riches of full assurance and the knowledge of God's mystery, Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. He says this so no one deludes them with plausible arguments.
2.big: Every treasure of wisdom is found in Christ, so nothing needs to be added to him.
2.h: Absent in Body, Present in Spirit

2.ctx: The heart of the letter's warning. The exact nature of the 'Colossian heresy' is debated, but it seems to have mixed Jewish ritual, mystical visions and ascetic rules.
2.mean: Paul says to walk in Christ as they received him, rooted and built up in him. Do not be taken captive by philosophy and empty deceit according to human tradition, for in Christ the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily, and they have been filled in him. They were buried with him in baptism and raised with him through faith. God forgave all their trespasses, cancelling the record of debt against them by nailing it to the cross, and disarmed the rulers and authorities. So let no one pass judgement on them over food, drink, festivals or Sabbaths, which were a shadow of things to come; the substance belongs to Christ. Rules like 'do not handle, do not taste' have an appearance of wisdom but no value against the indulgence of the flesh.
2.big: Because all God's fullness dwells bodily in Christ, believers are complete in him and need no additions.
2.diff: Verse 9, 'the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily', is among the clearest New Testament statements that Christ is fully God and fully human — the two natures in one person (see Mark 4:35). Christians differ over whether the Sabbath commandment still binds believers in some form; Reformed churches have historically kept the Lord's Day as the Christian Sabbath, while others read verse 16 as ending any Sabbath obligation.

3.ctx: The practical section begins. As in Ephesians, what believers are in Christ comes first, then how they should live.
3.mean: Paul says that since they have been raised with Christ, they should seek the things above, where Christ is seated at God's right hand. Their life is hidden with Christ in God. So put to death what is earthly: sexual immorality, impurity, covetousness, which is idolatry, and anger, slander and lying. They have put off the old self and put on the new, in which there is not Greek and Jew, slave and free, but Christ is all and in all. Put on compassion, kindness, humility, meekness, patience, forgiveness as the Lord forgave, and above all love. Let the peace of Christ rule and the word of Christ dwell richly, singing with thankfulness, and doing everything in the name of the Lord Jesus.
3.big: Because believers' true life is now hidden with Christ, they are to put off the old self and put on the character of Christ.

3.ctx: The household code, parallel to Ephesians 5:21–6:9 but shorter.
3.mean: Paul tells wives to submit to their husbands as fitting in the Lord, and husbands to love their wives and not be harsh with them. Children are to obey their parents in everything, and fathers not to provoke their children, lest they become discouraged.
3.big: Christ's lordship reshapes every relationship in the home.
3.diff: As at Ephesians 5, Christians differ over how the call for wives to submit applies today. Complementarian and egalitarian readings are both held by evangelicals; all agree the husband's call to love rules out harshness.

3.ctx: Slavery was common in the Roman world. Onesimus, a runaway slave from Colossae, carries this letter with Tychicus (4:9), which makes the passage pointed.
3.mean: Paul tells slaves to obey their earthly masters sincerely, working heartily as for the Lord rather than for people, knowing that from the Lord they will receive the inheritance as their reward. Whoever does wrong will be paid back, and there is no partiality.
3.big: All work, even under an unjust system, can be done for the Lord who sees and rewards.

4.ctx: The instruction to masters completes the household code, then Paul turns to prayer and speech toward outsiders.
4.mean: Paul tells masters to treat their slaves justly and fairly, knowing they too have a Master in heaven. He urges steadfast, watchful prayer with thanksgiving, and prayer for an open door for the gospel. Walk in wisdom toward outsiders, making the best use of the time; let speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so they know how to answer each person.
4.big: Believers are to pray for gospel opportunities and speak graciously to those outside the church.
4.diff: Verse 1's reminder that masters have a Master in heaven is one of the principles later Christians drew on in opposing slavery.

4.ctx: A list of Paul's companions, many of whom appear in Philemon and Acts.
4.mean: Paul commends Tychicus and Onesimus, who will bring news. He sends greetings from Aristarchus, Mark the cousin of Barnabas, Jesus called Justus, Epaphras who struggles in prayer for them, Luke the beloved physician, and Demas.
4.big: The gospel advances through a network of ordinary, named co-workers.
4.diff: The Mark named here is widely identified with John Mark, who deserted Paul on his first journey and whom Paul now commends — the same Mark traditionally linked with the Gospel of Mark.

4.ctx: The letter closes with greetings to the neighbouring church at Laodicea, about ten miles away.
4.mean: Paul greets Nympha and the church in her house, and asks that this letter be read also at Laodicea, and that they read the letter from Laodicea. He tells Archippus to fulfil his ministry, and signs the greeting in his own hand: remember my chains. Grace be with you.
4.big: Paul's letters were meant to be shared and read aloud across the churches.
4.diff: The 'letter from Laodicea' has not survived. Some scholars suggest it may be our Ephesians, if that was a circular letter.

1.ctx: James, the brother of Jesus and leader of the Jerusalem church (Acts 15, Galatians 1:19), writes to Jewish Christians scattered outside Judea. Many scholars date it early, perhaps in the 40s, making it among the first New Testament writings.
1.mean: James introduces himself simply as a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, and greets the twelve tribes in the dispersion.
1.big: The brother of Jesus calls himself only his servant.
1.diff: Some scholars think a later writer used James's name. The traditional view that James the Lord's brother wrote it remains widely held and is supported by the letter's early, Jewish character.

1.ctx: The letter reads more like a collection of practical wisdom than a structured argument, often compared to Proverbs and the Sermon on the Mount.
1.mean: James says to count it all joy when meeting trials, because testing produces steadfastness, which makes believers mature and complete. Anyone lacking wisdom should ask God, who gives generously, but must ask in faith without doubting. The lowly should boast in their exaltation and the rich in their humiliation, since wealth fades like a flower. Blessed is the one who remains steadfast under trial.
1.big: Trials, rightly received, are God's means of growing mature faith.

1.ctx: Having spoken about testing, James clarifies where temptation to sin comes from.
1.mean: James says no one should say they are tempted by God, for God cannot be tempted with evil and tempts no one. Each person is tempted when lured by their own desire, which gives birth to sin, and sin to death. Every good and perfect gift comes from the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation. He brought us forth by the word of truth.
1.big: Sin comes from our own desires; only good comes from God.

1.ctx: The theme of hearing and doing, central to the whole letter.
1.mean: James says to be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger. Receive the implanted word with meekness. Be doers of the word, not hearers only, deceiving yourselves — like someone who looks in a mirror and forgets what he saw. Religion that is pure is to visit orphans and widows in their affliction and keep oneself unstained from the world.
1.big: Hearing God's word without doing it is self-deception.

2.ctx: Early Christian gatherings met in homes or synagogue-style assemblies, where seating reflected status.
2.mean: James condemns favouritism: giving the rich man a good seat and telling the poor man to stand. God has chosen the poor to be rich in faith, while the rich often oppress believers. Fulfilling the royal law — love your neighbour as yourself — is doing well, but showing partiality is sin, and breaking one point of the law makes someone accountable for all of it. Mercy triumphs over judgement.
2.big: Favouring the rich contradicts the faith of a Lord who chose the poor.

2.ctx: One of the most discussed passages in the New Testament, because it can seem to contradict Paul.
2.mean: James says faith without works is dead. If a brother is without clothes or food and someone says 'go in peace, be warmed and filled' but gives nothing, what good is that? Even demons believe that God is one, and shudder. Abraham was justified by works when he offered Isaac, and faith was completed by works. A person is justified by works and not by faith alone.
2.big: Real faith is never alone; it always shows itself in action.
2.diff: James and Paul both quote Genesis 15:6, and Martin Luther once called James 'an epistle of straw' because of this passage. The historic Protestant and Reformed understanding is that they answer different questions: Paul asks how a sinner is declared righteous before God (by faith alone, apart from works), while James asks what genuine faith looks like (it is never alone, but produces works). James uses 'justified' in the sense of shown to be righteous. Luther himself did not remove James from his Bible.

3.ctx: Teachers were honoured in Jewish communities, and many wanted the role.
3.mean: James says not many should become teachers, since teachers will be judged more strictly. We all stumble, especially with our words. The tongue is small like a ship's rudder or a spark, but can set a forest on fire. No human can tame it. With it we bless God and curse people made in his likeness — this ought not to be.
3.big: The tongue reveals and shapes the whole person, and cannot be controlled without God's help.

3.ctx: A contrast between two kinds of wisdom, in the tradition of Proverbs.
3.mean: James says the wise should show it by good conduct in the meekness of wisdom. Jealousy and selfish ambition are earthly, unspiritual, even demonic, and produce disorder. The wisdom from above is pure, peaceable, gentle, open to reason, full of mercy and good fruits, impartial and sincere. A harvest of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace.
3.big: True wisdom is shown in gentle, peace-making character rather than cleverness or ambition.

4.ctx: James addresses quarrelling within the Christian communities.
4.mean: James says fights come from passions at war within them. They desire and do not have, so they fight. They do not have because they do not ask, or they ask wrongly to spend it on their pleasures. Friendship with the world is enmity with God. But God gives more grace: God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.
4.big: Conflict among believers springs from selfish desire, and the remedy is humble dependence on God's grace.

4.ctx: Following the warning that God opposes the proud (4:6, quoting Proverbs 3:34), James gives ten short commands in a row — the most concentrated call to repentance in the letter.
4.mean: James says submit to God, resist the devil and he will flee. Draw near to God and he will draw near. Cleanse your hands and purify your hearts. Humble yourselves before the Lord, and he will exalt you. Do not speak evil against one another, for only God is Judge.
4.big: Humble submission to God is the way to draw near to him.

4.ctx: Merchants travelling between cities were common in the Roman world.
4.mean: James rebukes those who plan business ventures confidently: you do not know what tomorrow brings; you are a mist that appears for a little while and vanishes. Instead say, 'If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that.' Boasting in arrogance is evil. Knowing the right thing to do and failing to do it is sin.
4.big: All plans should be made in humble dependence on God's will, since life is brief.

5.ctx: Sharp prophetic words, like those of Amos, aimed at wealthy landowners.
5.mean: James says the rich should weep for the miseries coming on them. Their riches have rotted; they have hoarded wealth in the last days. The wages withheld from labourers cry out, and the cries have reached the Lord of hosts. They have lived in luxury and condemned the righteous.
5.big: God hears the cry of exploited workers and will judge those who oppress them.

5.ctx: Addressed to believers suffering, perhaps from the oppression just described.
5.mean: James urges patience until the coming of the Lord, like a farmer waiting for rain. Do not grumble against one another. Take the prophets and Job as examples of patience; the Lord is compassionate and merciful. Do not swear oaths; let your yes be yes and your no be no.
5.big: Believers endure suffering patiently because the Lord is coming and is merciful.

5.ctx: The letter closes with instructions on prayer in every circumstance.
5.mean: James says anyone suffering should pray, anyone cheerful sing praise. Anyone sick should call the elders to pray and anoint him with oil in the Lord's name, and the prayer of faith will save the sick, and any sins will be forgiven. Confess sins to one another and pray for one another. The prayer of a righteous person has great power, as Elijah's did.
5.big: Prayer is the believer's response to every situation, and God hears it.
5.diff: Christians read verses 14–16 differently: as a promise of healing now, as including final resurrection, or as a general principle rather than a guarantee. Anointing with oil has been understood as medicinal, symbolic, or sacramental. Scripture never treats a lack of healing as proof of weak faith.

5.ctx: The letter ends abruptly, without greetings, on the theme of restoring someone who has strayed.
5.mean: James says that if anyone wanders from the truth and someone brings him back, whoever does so will save his soul from death and cover a multitude of sins.
5.big: Bringing back a brother who has wandered is among the most important things a believer can do.

1.ctx: Written by John the apostle according to early tradition, probably late in the first century from Ephesus, to churches shaken by teachers who had left them and denied that Jesus came in the flesh.
1.mean: John says he writes about what was from the beginning, which he has heard, seen with his eyes, looked upon and touched with his hands — the word of life. That life was made manifest, and he proclaims it so that his readers may have fellowship with the apostles, and their fellowship is with the Father and the Son.
1.big: The eternal life of God became a real, touchable human being, and that is the foundation of fellowship.
1.diff: The letter does not name its author, but its language closely matches John's Gospel, and early tradition ascribes it to John the apostle. The strong emphasis on touching and seeing answers teachers who denied Christ's real humanity — the church's teaching of his two natures (see Mark 4:35).

1.ctx: The first main theme: God is light, and fellowship with him cannot coexist with walking in darkness.
1.mean: John says God is light and in him is no darkness at all. If we claim fellowship with him while walking in darkness, we lie. But if we walk in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus cleanses us from all sin. If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us and cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
1.big: Honest confession, not claims of sinlessness, is the mark of walking in God's light.

2.ctx: John balances the call to holiness with provision for failure.
2.mean: John writes so that they may not sin; but if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous. He is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only but also for the sins of the whole world. We know we have come to know him if we keep his commandments.
2.big: When believers sin, Jesus stands as their advocate and the sacrifice that turned God's wrath away.
2.diff: 'Propitiation' means a sacrifice that turns away God's wrath; some translations use 'atoning sacrifice' or 'expiation'. How 'the whole world' relates to the extent of the atonement is debated: Reformed theology generally reads it as Christ's sacrifice being sufficient for all and applied to believers from every nation; others read it as an atonement made for every person. Both sides preach Christ freely to all.

2.ctx: John's second test of genuine faith, alongside obedience: love for fellow believers.
2.mean: John says he writes no new commandment but an old one, yet it is new because the darkness is passing and the true light is already shining. Whoever says he is in the light but hates his brother is still in darkness. He then addresses children, fathers and young men, assuring them their sins are forgiven and they have overcome the evil one.
2.big: Love for fellow believers is evidence that someone truly walks in the light.

2.ctx: 'The world' in John often means human society organised in opposition to God, not creation or people as such.
2.mean: John says not to love the world or the things in it. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him. All that is in the world — the desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes and the pride of life — is not from the Father. The world is passing away, but whoever does the will of God abides for ever.
2.big: The world's desires are passing away, so love for God must come before them.

2.ctx: The false teachers had left the churches; John calls them antichrists.
2.mean: John says it is the last hour, and many antichrists have come. They went out from us, but they were not of us; if they had been, they would have continued with us. Who is the liar but he who denies that Jesus is the Christ? No one who denies the Son has the Father.
2.big: Denying the Son means denying the Father, whatever religious claims are made.
2.diff: Verse 19 is often cited in Reformed discussion of perseverance: those who finally leave the faith show they never truly belonged. Others emphasise the passage's pastoral purpose of reassuring those who stayed. The singular 'antichrist' has been interpreted as a future individual, and 'antichrists' as present false teachers; John applies the term chiefly to those denying Christ in his own day.

2.ctx: Continuing the warning, John turns to what keeps believers secure against false teaching.
2.mean: John says to let what they heard from the beginning abide in them. The anointing they received from him abides in them and teaches them, so they have no need for anyone to teach them otherwise. Abide in him, so that when he appears they may have confidence and not shrink from him in shame.
2.big: The Spirit and the original apostolic message keep believers secure against error.
2.diff: The 'anointing' is widely understood as the Holy Spirit. 'No need for anyone to teach you' does not reject teachers — John is teaching them — but means they need no new revelation beyond the apostolic gospel.

3.ctx: John turns from warning to assurance about believers' identity.
3.mean: John says see what kind of love the Father has given us, that we should be called children of God — and so we are. What we will be has not yet appeared, but when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is. Everyone who hopes in him purifies himself. No one who abides in him keeps on sinning; whoever practises righteousness is righteous.
3.big: Believers are God's children now, and the hope of seeing Christ makes them pursue purity.
3.diff: Verses 6 and 9 ('no one born of God makes a practice of sinning') have troubled readers, since 1:8 says believers do sin. Most interpreters read them as describing settled, habitual sin as a way of life, not every failure.

3.ctx: John returns to the command Jesus gave on the night before he died (John 13:34). Cain, the first murderer (Genesis 4), serves as the picture of hatred among brothers.
3.mean: John says not to be like Cain, who murdered his brother. Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer. We know love by this: Christ laid down his life for us, so we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers. If anyone has the world's goods and sees a brother in need but closes his heart, how does God's love abide in him? Let us love in deed and in truth, not only in word. Whenever our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart.
3.big: Love is defined by Christ's self-giving and proved by practical help to those in need.

4.ctx: The false teachers claimed spiritual authority, so John gives a test.
4.mean: John says do not believe every spirit, but test them. Every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God; every spirit that does not is the spirit of antichrist. He who is in you is greater than he who is in the world.
4.big: Teaching must be tested by what it says about Jesus Christ coming in the flesh.
4.diff: The test targets teachers who denied Christ's real humanity. Christians have long applied it more widely: any teaching must be measured against the apostolic confession of who Jesus is, fully God and fully man (see Mark 4:35).

4.ctx: The high point of the letter's teaching on love. The false teachers apparently claimed superior spiritual knowledge while treating other believers with contempt.
4.mean: John says love is from God, and whoever loves has been born of God. God is love. God showed his love by sending his only Son so that we might live through him. In this is love: not that we loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins. No one has ever seen God, but if we love one another, God abides in us. Perfect love casts out fear. We love because he first loved us. Whoever loves God must also love his brother.
4.big: God's love, shown in sending his Son, is the source and pattern of all true love.

5.ctx: John draws the threads of faith, love and obedience together.
5.mean: John says everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God, and everyone who loves the Father loves his children. His commandments are not burdensome, because everyone born of God overcomes the world, and the victory is our faith. Jesus came by water and blood, not by the water only.
5.big: Faith in Jesus as the Son of God is the victory that overcomes the world.
5.diff: 'Water and blood' has been read as Jesus' baptism and death, as the water and blood from his side, or as the sacraments. The first is most common: against teachers who said the divine Christ left Jesus before the cross, John insists the Son came through both baptism and death.

5.ctx: Jewish law required two or three witnesses to establish a matter (Deuteronomy 19:15). John has just named three — the Spirit, the water and the blood — and now appeals to God's own witness.
5.mean: John says if we receive human testimony, the testimony of God is greater, and this is the testimony: God gave us eternal life, and this life is in his Son. Whoever has the Son has life; whoever does not have the Son of God does not have life.
5.big: Eternal life is found in the Son and nowhere else.
5.diff: Older English Bibles include words in verses 7–8 about three witnesses in heaven. They appear in no Greek manuscript before the late Middle Ages and are omitted by modern translations. The Trinity is taught throughout Scripture without them.

5.ctx: John states the purpose of the whole letter, echoing the purpose statement of his Gospel (John 20:31), which was written so that readers might believe; this letter, so that believers might know.
5.mean: John says he writes so that those who believe in the name of the Son of God may know that they have eternal life. We have confidence that if we ask anything according to his will he hears us. He urges prayer for a brother committing sin not leading to death, but speaks of sin that leads to death.
5.big: The letter is written so that believers may know, not merely hope, that they have eternal life.
5.diff: 'Sin that leads to death' is unexplained in the text. Suggestions include the apostasy of the false teachers, a sin bringing physical death as judgement, or deliberate persistent rejection of Christ. The pastoral point is to keep praying for fellow believers.

5.ctx: The letter closes with three confident statements, each beginning 'we know'.
5.mean: John says we know that everyone born of God does not keep on sinning, and the evil one does not touch him. We know that we are from God, and the whole world lies in the power of the evil one. We know that the Son of God has come and given us understanding, so that we may know him who is true; and we are in him who is true, in his Son Jesus Christ. He is the true God and eternal life. Little children, keep yourselves from idols.
5.big: Believers can know the true God through his Son, who is himself the true God and eternal life.
5.diff: Whether 'He is the true God' in verse 20 refers to the Father or to Jesus Christ is debated grammatically. Many interpreters, historically and today, take it as referring to Jesus Christ, the nearest antecedent, making it a direct statement of his deity.

1.ctx: John's Gospel is traditionally attributed to John the apostle, 'the disciple whom Jesus loved', writing late in the first century, probably from Ephesus. It opens not in Bethlehem but before creation, echoing the first words of Genesis.
1.mean: John says that in the beginning was the Word, the Word was with God, and the Word was God. All things were made through him; in him was life, and the life was the light of men. The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it. 'Word' (logos) meant God's creative speech to Jewish readers and the ordering reason of the universe to Greek ones.
1.big: The one John will write about existed before creation, is distinct from God the Father, and is himself God.
1.diff: Jehovah's Witnesses translate verse 1 'the Word was a god', arguing from the absence of the Greek article. The grammatical work is published and checkable. Philip Harner, in the Journal of Biblical Literature 92 (1973), concluded that a predicate noun in this position is primarily qualitative — stating what the Word is by nature — and Daniel Wallace's Greek Grammar Beyond the Basics agrees. Honesty requires noting that some writers use Harner's 'qualitative' finding to argue for 'a god' instead. The decisive point is easier to check: the New World Translation renders the same grammatical construction as 'God' elsewhere in this very chapter, at verses 6, 12, 13 and 18, and only at verse 1 as 'a god'. See also Bruce Metzger in Theology Today 10 (1953) and Murray Harris, Jesus as God (1992). Authorship is also discussed; some scholars think a disciple other than the son of Zebedee is 'the beloved disciple', though the traditional view remains widely held.

1.ctx: John the Baptist appears within the prologue itself, carefully distinguished from the Word.
1.mean: John says a man was sent from God named John, who came as a witness to the light, but was not the light. The true light, which gives light to everyone, was coming into the world. He came to his own, and his own did not receive him. But to all who received him, who believed in his name, he gave the right to become children of God — born not of blood or human will, but of God.
1.big: Becoming a child of God comes by receiving Christ, and is God's doing rather than human descent or decision.
1.diff: Reformed interpreters see in verse 13 a statement that the new birth is God's sovereign work; others stress verse 12's emphasis on receiving and believing. John holds the two together.

1.ctx: The climax of the prologue. 'Dwelt' literally means 'pitched his tent', recalling the tabernacle where God's glory lived among Israel.
1.mean: John says the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory, the glory of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth. The law came through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. No one has ever seen God; the only God, who is at the Father's side, has made him known.
1.big: The eternal Word did not merely appear human; he became fully human, and in him God is made known.
1.diff: This verse is the foundation of the church's teaching on the incarnation and the two natures of Christ (see Mark 4:35). In verse 18 the best manuscripts read 'the only God' or 'the only-begotten God'; others read 'the only Son'. Most modern scholars prefer 'God', which makes the verse another direct statement of Christ's deity.

1.ctx: Priests and Levites are sent from Jerusalem to investigate John, whose baptising had drawn crowds.
1.mean: John the Baptist denies being the Christ, Elijah or the Prophet. He is the voice crying in the wilderness from Isaiah 40:3, and says one is coming after him whose sandal strap he is not worthy to untie.
1.big: The greatest prophet of his time defines himself entirely by the one coming after him.
1.h: The Mission of John the Baptist

1.ctx: The next day, at Bethany beyond the Jordan. Passover lambs were sacrificed each year in Jerusalem, and Isaiah 53:7 pictures God's servant led like a lamb to the slaughter.
1.mean: John sees Jesus and says: behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world. He testifies that he saw the Spirit descend and remain on him, and that this is the Son of God. The 'lamb' evokes the Passover lamb and the servant led like a lamb to slaughter in Isaiah 53.
1.big: From the start, Jesus is identified as the sacrifice who will take away sin.

1.ctx: Two of John's disciples, one of them Andrew, leave John to follow Jesus.
1.mean: John says Jesus asked them what they were seeking, and they asked where he was staying. 'Come and you will see.' Andrew then finds his brother Simon and tells him they have found the Messiah; Jesus renames Simon 'Cephas', Peter, meaning rock.
1.big: The first disciples come by invitation and immediately bring others.

1.ctx: Jesus moves north to Galilee. Philip and Nathanael came from Bethsaida and Cana. Sitting under a fig tree was a common image of study and reflection on Scripture.
1.mean: Jesus calls Philip, who finds Nathanael. Nathanael doubts anything good can come from Nazareth, but when Jesus shows he knew him under the fig tree, he confesses Jesus as Son of God and King of Israel. Jesus promises he will see heaven opened and angels ascending and descending on the Son of Man — echoing Jacob's ladder in Genesis 28.
1.big: Jesus is the meeting point between heaven and earth that Jacob's ladder foreshadowed.

2.ctx: Cana, a village in Galilee. A wedding feast could last a week, and running out of wine would shame the family.
2.mean: John says Jesus turned about 120 gallons of water, in stone jars used for Jewish purification, into the best wine. John calls it the first of his 'signs', which revealed his glory, and his disciples believed.
2.big: Jesus' first sign shows the abundance he brings, replacing ritual washing with the new wine of the kingdom.
2.diff: Jesus addressing his mother as 'woman' was not rude in its setting, but it does mark distance. Traditions differ over what Mary's role in this scene implies; the text's focus is Jesus' own 'hour', which is his death and glorification.

2.ctx: Jerusalem at Passover. Traders sold animals for sacrifice and exchanged currency in the temple courts.
2.mean: Jesus drives out the traders with a whip of cords. Asked for a sign, he says: destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it. John explains he was speaking of the temple of his body, which the disciples understood after the resurrection.
2.big: Jesus' body replaces the temple as the place where God meets his people.
2.diff: The Synoptic Gospels place a temple cleansing in Jesus' final week. Some hold there were two cleansings; others think John placed it early for theological reasons.

3.ctx: Nicodemus was a Pharisee and member of the Sanhedrin who came at night, perhaps for privacy, perhaps symbolising his spiritual darkness.
3.mean: Jesus tells Nicodemus that unless someone is born again — or 'from above', the Greek means both — he cannot see the kingdom of God. One must be born of water and the Spirit; the Spirit blows like the wind, where it wills. As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, the Son of Man must be lifted up. For God so loved the world that he gave his only Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life.
3.big: No one enters God's kingdom without a new birth from above, which comes through faith in the lifted-up Son.
3.diff: 'Water and the Spirit' has been read as baptism and the Spirit, as natural birth and spiritual birth, or — as many Reformed interpreters hold — as the cleansing and renewal promised in Ezekiel 36:25–27. Scholars also differ over whether Jesus' words end at verse 15 or verse 21. Reformed theology stresses the Spirit's sovereign work in the new birth (verse 8).

3.ctx: Jesus' disciples are baptising in Judea while John continues nearby. John's followers see the crowds moving to Jesus and feel their own leader is being overshadowed.
3.mean: John the Baptist's disciples complain that everyone is going to Jesus. John answers that he is only the friend of the bridegroom, and his joy is complete: he must increase, but I must decrease. The one who comes from above is above all, and whoever believes in the Son has eternal life.
3.big: The faithful messenger rejoices to be eclipsed by the one he points to.

4.ctx: Jews and Samaritans were bitterly divided, and Jewish men did not normally speak with women in public. Jesus sits at Jacob's well at noon.
4.mean: John says Jesus, wearied from the journey, sat by the well and asked a Samaritan woman for a drink. He offered her living water welling up to eternal life, revealed he knew her history of five husbands, and told her that true worshippers will worship the Father in spirit and truth. When she spoke of the coming Messiah, he said: I who speak to you am he. His tiredness and thirst are real human needs, set beside knowledge no ordinary man could have (see Mark 4:35 on the two natures).
4.big: Jesus crosses every barrier to offer eternal life to an outsider, and reveals himself as Messiah to her.

4.ctx: The disciples return with food and are surprised to find him talking with a woman.
4.mean: The woman leaves her water jar and tells the town: come, see a man who told me everything I ever did. Jesus tells his disciples his food is to do the will of the one who sent him, and that the fields are already white for harvest.
4.big: Jesus sees a harvest where his disciples see only Samaritans.

4.ctx: Jesus stays two days in the Samaritan town of Sychar — remarkable, since most Jews travelling between Judea and Galilee would not even pass through Samaria.
4.mean: Many Samaritans believe because of the woman's testimony, and many more because of his own word. They say: we know that this is indeed the Saviour of the world.
4.big: Outsiders are the first in John's Gospel to call Jesus Saviour of the world.

4.ctx: Back in Cana. The official was probably in Herod Antipas's service at Capernaum, about twenty miles away.
4.mean: An official begs Jesus to heal his dying son. Jesus says 'Go; your son will live.' The man believed the word and went; his son recovered at the very hour. John calls it the second sign.
4.big: Jesus' word alone has power over sickness at a distance, and faith takes him at his word.

5.ctx: The pool of Bethesda in Jerusalem, with five colonnades; its remains have been excavated near St Anne's Church.
5.mean: Jesus heals a man who had been ill for thirty-eight years, telling him to take up his mat and walk. Because it was the Sabbath, the religious leaders object to him carrying the mat.
5.big: Jesus restores what decades of waiting could not.
5.diff: Verse 4, about an angel stirring the water, is absent from the earliest manuscripts and omitted by most modern translations.

5.ctx: The Sabbath healing leads to one of the clearest statements in the Gospels of Jesus' relationship to the Father.
5.mean: Jesus says his Father is working until now, and he is working. John says the leaders sought to kill him because he was making himself equal with God. Jesus says the Son does whatever the Father does; the Father has given all judgement to the Son, so that all may honour the Son as they honour the Father. The hour is coming when the dead will hear his voice and live.
5.big: Jesus claims to share the Father's work, authority and honour.

5.ctx: Jewish law required more than one witness to establish testimony.
5.mean: Jesus lists witnesses to himself: John the Baptist, the works the Father gave him to do, and the Father himself.
5.big: Jesus' identity is confirmed by a chain of witnesses, above all the Father.

5.ctx: Jesus addresses religious leaders who studied the Scriptures with great devotion, and who believed Moses would be their advocate before God.
5.mean: Jesus says they search the Scriptures because they think that in them they have eternal life, but those Scriptures bear witness about him, and they refuse to come to him. If they believed Moses, they would believe him, for Moses wrote of him.
5.big: Scripture's purpose is to lead people to Christ, and studying it without coming to him misses the point.

6.ctx: Near Passover, on the far side of the Sea of Galilee. The only miracle besides the resurrection recorded in all four Gospels.
6.mean: Jesus feeds five thousand men from five barley loaves and two fish, with twelve baskets left over. The people say he is the Prophet who is to come and want to make him king by force, so he withdraws to the mountain alone.
6.big: Jesus provides for his people in the wilderness, but refuses the political kingship the crowd wants.
6.h: The Feeding of the Five Thousand

6.ctx: That evening, after the crowd tried to make him king, the disciples row across the lake. The Sea of Galilee is prone to sudden strong winds.
6.mean: They see Jesus walking on the sea and are frightened. He says 'It is I; do not be afraid' — literally 'I am'. Then they were willing to take him into the boat, and immediately the boat reached the land.
6.big: Jesus does what only God does in the Old Testament, and speaks with the divine name.

6.ctx: The next day at Capernaum, a long discourse in the synagogue, following the feeding.
6.mean: Jesus says they seek him because they ate their fill. The work of God is to believe in the one he sent. He is the bread of life; whoever comes to him will not hunger. All that the Father gives him will come to him, and he will never cast out whoever comes. No one can come unless the Father draws him. Unless they eat his flesh and drink his blood, they have no life; whoever does so has eternal life, and he will raise him up on the last day.
6.big: Jesus is the true bread from heaven, and life comes only from receiving him.
6.diff: Verses 37–44 are central to debates about election: Reformed theology holds that the Father's drawing effectively brings those he has given to the Son; other traditions understand the drawing as an influence that can be resisted. Verses 53–58 have been read as referring to the Lord's Supper, or as vivid language for believing in Christ's death; many Protestant interpreters take the second, noting the Supper had not yet been instituted.

6.ctx: The reaction in the synagogue at Capernaum to the bread of life discourse. The language of eating flesh and drinking blood deeply offended Jewish hearers, since the law forbade consuming blood.
6.mean: Many disciples say this is a hard saying, who can listen to it? Jesus says the Spirit gives life, the flesh is of no help, and no one can come to him unless granted by the Father. After this many of his disciples turned back.
6.big: Jesus' teaching divides even his followers, and he does not soften it to keep them.

6.ctx: After many disciples leave, Jesus turns to the Twelve. This is John's equivalent of Peter's confession at Caesarea Philippi in the other Gospels.
6.mean: Jesus asks if they want to go away too. Peter answers: Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life, and we have believed and know that you are the Holy One of God. Jesus says one of them is a devil, meaning Judas.
6.big: Faith sometimes stays not because everything is clear, but because there is nowhere else to go.

7.ctx: The Feast of Tabernacles in autumn, remembering Israel's wilderness years with temporary shelters, water rituals and great lamps.
7.mean: Jesus' brothers, who did not believe in him, urge him to show himself publicly. He goes up privately, then teaches in the temple mid-feast. The crowd is divided. He says his teaching is not his own but from the one who sent him.
7.big: Even Jesus' own family did not yet believe, and his teaching divides the crowds.
7.diff: Jesus' brothers are understood as later children of Mary in most Protestant traditions, and as cousins or Joseph's children by another marriage in Catholic and Orthodox traditions.

7.ctx: Jerusalem residents debate whether the authorities have recognised him.
7.mean: Some ask whether this could be the Christ, but say they know where he comes from. Jesus says they do not know the one who sent him. Officers are sent to arrest him, but no one lays a hand on him, because his hour had not yet come.
7.big: Jesus' life runs on God's timetable, not his enemies'.

7.ctx: The last day of the feast, when water was poured out at the altar in a ceremony recalling the water from the rock.
7.mean: Jesus stands and cries out: if anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink; whoever believes in me, out of his heart will flow rivers of living water. John explains that he meant the Spirit, not yet given because Jesus was not yet glorified.
7.big: Jesus is the true source of the life the water ceremony only pictured, given through the Spirit.

7.ctx: On the last day of the Feast of Tabernacles, the crowd divides over Jesus' identity. Micah 5:2 said the Messiah would come from Bethlehem, and most thought Jesus was simply from Galilee.
7.mean: Some say he is the Prophet, others the Christ; others object that the Christ comes from Bethlehem, not Galilee. John, whose readers knew Jesus was born in Bethlehem, lets the irony stand.
7.big: The crowd's objections rest on what they do not know about Jesus.

7.ctx: The temple officers sent in 7:32 return without Jesus. Nicodemus, who first came by night in chapter 3, now speaks cautiously on Jesus' behalf in the council.
7.mean: The officers say no one ever spoke like this man. The Pharisees scorn them and the crowd. Nicodemus asks whether the law judges a man without hearing him, and is mocked.
7.big: Those sent to arrest Jesus are arrested by his words instead.
7.h: The Unbelief of the Jewish Leaders

8.ctx: This passage (7:53–8:11) is set apart in most modern Bibles.
8.mean: Scribes and Pharisees bring a woman caught in adultery to test Jesus. He writes on the ground and says: let him who is without sin among you be the first to throw a stone. They leave one by one. Jesus says: neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more.
8.big: Jesus refuses both condemnation and approval: he forgives and calls to a new life.
8.diff: The passage is absent from the earliest and best manuscripts of John, appears in different places in others, and differs in style. Many scholars think it records a genuine incident preserved separately before being placed here. No doctrine depends on it.

8.ctx: At the Feast of Tabernacles, great lamps were lit in the temple court.
8.mean: Jesus says: I am the light of the world; whoever follows me will not walk in darkness. The Pharisees say his testimony is invalid; he answers that the Father also bears witness. He says that unless they believe that 'I am', they will die in their sins.
8.big: Jesus claims to be the light the festival lamps only symbolised.
8.h: Jesus the Light of the World

8.ctx: Many believe in him, and Jesus addresses these new believers.
8.mean: Jesus says if they abide in his word they are truly his disciples, and they will know the truth, and the truth will set them free. They protest they are Abraham's offspring and have never been slaves. Jesus says everyone who practises sin is a slave to sin; if the Son sets them free, they will be free indeed.
8.big: True freedom comes from the Son, not from descent or religious heritage.
8.h: The Truth Will Set You Free

8.ctx: The argument with those who had believed (8:31) turns hostile. Calling Jesus a Samaritan and demon-possessed were serious insults.
8.mean: Jesus says that if anyone keeps his word, he will never see death, and that Abraham rejoiced to see his day. When they object that he is not yet fifty, he says: truly, before Abraham was, I am. They pick up stones to throw at him. 'I am' echoes God's name in Exodus 3:14 and the 'I am he' of Isaiah.
8.big: Jesus claims to have existed before Abraham, using the divine name, and his hearers understand the claim.
8.diff: Some translations, including the New World Translation, render verse 58 'I have been'. Most scholars hold that 'I am' is the correct and intended translation, and the listeners' attempt to stone him for blasphemy shows how they understood it.
8.h: Before Abraham Was Born, I Am

9.ctx: A man blind from birth, in Jerusalem, on a Sabbath. Many at the time believed disability was a punishment for sin, either the person's own or their parents'.
9.mean: The disciples ask whose sin caused his blindness. Jesus says neither his nor his parents', but that the works of God might be displayed. He makes mud, puts it on the man's eyes and tells him to wash in the pool of Siloam, and he comes back seeing.
9.big: Suffering is not always the result of a specific sin; Jesus brings light into it.
9.h: Jesus Heals the Man Born Blind

9.ctx: The healed man is questioned by the Pharisees, his parents are questioned, and he is questioned again.
9.mean: The Pharisees are divided. His parents, afraid of being put out of the synagogue, refer them to him. He says: one thing I know, that though I was blind, now I see. He argues that if Jesus were not from God he could do nothing, and they cast him out.
9.big: The man's understanding grows as he is pressured, while the religious leaders' blindness deepens.

9.ctx: The healed man has just been cast out of the synagogue for defending Jesus — a serious social exclusion. Jesus seeks him out.
9.mean: Jesus asks if he believes in the Son of Man. He says 'Lord, I believe,' and worships him. Jesus says he came so that the blind may see and those who see may become blind; the Pharisees who claim to see remain guilty.
9.big: The healed man ends in worship; those who claim sight prove blind.

10.ctx: Continuing from chapter 9, against the background of Ezekiel 34, where God condemns Israel's false shepherds and promises to shepherd his flock himself.
10.mean: Jesus says he is the door of the sheep and the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep. The sheep hear his voice and he calls them by name. He has other sheep not of this fold, and there will be one flock and one shepherd. No one takes his life from him; he lays it down of his own accord and takes it up again.
10.big: Jesus is the promised shepherd, who gives his life freely for his sheep.
10.diff: 'Other sheep' is usually understood as Gentile believers. Reformed theology has often seen in 'I lay down my life for the sheep' support for Christ's death being particularly for his people; others read the image without that implication.

10.ctx: The Feast of Dedication (Hanukkah) in winter, remembering the rededication of the temple in 164 BC.
10.mean: Asked plainly if he is the Christ, Jesus says his works bear witness, but they do not believe because they are not his sheep. His sheep hear his voice, he gives them eternal life, and no one will snatch them out of his hand or the Father's. I and the Father are one. They pick up stones, saying he, being a man, makes himself God.
10.big: Jesus' sheep are held securely by both Son and Father, who are one.
10.diff: Verses 28–29 are a key text for the Reformed doctrine of the perseverance of the saints. 'I and the Father are one' is read by the historic church as unity of nature, not only of purpose — which is how his hearers understood it.
10.h: Jesus at the Feast of Dedication

10.ctx: Jesus withdraws across the Jordan to where John first baptised.
10.mean: Many come to him and say that John did no sign, but everything John said about this man was true. And many believed in him there.
10.big: The Baptist's witness is vindicated where it began.

11.ctx: Bethany, about two miles from Jerusalem, home of Lazarus, Martha and Mary, whom John says Jesus loved.
11.mean: When told Lazarus is ill, Jesus says the illness will not end in death but is for the glory of God, and then deliberately stays two more days. He tells the disciples Lazarus has died, and that he is glad for their sake, so that they may believe. Thomas says: let us also go, that we may die with him.
11.big: Jesus' delay is purposeful, aimed at revealing God's glory and strengthening faith.

11.ctx: Lazarus has been in the tomb four days; Jewish belief held the soul lingered three days, so hope was gone.
11.mean: Martha says if Jesus had been there her brother would not have died. Jesus says: I am the resurrection and the life; whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live. Martha confesses him as the Christ, the Son of God. When Jesus sees Mary and the mourners weeping, he is deeply moved and troubled, and Jesus wept.
11.big: Jesus is himself the resurrection, and he grieves genuinely with those who grieve.
11.diff: Jesus weeps knowing he is about to raise Lazarus — a clear instance of the full humanity held together with divine power that the church calls the two natures (see Mark 4:35).

11.ctx: At the tomb, a cave with a stone across its entrance, typical of wealthier Jewish burials. Lazarus has been dead four days, and decomposition would have begun.
11.mean: Jesus tells them to take away the stone, prays aloud to the Father for the crowd's sake, and cries: Lazarus, come out. The dead man comes out, bound in grave cloths. Jesus says: unbind him, and let him go.
11.big: Jesus' word has power over death itself — the greatest sign in John's Gospel.

11.ctx: The raising of Lazarus becomes the immediate trigger for the plot to kill Jesus.
11.mean: The Sanhedrin fears everyone will believe in him and the Romans will destroy the nation. Caiaphas, the high priest, says it is better that one man should die for the people. John comments that he prophesied, without realising it, that Jesus would die for the nation and to gather the scattered children of God.
11.big: Jesus' enemies unknowingly announce the purpose of his death: one dying for many.

12.ctx: Six days before Passover, at a dinner in Bethany given in Jesus' honour. Lazarus, recently raised, is at the table. Nard was imported from India and extremely costly.
12.mean: Mary anoints Jesus' feet with expensive nard and wipes them with her hair. Judas objects that it could have been sold for the poor — John notes he was a thief. Jesus says she kept it for the day of his burial.
12.big: Extravagant devotion is honoured by Jesus, whose burial is near.

12.ctx: Pilgrims arriving for Passover come to Bethany to see both Jesus and Lazarus, whose raising had become widely known.
12.mean: The chief priests plan to kill Lazarus as well, because on his account many were believing in Jesus.
12.big: The evidence of Jesus' power is so threatening that his enemies plan to destroy it.

12.ctx: The next day, crowds come out with palm branches, symbols of national victory.
12.mean: They cry 'Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, even the King of Israel.' Jesus sits on a young donkey, fulfilling Zechariah 9:9. The disciples understood this only after he was glorified.
12.big: Jesus enters Jerusalem as the humble king the prophets promised.

12.ctx: Some Greeks at the feast ask to see Jesus — a sign that the Gentiles are coming.
12.mean: Jesus says the hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified. Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit. His soul is troubled, but he will not ask to be saved from this hour. A voice from heaven says: I have glorified it, and will glorify it again. When he is lifted up, he will draw all people to himself.
12.big: Jesus' glory is found in his death, which will bear fruit among all peoples.
12.diff: 'Draw all people' is read by some as every individual and by Reformed interpreters as people of every kind and nation, Jew and Gentile — prompted in context by the Greeks' arrival.

12.ctx: John closes the account of Jesus' public ministry, which began at 1:19. From chapter 13, Jesus speaks privately to his disciples before his death.
12.mean: John says that though Jesus had done so many signs, they still did not believe, fulfilling Isaiah 53:1 and 6:10. Isaiah said these things because he saw his glory and spoke of him. Many of the authorities believed, but would not confess it for fear of the Pharisees, for they loved the glory that comes from man more than the glory that comes from God.
12.big: Unbelief in the face of clear signs is both human refusal and, as Isaiah foretold, divine hardening.
12.diff: Verse 41 says Isaiah saw Jesus' glory — referring to the vision of the LORD on his throne in Isaiah 6. Christians have long cited this as identifying Jesus with the LORD of Isaiah's vision.

13.ctx: The evening before Passover. Chapters 13–17 form the 'upper room discourse', Jesus' private teaching before his death.
13.mean: Knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, Jesus rises from supper, takes a towel, and washes the disciples' feet — the job of the lowest servant. Peter refuses, then asks to be washed all over. Jesus says: if I, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another's feet.
13.big: The one with all authority takes the lowest place, and calls his followers to do the same.
13.diff: Most churches read this as an example of humble service rather than an ordinance to repeat; some traditions practise foot washing literally.

13.ctx: Still at the supper. Reclining at table, the disciple Jesus loved was beside him. Giving someone a morsel of bread from the dish was a gesture of honour and friendship.
13.mean: Jesus quotes Psalm 41:9 — he who ate my bread has lifted his heel against me. Troubled in spirit, he says one of them will betray him, and gives the morsel to Judas. John says Satan entered him, and Judas went out, and it was night.
13.big: The betrayal happens within the circle of friendship, and Jesus knows it in advance.

13.ctx: Judas has gone out into the night. From here Jesus speaks only to the eleven, and the long farewell teaching of chapters 14–17 begins.
13.mean: Jesus says now is the Son of Man glorified. He gives a new commandment: love one another as I have loved you. By this all people will know that you are my disciples.
13.big: The mark of Jesus' disciples is love for one another, measured by his love for them.

13.ctx: Peter has just heard that Jesus is going where they cannot follow. He protests his loyalty, which Jesus answers by predicting his denial.
13.mean: Peter says he will lay down his life for Jesus. Jesus answers: will you? The rooster will not crow till you have denied me three times.
13.big: Jesus knows his followers' weakness better than they do.

14.ctx: Continuing the upper room discourse, spoken to troubled disciples.
14.mean: Jesus says: let not your hearts be troubled; believe in God, believe also in me. In my Father's house are many rooms. I go to prepare a place for you, and I will come again and take you to myself.
14.big: Jesus comforts his followers with the promise of a place with him and his return to bring them there.
14.h: In My Father's House Are Many Rooms

14.ctx: Thomas says they do not know where Jesus is going, so how can they know the way? Jesus answers with the sixth of his seven 'I am' sayings in John.
14.mean: Jesus says: I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me. If you had known me, you would have known my Father. Whoever has seen me has seen the Father. Whoever believes in me will do the works I do, and greater works than these.
14.big: Jesus is the only way to the Father, because in him the Father is seen.
14.diff: 'Greater works' is usually understood as the wider reach of the gospel through the church after Pentecost, rather than more spectacular miracles.
14.h: The Way, the Truth, and the Life

14.ctx: The first of several promises of the Spirit in these chapters.
