14.mean: Jesus says he will ask the Father, and he will give another Helper to be with them for ever, the Spirit of truth. He will not leave them as orphans. The Helper, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in his name, will teach them all things and bring to remembrance all that he said.
14.big: Jesus promises the Spirit as another Helper like himself, who will live in his people and teach them.
14.diff: 'Another Helper' implies one like Jesus himself — a personal being, not an impersonal force — which is significant in discussions with Jehovah's Witnesses. The Greek word, parakletos, means one called alongside to help, advise or advocate.

14.ctx: The discourse moves toward its close. 'Peace' (shalom) was the ordinary Jewish greeting and farewell, but it also meant the wholeness God promised.
14.mean: Jesus says: peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you; not as the world gives. He says the Father is greater than he, and that the ruler of this world is coming but has no claim on him.
14.big: Jesus gives a peace the world cannot give, grounded in his victory.
14.diff: 'The Father is greater than I' is cited by some to deny Christ's deity. The historic understanding is that Jesus speaks of his role and position as the incarnate Son, sent and obedient, not of a lesser nature — consistent with 10:30 and 20:28.

15.ctx: Israel was often pictured as God's vine or vineyard (Psalm 80, Isaiah 5).
15.mean: Jesus says he is the true vine and his Father the vinedresser. Every branch that does not bear fruit is taken away; every fruitful branch is pruned. Abide in me, and I in you; apart from me you can do nothing. If anyone does not abide, he is thrown away like a branch and withers.
15.big: Fruitfulness comes only from remaining connected to Jesus.
15.diff: Verses 2 and 6 are debated in relation to whether true believers can finally fall away. Reformed interpreters generally read them as describing those who were outwardly attached but never truly united to Christ; others see a real possibility of apostasy.

15.ctx: Continuing the vine discourse. In the ancient world, a friend of a king was a close adviser, trusted with his plans — more than a servant.
15.mean: Jesus says as the Father loved him, so he has loved them; abide in my love. Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends. They are his friends if they do what he commands. They did not choose him; he chose them and appointed them to bear lasting fruit.
15.big: Jesus' love, shown in laying down his life, makes his disciples his friends.
15.diff: 'You did not choose me, but I chose you' refers directly to the apostles' calling; Reformed theology also sees in it a principle of God's gracious initiative in salvation.

15.ctx: Jesus prepares the disciples for hostility. When John wrote, Christians were already being expelled from synagogues and facing persecution from Roman authorities.
15.mean: Jesus says if the world hates them, it hated him first. A servant is not greater than his master. When the Helper comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness about me.
15.big: Opposition is to be expected, and the Spirit will bear witness to Christ through his people.
15.diff: Verse 26 is central to the 'filioque' debate. Eastern Orthodox churches hold that the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone, citing this verse. Western churches, including Reformed churches and this group, hold that he proceeds from the Father and the Son, noting that here the Son sends the Spirit. Both agree the Spirit is fully God.

16.ctx: Jesus warns the disciples plainly about persecution. Saul of Tarsus, before his conversion, is an example of someone who thought killing Christians was serving God.
16.mean: Jesus says they will be put out of the synagogues, and whoever kills them will think he is offering service to God. He tells them now so that they will remember when it happens.
16.big: Jesus forewarns his followers so that persecution will not shake their faith.

16.ctx: The fullest teaching in the Gospels about the Holy Spirit's work. The disciples are grieved that Jesus is leaving; he tells them his going will bring the Spirit.
16.mean: Jesus says it is to their advantage that he goes away, for otherwise the Helper will not come. The Spirit will convict the world concerning sin, righteousness and judgement. He will guide them into all the truth; he will not speak on his own authority but will glorify Jesus, taking what is his and declaring it.
16.big: The Spirit's work is to convict the world and to glorify Christ by making him known.
16.diff: Verses 13–15 are often cited in describing the Spirit's role: he points to Christ rather than drawing attention to himself. This is part of why Christian prayer is usually directed to the Father through the Son in the Spirit.
16.h: The Promise of the Holy Spirit

16.ctx: The disciples are confused by 'a little while', referring to his death and resurrection. They are about to experience exactly what he describes: grief, then joy.
16.mean: Jesus says they will weep and lament while the world rejoices, but their sorrow will turn into joy, like a woman in labour whose anguish gives way to joy. No one will take their joy from them.
16.big: The grief of Jesus' death will turn into a joy that cannot be taken away.

16.ctx: The discourse draws to its close. After the resurrection, the disciples' relationship with the Father would change; they would pray to him in Jesus' name.
16.mean: Jesus says whatever they ask the Father in his name, he will give them. The Father himself loves them. In the world they will have tribulation, but take heart: I have overcome the world.
16.big: Believers may pray confidently to a Father who loves them, and face trouble knowing Christ has already won.
16.diff: 'In my name' means according to Christ's character and purposes, not a formula that guarantees any request.

17.ctx: Often called Jesus' 'high priestly prayer', prayed aloud before the disciples.
17.mean: Jesus prays: Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son that the Son may glorify you. Eternal life is this: that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent. He asks to be glorified with the glory he had with the Father before the world existed.
17.big: Eternal life consists in knowing the Father and the Son, and Jesus shared the Father's glory before creation.
17.diff: 'The only true God' is cited by some to exclude the Son. The historic reading is that Jesus distinguishes himself from the Father as a person while in the same prayer claiming eternal shared glory — which no created being could.

17.ctx: The second part of the prayer. Jesus prays for the eleven, who are about to face the shock of his arrest and death.
17.mean: Jesus says he has manifested the Father's name to those the Father gave him out of the world. He prays that the Father keep them in his name, that they may be one, and keep them from the evil one. Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth. As you sent me into the world, so I have sent them.
17.big: Jesus prays that his people be kept, united and made holy by God's word as they are sent into the world.

17.ctx: The final part of the prayer, extending to all who would later believe through the apostles' message — which includes every Christian since.
17.mean: Jesus prays for those who will believe through the apostles' word, that they may all be one, just as the Father is in him and he in the Father, so that the world may believe. He desires that they be with him to see his glory.
17.big: Jesus prayed for every future believer, asking that their unity would show the world who he is.

18.ctx: A garden across the Kidron valley on the Mount of Olives, where Jesus often met with his disciples, which is why Judas knew where to find him.
18.mean: Judas brings a band of soldiers and officers. Jesus steps forward and asks whom they seek; when he says 'I am he', they draw back and fall to the ground. He asks that the disciples be let go. Peter cuts off the ear of Malchus, and Jesus tells him to put away his sword: shall I not drink the cup the Father has given me?
18.big: Jesus is not captured but hands himself over, in command even at his arrest.

18.ctx: The courtyard of the high priest's house. 'Another disciple', usually identified as John himself, was known to the high priest and got Peter admitted.
18.mean: Peter follows with another disciple known to the high priest. When the servant girl at the door asks if he is one of Jesus' disciples, Peter says 'I am not.'
18.big: Peter's denial begins with a small question from a servant girl.

18.ctx: An informal hearing before Annas, the former high priest and father-in-law of Caiaphas.
18.mean: Annas questions Jesus about his disciples and teaching. Jesus says he has spoken openly; ask those who heard him. An officer strikes him. Annas sends him bound to Caiaphas.
18.big: Jesus answers with dignity while being treated unjustly.

18.ctx: Back in the courtyard, while the hearing before Annas goes on. John interweaves the two scenes so that Jesus' faithfulness and Peter's failure happen side by side.
18.mean: Peter is asked again and denies it; a relative of Malchus asks whether he saw him in the garden, and Peter denies it again. At once a rooster crowed.
18.big: Peter fails exactly as Jesus said he would.

18.ctx: Early morning at the governor's headquarters. The Jewish leaders do not enter, to avoid ritual defilement before Passover.
18.mean: Pilate asks if Jesus is the King of the Jews. Jesus says his kingdom is not of this world; if it were, his servants would fight. He came to bear witness to the truth. Pilate asks 'What is truth?', finds no guilt in him, and offers to release him; the crowd chooses Barabbas.
18.big: Jesus' kingdom is real but of another kind, and its king stands on trial before a governor who cannot see the truth in front of him.

19.ctx: Pilate has Jesus flogged, perhaps hoping to satisfy the crowd.
19.mean: The soldiers crown him with thorns, dress him in purple and strike him. Pilate brings him out: behold the man. The chief priests cry 'crucify him'; they say he claimed to be the Son of God. Pilate, afraid, questions him again. Jesus says Pilate would have no authority unless it had been given from above. They cry 'We have no king but Caesar,' and Pilate hands him over.
19.big: Jesus is condemned as king by people who in that moment disown God as their king.

19.ctx: Golgotha, 'place of a skull', outside the city walls. Condemned men usually carried the crossbeam to the place of execution.
19.mean: Jesus goes out bearing his own cross, and is crucified between two others. Pilate's sign reads 'Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews' in Aramaic, Latin and Greek, and he refuses to change it. The soldiers divide his garments and cast lots for his tunic, fulfilling Psalm 22:18. Jesus entrusts his mother to the disciple he loved.
19.big: Even at the cross, Scripture is fulfilled and Jesus cares for those he loves.

19.ctx: The last moments on the cross. Crucifixion caused intense thirst through blood loss and exposure. Psalm 69:21 speaks of being given sour wine to drink.
19.mean: Knowing that all was now finished, Jesus says 'I thirst', to fulfil Scripture, and is given sour wine. Then he says 'It is finished', bows his head and gives up his spirit. His thirst is real human suffering, and his death a real human death (see Mark 4:35 on the two natures).
19.big: Jesus dies having completed the work he came to do.
19.diff: 'It is finished' translates a word also used on receipts to mean 'paid in full'. Christians have understood it as declaring the completed work of atonement.

19.ctx: The Sabbath was near, and bodies were not to remain on crosses (Deuteronomy 21:23).
19.mean: The soldiers break the legs of the other two, but finding Jesus already dead, do not break his. One pierces his side with a spear, and blood and water come out. John insists he saw this and testifies so that his readers may believe. Scripture is fulfilled: not a bone of him will be broken (the Passover lamb, Exodus 12:46), and they will look on him whom they pierced (Zechariah 12:10).
19.big: John bears eyewitness testimony that Jesus truly died, as the Passover lamb and the one they pierced.
19.diff: The blood and water have been read symbolically as the sacraments, or as evidence of death. John's own emphasis is on the reality of the death, against those who denied it.

19.ctx: Joseph of Arimathea, a council member and secret disciple, and Nicodemus, who first came to Jesus by night. Burial had to be completed before the Sabbath began at sunset.
19.mean: Joseph asks Pilate for the body; Nicodemus brings about seventy-five pounds of myrrh and aloes — a royal quantity. They bind the body in linen with the spices and lay it in a new tomb in a garden nearby.
19.big: Two secret disciples come into the open to bury Jesus as a king.

20.ctx: Early on the first day of the week, while still dark. The Sabbath had prevented any visit to the tomb. Women's testimony carried little legal weight, yet all four Gospels name them as first witnesses.
20.mean: Mary Magdalene finds the stone taken away and runs to Peter and the beloved disciple. They run to the tomb and find the linen cloths lying there, and the face cloth folded separately. The other disciple saw and believed.
20.big: The empty tomb and the grave cloths left behind point to resurrection, not theft.
20.diff: The detail of the folded cloths is often noted as an eyewitness touch; grave robbers would not have unwrapped the body.

20.ctx: Mary stays at the tomb weeping after the two disciples go home. She was from Magdala on the Sea of Galilee, and Jesus had delivered her from seven demons (Luke 8:2).
20.mean: Two angels ask why she is weeping. She turns and sees Jesus but thinks he is the gardener, until he says her name. He tells her not to cling to him, for he has not yet ascended, but to go and tell his brothers: I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.
20.big: The risen Jesus is recognised when he calls a grieving follower by name, and a woman is the first witness sent to tell the apostles.

20.ctx: That evening, behind locked doors for fear of the Jewish leaders.
20.mean: Jesus stands among them: peace be with you. He shows them his hands and side. As the Father sent me, so I send you. He breathes on them: receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven.
20.big: The risen Jesus sends his disciples as the Father sent him, and gives them the Spirit.
20.diff: How this gift of the Spirit relates to Pentecost in Acts 2 is discussed — a foretaste, a symbolic promise, or a distinct giving. Verse 23 is read by some traditions as priestly authority to absolve, and by most Protestants as authority to declare forgiveness through the gospel.

20.ctx: Thomas, called the Twin, was absent when Jesus first appeared. Earlier he had said, 'Let us also go, that we may die with him' (11:16).
20.mean: Thomas says unless he sees and touches the wounds, he will not believe. Eight days later Jesus invites him to do exactly that. Thomas answers: my Lord and my God. Jesus says: blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.
20.big: The Gospel's climax is a disciple addressing the risen Jesus as Lord and God — and Jesus accepting it.
20.diff: Thomas's words are among the clearest direct confessions of Christ's deity in the New Testament. Some have suggested they are an exclamation addressed to God; this is grammatically unlikely, since John says he said them 'to him'.

20.ctx: John states the purpose of his Gospel. He has chosen seven signs from many possible, arranging his material to lead readers to faith.
20.mean: John says Jesus did many other signs not written in this book, but these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name.
20.big: The whole Gospel is written so that its readers will believe in Jesus and have life.

21.ctx: Beside the Sea of Galilee (Tiberias). Many scholars see chapter 21 as an epilogue added after 20:31, though all manuscripts include it.
21.mean: Seven disciples fish all night and catch nothing. A man on shore tells them to cast the net on the right side, and they catch 153 fish. The beloved disciple says: it is the Lord. Peter jumps into the sea. Jesus has a charcoal fire with fish and bread and gives them breakfast.
21.big: The risen Jesus meets his disciples in their ordinary work and feeds them.
21.diff: The number 153 has been given many symbolic interpretations; many scholars think it is simply an eyewitness detail.
21.h: Jesus Appears by the Sea of Tiberias

21.ctx: Beside another charcoal fire — the same word used for the fire where Peter denied Jesus (18:18).
21.mean: Three times Jesus asks Peter: do you love me? Three times Peter answers yes, and Jesus tells him to feed his lambs and tend his sheep. Jesus foretells that Peter will be led where he does not want to go, signifying the death by which he would glorify God. Then: follow me.
21.big: Jesus restores Peter three times for his three denials, and recommissions him.
21.diff: Two different Greek words for 'love' are used, and some build a contrast between them; many scholars think John uses them interchangeably, as he does elsewhere.

21.ctx: Peter sees the beloved disciple and asks: what about this man?
21.mean: Jesus says: if it is my will that he remain until I come, what is that to you? You follow me. John corrects a rumour that he would not die. He says he is the disciple who wrote these things, and his testimony is true. If everything Jesus did were written, the world could not contain the books.
21.big: Each disciple is to follow Jesus without comparing his path with another's.
21.diff: The closing verses identify the beloved disciple as the Gospel's source and witness. Whether he wrote it himself or others completed it under his testimony is debated.

1.ctx: Paul writes from Corinth around AD 57 to a church in Rome he has not yet visited. The church there was mixed, Jewish and Gentile, and Jews had recently returned after being expelled from Rome under Claudius in AD 49.
1.mean: Paul introduces himself as set apart for the gospel of God, promised beforehand in the Scriptures, concerning God's Son, descended from David according to the flesh and declared to be the Son of God in power by his resurrection. Verses 3–4 hold together Christ's human descent and his divine sonship (see Mark 4:35 on the two natures).
1.big: The gospel is God's long-promised news about his Son, both David's descendant and Son of God.
1.h: Paul Greets the Saints in Rome

1.ctx: Paul's thanksgiving leads straight into the theme of the whole letter.
1.mean: Paul says he longs to visit them. Then the thesis: he is not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek. In it the righteousness of God is revealed from faith for faith; as it is written, the righteous shall live by faith (Habakkuk 2:4).
1.big: The gospel reveals God's righteousness and saves everyone who believes, Jew and Gentile alike.
1.diff: 'The righteousness of God' is one of the most debated phrases in Paul. The Reformation reading, following Luther, takes it chiefly as the righteous standing God gives to believers; others emphasise God's own saving faithfulness to his covenant promises. Many scholars see both in view.

1.ctx: Paul begins to show why everyone needs the gospel, starting with the pagan world.
1.mean: Paul says God's wrath is revealed against all ungodliness of those who suppress the truth. What can be known about God is plain from creation, so they are without excuse. Though they knew God, they did not honour him, and exchanged the glory of God for images. Three times Paul says 'God gave them over' — to impurity, to dishonourable passions, and to a debased mind.
1.big: Humanity has rejected the God it could see in creation, and God's judgement is to give people over to what they chose.
1.diff: Verses 26–27 are central to Christian debates about sexuality. The historic teaching of the church across all major traditions, held by most evangelical and Reformed scholars, reads them as teaching that same-sex sexual activity is contrary to God's design. Some recent scholars argue Paul had only exploitative practices in view. Paul's point in the chapter is that all humanity is guilty, and he immediately turns in chapter 2 on those who judge others.

2.ctx: Paul turns to a reader who agrees with chapter 1 and feels superior — probably a moral Jewish reader, though Paul does not name him yet.
2.mean: Paul says whoever judges others condemns himself, because he does the same things. God's kindness is meant to lead to repentance. God will render to each according to his works; there is no partiality with him. Gentiles who do not have the law show that the work of the law is written on their hearts.
2.big: Those who condemn others while doing the same things are equally under God's judgement.
2.diff: Verses 6–16, about judgement according to works, are read in different ways: as describing a hypothetical standard no one meets (setting up 3:20), as referring to Gentile Christians who fulfil the law through the Spirit, or as the evidence of genuine faith at the final judgement. Most Reformed interpreters take the first or third.

2.ctx: Paul now names the reader he has been addressing since 2:1: a Jew confident in having the law, circumcision and knowledge of God's will, and in being a guide to the Gentiles.
2.mean: Paul says if you call yourself a Jew and rely on the law, teaching others, do you teach yourself? The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you. Circumcision is of value only if you keep the law. A true Jew is one inwardly, and circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit.
2.big: Having God's law and its marks is no protection for those who break it.

3.ctx: Paul anticipates objections a Jewish reader would raise to chapter 2: if being a Jew gives no protection from judgement, what was the point of God's covenant with Israel?
3.mean: Paul asks what advantage the Jew has, and answers: much — they were entrusted with God's words. Their unfaithfulness does not nullify God's faithfulness. Let God be true though every man a liar.
3.big: Human failure does not undo God's faithfulness to his promises.

3.ctx: The conclusion of Paul's case from 1:18. He strings together Old Testament quotations, mostly from the Psalms.
3.mean: Paul says Jews and Greeks are all under sin: none is righteous, no, not one. Whatever the law says, it speaks to those under the law, so that every mouth may be stopped and the whole world held accountable to God. By works of the law no human being will be justified, since through the law comes knowledge of sin.
3.big: The whole human race stands guilty before God, and the law can expose sin but cannot remove it.
3.diff: Reformed theology draws on this passage for the doctrine of total depravity: not that people are as bad as possible, but that sin affects every part of human nature, so that no one seeks God on their own.

3.ctx: The turning point of the letter. 'But now' marks the arrival of God's answer to the problem of 1:18–3:20.
3.mean: Paul says the righteousness of God has been revealed apart from the law, through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe. All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and are justified by his grace as a gift, through the redemption in Christ Jesus, whom God put forward as a propitiation by his blood. This was to show God's righteousness, so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus. Boasting is excluded; a person is justified by faith apart from works of the law.
3.big: God solves the problem of sin in a way that is both just and merciful: Christ's death satisfies justice, and believers are declared righteous as a gift.
3.diff: This passage is at the heart of Reformation theology. Reformed and evangelical theology reads 'propitiation' as Christ's death turning away God's just wrath by bearing it in our place (penal substitution); some prefer 'expiation' (removing sin) or 'mercy seat' (the lid of the ark). As at Galatians 2:16, 'faith in Jesus' may also be translated 'faithfulness of Jesus'.

4.ctx: Paul tests his teaching against the example every Jewish reader revered: Abraham.
4.mean: Paul says Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness (Genesis 15:6). To one who works, wages are counted as due; but to one who does not work but trusts him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted as righteousness. David speaks of the blessing of the one to whom God counts righteousness apart from works (Psalm 32). And Abraham was counted righteous before he was circumcised.
4.big: Abraham himself was declared righteous by faith, before and apart from any works of the law.
4.diff: Reformed theology sees here the doctrine of imputation — righteousness credited to the believer. Some New Perspective scholars emphasise instead that Paul is showing Abraham to be father of Gentile as well as Jewish believers. Both readings recognise that faith, not law-keeping or circumcision, is the ground.

4.ctx: Paul continues the argument from Abraham. Jewish tradition often linked Abraham's blessing to his obedience to the law; Paul points out the promise came centuries before the law was given.
4.mean: Paul says the promise to Abraham came through the righteousness of faith, not the law, so that it rests on grace and is guaranteed to all his offspring. Abraham, against hope, believed that he would become the father of many nations, not weakening in faith though his body was as good as dead. His faith was counted to him as righteousness — and the words were written for our sake too, who believe in him who raised Jesus our Lord, delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification.
4.big: Believers share Abraham's faith in the God who gives life to the dead.

5.ctx: Having shown in chapters 3–4 how believers are justified, Paul turns in chapters 5–8 to what justification brings and how secure it is. Chapter 5 is often seen as a bridge between the two halves.
5.mean: Paul says since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, access into grace, and hope of the glory of God. We rejoice even in sufferings, because suffering produces endurance, endurance character, and character hope, and hope does not put us to shame, because God's love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit.
5.big: Justification brings peace with God and a hope that survives suffering.

5.ctx: Paul explains the depth of God's love shown at the cross. In the ancient world, dying for a good person was admired but rare; dying for enemies was unheard of.
5.mean: Paul says while we were still weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly. God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. Since we are now justified by his blood, much more shall we be saved by him from the wrath of God, and reconciled, saved by his life.
5.big: God's love was shown to his enemies, which is why believers can be certain of final salvation.

5.ctx: One of the most theologically significant passages in the New Testament, comparing Adam and Christ.
5.mean: Paul says sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin, and so death spread to all because all sinned. Adam was a type of the one to come. As one trespass led to condemnation for all, so one act of righteousness leads to justification and life for all. By one man's disobedience many were made sinners; by one man's obedience many will be made righteous. Where sin increased, grace abounded all the more.
5.big: Christ undoes, and far more than undoes, what Adam's sin brought on humanity.
5.diff: This passage underlies the doctrine of original sin. Reformed theology holds that Adam acted as the representative head of humanity, so that his guilt is counted to all his descendants, just as Christ's righteousness is counted to his people. Other traditions hold that people inherit a corrupted nature rather than Adam's guilt. The historicity of Adam is also discussed; the parallel with Christ has led most evangelical scholars to hold that Paul treats Adam as a real individual.
5.h: Death in Adam, Life in Christ

6.ctx: Paul answers the objection his teaching on grace invites. His opponents apparently accused him of encouraging sin (3:8), since if grace abounds where sin increases, why not sin more?
6.mean: Paul asks: shall we continue in sin that grace may abound? By no means! Those baptised into Christ were baptised into his death; buried with him so that, as Christ was raised, they too might walk in newness of life. Our old self was crucified with him. Consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus. Sin will have no dominion over you, since you are not under law but under grace.
6.big: Grace does not encourage sin; union with Christ in his death and resurrection breaks sin's rule.
6.diff: Christians differ over the mode and subjects of baptism, and over whether baptism conveys what it signifies. Paul's point here is union with Christ, which all traditions affirm baptism represents.
6.h: Dead to Sin, Alive to God

6.ctx: Paul uses the image of slavery, familiar in a city where perhaps a third of the population were slaves.
6.mean: Paul says you are slaves of whomever you obey — either sin, leading to death, or obedience, leading to righteousness. Having been set free from sin, they have become slaves of righteousness and of God. The wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.
6.big: Everyone serves a master; freedom in Christ means serving God, whose gift is eternal life.

7.ctx: Paul now explains how believers relate to the law of Moses, using marriage law as an illustration.
7.mean: Paul says a wife is bound to her husband only while he lives. Likewise believers have died to the law through the body of Christ, so that they may belong to another, who has been raised, and bear fruit for God. They now serve in the new way of the Spirit, not the old way of the written code.
7.big: Believers are released from the law's authority to belong to the risen Christ.

7.ctx: Paul guards against the conclusion that the law itself is sinful.
7.mean: Paul asks: is the law sin? By no means! He would not have known sin except through the law — he would not have known coveting if the law had not said 'you shall not covet'. Sin seized the opportunity through the commandment. So the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good.
7.big: The law is good; the problem is sin, which uses the law to provoke and expose itself.

7.ctx: Paul explains how the good law became an instrument of death. He switches to the present tense and the first person, which is why the passage has been read so differently.
7.mean: Paul says the law is spiritual, but he is of the flesh, sold under sin. He does not do what he wants, but the very thing he hates. Nothing good dwells in his flesh; he delights in God's law in his inner being, but sees another law waging war. Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord!
7.big: The struggle with sin is real and painful, and deliverance comes only through Christ.
7.diff: Christians have long divided over whether the 'I' here is Paul as a mature Christian, Paul before conversion, or a representative figure such as Israel under the law. Augustine, Luther, Calvin and many Reformed interpreters read it as the ongoing struggle of the believer; many other scholars read it as life under the law without the Spirit, pointing to the contrast with chapter 8. The first reading has comforted many Christians who find sin still at war in them.

8.ctx: The high point of the letter, and one of the most loved chapters in the Bible. The Holy Spirit, mentioned only once in chapter 7, appears nearly twenty times here.
8.mean: Paul says there is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. God has done what the law could not do: sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, he condemned sin in the flesh, so that the law's requirement might be fulfilled in those who walk according to the Spirit. The mind set on the flesh is death; the mind set on the Spirit is life and peace. Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him.
8.big: Because Christ bore condemnation, those in him face none, and the Spirit gives them new life.
8.diff: 'The likeness of sinful flesh' affirms that Christ was truly human while remaining without sin — part of the church's teaching on the two natures (see Mark 4:35).

8.ctx: Continuing the work of the Spirit. In Roman law adoption gave a son full legal rights as heir, often used by wealthy families without natural sons to secure an inheritance.
8.mean: Paul says those led by the Spirit are sons of God. They received not a spirit of slavery to fall back into fear, but the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry 'Abba! Father!' The Spirit bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God, and if children, then heirs — heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ, provided we suffer with him in order to be glorified with him.
8.big: The Spirit assures believers they are God's adopted children and heirs with Christ.

8.ctx: Paul sets present suffering in the light of future glory. Genesis 3:17 describes creation cursed because of human sin; Paul pictures it waiting to share in humanity's redemption.
8.mean: Paul says the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory to be revealed. Creation itself waits eagerly, subjected to futility but in hope of being set free from its bondage to decay. We groan inwardly as we wait for the redemption of our bodies. The Spirit helps us in our weakness; when we do not know what to pray, the Spirit intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words.
8.big: Present suffering is real, but it is the groaning before a new creation, and the Spirit prays for us in it.

8.ctx: One of the best known and most misused verses in Scripture, followed by what is often called 'the golden chain'.
8.mean: Paul says for those who love God all things work together for good, for those called according to his purpose. Those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son; those he predestined he called; those he called he justified; those he justified he glorified.
8.big: God's purpose for his people runs unbroken from before time to final glory, and he works everything toward it.
8.diff: Reformed theology reads verses 29–30 as teaching that God's foreknowledge is his prior loving choice of particular people, and that none who are called and justified will fail to be glorified. Arminian theology reads 'foreknew' as God's knowledge of who would believe. Verse 28 does not say every event is good, but that God works in all things for his people's good, defined in verse 29 as becoming like Christ.

8.ctx: The conclusion of the first eight chapters, in a series of questions and answers.
8.mean: Paul asks: who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, distress, persecution, famine, danger or sword? In all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us. Neither death nor life, nor angels nor rulers, nor anything in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord.
8.big: Nothing in all creation can separate God's people from his love in Christ.

9.ctx: Paul turns to the question of Israel, which occupies chapters 9–11. If God's promises are sure, why have most of Israel not believed?
9.mean: Paul says he has great sorrow and unceasing anguish, and could wish himself cut off from Christ for the sake of his people. To them belong the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the law, the worship and the promises; from their race, according to the flesh, is the Christ, who is God over all, blessed for ever.
9.big: Israel's unbelief grieves Paul deeply, because to Israel belong all God's privileges, including the Messiah himself.
9.diff: Verse 5 can be punctuated to call Christ 'God over all', or to make a separate doxology to God. Many scholars, ancient and modern, take the first, making it a direct statement of Christ's deity.

9.ctx: Paul argues that God's word has not failed, because not all descended from Israel are Israel.
9.mean: Paul says God chose Isaac over Ishmael and Jacob over Esau before they were born or had done anything good or bad, so that his purpose of election might continue, not because of works but because of him who calls. Is there injustice with God? By no means! He will have mercy on whom he will have mercy. So it depends not on human will or exertion, but on God, who has mercy. He hardened Pharaoh. The potter has the right over the clay.
9.big: God's choosing rests on his own free mercy, not on anything in those he chooses.
9.diff: This is the passage Christians argue over most. Reformed theology reads it as teaching God's unconditional election of individuals to salvation. Others read it as concerning nations or roles in history (Jacob and Esau as peoples), or as election based on foreseen faith. Paul anticipates the objection that this is unjust and answers with God's freedom, while holding it together with his own anguish in verses 1–3.

9.ctx: Having explained Israel's unbelief from God's side in 9:6–29, Paul now looks at it from the human side, showing that Israel is responsible for rejecting the Messiah.
9.mean: Paul says Gentiles who did not pursue righteousness have attained it by faith, while Israel, pursuing a law that would lead to righteousness, did not succeed, because they pursued it as if by works. They stumbled over the stumbling stone, as Isaiah said.
9.big: Israel stumbled by seeking righteousness through works instead of receiving it by faith.

10.ctx: Paul continues to explain Israel's unbelief, while still praying for their salvation.
10.mean: Paul says Israel has a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge; seeking to establish their own righteousness, they did not submit to God's. Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes. If you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved. How will they call on him in whom they have not believed, or hear without someone preaching?
10.big: Salvation comes to anyone, Jew or Gentile, who confesses Jesus as Lord and believes God raised him — which is why the message must be preached.
10.diff: 'Christ is the end of the law' can mean its goal, its termination as a way to righteousness, or both. In verse 13 Paul applies Joel 2:32 — 'the LORD' — to Jesus, which Christians have long noted as a sign of his divine identity.

11.ctx: Paul answers the question his argument has raised: has God rejected his people? He answers first from his own experience as a believing Jew.
11.mean: Paul says by no means — he himself is an Israelite. As in Elijah's time, God has kept a remnant, chosen by grace; and if by grace, it is no longer on the basis of works. The rest were hardened.
11.big: God has not abandoned Israel; a remnant remains, chosen by grace.

11.ctx: Paul uses the image of an olive tree, with natural branches broken off and wild branches grafted in.
11.mean: Paul says through Israel's stumbling, salvation has come to the Gentiles, to make Israel jealous. Some natural branches were broken off because of unbelief, and Gentiles grafted in by faith. Gentiles must not be arrogant, for God is able to graft the natural branches in again.
11.big: Gentile believers share Israel's root by grace alone and have no grounds for pride.
11.diff: Verses 20–22 ('otherwise you too will be cut off') are discussed in relation to perseverance. Reformed interpreters generally read them as addressed to Gentiles as a group, or as the means by which God keeps true believers; others see a real possibility of individual apostasy.

11.ctx: Paul reveals a 'mystery' — in the New Testament, something previously hidden and now made known by God — about Israel's future, addressed especially to Gentile believers tempted to look down on Israel.
11.mean: Paul says a partial hardening has come on Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, and in this way all Israel will be saved. As regards the gospel they are enemies for your sake; as regards election they are beloved for the sake of their fathers. The gifts and calling of God are irrevocable. God has consigned all to disobedience, that he may have mercy on all.
11.big: God's purposes for Israel are not finished, because his calling is irrevocable.
11.diff: 'All Israel will be saved' is interpreted as a large-scale future turning of Jewish people to Christ, as the total of elect Jews across history, or as the whole people of God, Jew and Gentile. The first has been the most common reading in the Reformed tradition and is probably the most natural here.

11.ctx: Paul breaks into praise after the hardest chapters of the letter.
11.mean: Paul says: oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgements and inscrutable his ways! Who has known the mind of the Lord? From him and through him and to him are all things. To him be glory for ever.
11.big: The right response to God's sovereign purposes is not a solved puzzle but worship.

12.ctx: The turn to practical living. 'Therefore' connects everything that follows to the mercies of God set out in chapters 1–11.
12.mean: Paul says: I appeal to you, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship. Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind. He then describes the church as one body with many members and different gifts — prophecy, service, teaching, exhortation, giving, leading, mercy.
12.big: In response to God's mercy, believers offer their whole lives as worship and serve one another with their different gifts.

12.ctx: A series of short commands on life together. Verses 10–13 are among the passages the Community of Brothers takes as a description of brotherhood.
12.mean: Paul says let love be genuine. Abhor what is evil; hold fast to what is good. Love one another with brotherly affection; outdo one another in showing honour. Do not be slothful in zeal; be fervent in spirit, serve the Lord. Rejoice in hope, be patient in tribulation, be constant in prayer. Contribute to the needs of the saints and seek to show hospitality.
12.big: Genuine love shows itself in honour, zeal, patience, prayer and hospitality among believers.

12.ctx: Paul turns to relationships with those outside the church, including enemies.
12.mean: Paul says bless those who persecute you. Live in harmony with one another. Repay no one evil for evil. If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all. Never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God. If your enemy is hungry, feed him. Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.
12.big: Believers overcome evil not by revenge but by doing good, leaving justice to God.

13.ctx: Paul writes under the emperor Nero, early in his reign, before the persecution of Christians began.
13.mean: Paul says let every person be subject to the governing authorities, for there is no authority except from God. Rulers are God's servants for good, bearing the sword to punish wrongdoing. Therefore pay taxes and give respect and honour to whom they are owed.
13.big: Civil government is ordained by God, and believers should respect and support it.
13.diff: Christians differ over the limits of this instruction. The New Testament itself shows that when authorities command what God forbids, believers must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29). How this applies to unjust governments, protest and resistance has been discussed throughout church history.

13.ctx: Following instruction about paying what is owed to governing authorities, Paul turns to the one debt that can never be fully paid: the debt of love.
13.mean: Paul says owe no one anything, except to love each other. Adultery, murder, theft and coveting are all summed up in this word: you shall love your neighbour as yourself. Love does no wrong to a neighbour; therefore love is the fulfilling of the law.
13.big: Love for neighbour fulfils everything the law requires in our dealings with others.

13.ctx: Paul gives the reason for urgency. The early church lived in expectation of Christ's return, and Paul uses the image of dawn approaching after a long night.
13.mean: Paul says it is the hour to wake from sleep, for salvation is nearer now than when we first believed. The night is far gone; the day is at hand. Cast off the works of darkness and put on the armour of light. Put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh.
13.big: Because Christ's return draws nearer every day, believers should live as people of the day.
13.diff: Augustine was converted on reading verses 13–14, one of the most famous conversions in church history.

14.ctx: The Roman church had disputes, probably between Jewish and Gentile believers, over food laws and holy days.
14.mean: Paul says welcome the one who is weak in faith, but not to quarrel over opinions. One person eats anything, another only vegetables; one esteems one day above another. Each should be fully convinced in his own mind. Why do you judge your brother? We will all stand before God's judgement seat.
14.big: On disputable matters, believers must not despise or judge one another, since each answers to the Lord.
14.diff: Christians disagree about which issues count as 'disputable matters'. Paul's category covers practices neither commanded nor forbidden in the gospel, not matters of core doctrine or clear moral teaching.

14.ctx: Paul turns from not judging to not causing others to stumble.
14.mean: Paul says decide never to put a stumbling block in the way of a brother. Nothing is unclean in itself, but if your brother is grieved by what you eat, you are no longer walking in love. The kingdom of God is not food and drink but righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit. Whatever does not proceed from faith is sin.
14.big: Christian freedom is limited by love for fellow believers whose consciences are weaker.

15.ctx: Continuing the instruction about 'the strong' — those who felt free to eat anything and ignore special days — and 'the weak', who kept food laws and holy days.
15.mean: Paul says the strong should bear with the failings of the weak and not please themselves, for Christ did not please himself. He prays that God would grant them to live in harmony, so that together, with one voice, they may glorify God. Verses 5–7 are among the passages the Community of Brothers returns to.
15.big: Following Christ's example, believers are to put others first so that the church glorifies God together.

15.ctx: The practical section reaches its theological conclusion, linking the call to welcome one another with Christ's ministry to both Jews and Gentiles.
15.mean: Paul says welcome one another as Christ has welcomed you, for the glory of God. Christ became a servant to the circumcised to confirm God's promises to the patriarchs, and so that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy. He quotes four Old Testament passages about the Gentiles praising God, and prays that the God of hope fill them with joy and peace in believing.
15.big: Christ welcomed Jews and Gentiles alike, so his people must welcome one another.
15.h: Christ the Servant of Jews and Gentiles

15.ctx: Paul explains his boldness in writing to a church he did not found.
15.mean: Paul says he is satisfied they are full of goodness, but has written boldly because of the grace given him to be a minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles. From Jerusalem to Illyricum he has fully proclaimed the gospel, making it his ambition to preach where Christ has not been named.
15.big: Paul's ambition is to take the gospel where Christ is not yet known.
15.h: Paul the Minister to the Gentiles

15.ctx: Paul's travel plans. He is about to take a collection from Gentile churches to the poor in Jerusalem.
15.mean: Paul says he hopes to see them on his way to Spain, after delivering the collection to Jerusalem. He asks them to pray that he may be delivered from unbelievers in Judea and that his service will be acceptable.
15.big: Paul's plans are made in dependence on prayer.
15.diff: Acts records that Paul reached Rome as a prisoner after arrest in Jerusalem. Whether he ever reached Spain is uncertain; some early writers say he did.

16.ctx: Phoebe probably carried the letter from Cenchreae, the port of Corinth, to Rome.
16.mean: Paul commends Phoebe, a deacon (or servant) of the church at Cenchreae and patron of many, and greets a long list of people by name — including Prisca and Aquila, and Andronicus and Junia, 'well known to the apostles'. Around a third of those named are women.
16.big: The early church was a network of named, valued men and women serving together.
16.diff: Whether Phoebe held the office of deacon, and whether Junia was counted 'among the apostles' or 'well known to' them, are debated and bear on discussions of women's roles in the church.

16.ctx: A brief, sharp warning near the end of the letter, possibly about teachers similar to those Paul opposed in Galatia or Philippi.
16.mean: Paul says watch out for those who cause divisions contrary to the teaching they received, and avoid them. They serve their own appetites and deceive the naive with smooth talk. The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet — an echo of Genesis 3:15.
16.big: Believers must guard the church's unity against divisive teachers, trusting God's victory over evil.

16.ctx: Greetings from those with Paul in Corinth, where he wrote the letter. Letters were normally written down by a secretary, who occasionally added his own greeting.
16.mean: Timothy, several relatives of Paul, Gaius his host, and Erastus the city treasurer send greetings. Tertius, who wrote the letter down, adds his own.
16.big: The gospel had reached people of every rank, from secretaries to city officials.
16.diff: An inscription found in Corinth names an Erastus as a city official. Many scholars think it may be the same man.

16.ctx: The closing doxology, returning to themes from the opening verses of the letter: the gospel, promised in the prophets, bringing about the obedience of faith among all nations.
16.mean: Paul gives glory to God, who is able to strengthen them according to the gospel and the revelation of the mystery kept secret for long ages but now disclosed and made known to all nations, to bring about the obedience of faith — to the only wise God be glory for evermore through Jesus Christ.
16.big: The letter ends where it began: the gospel, promised long ago, now made known to all nations for God's glory.
16.diff: The doxology appears in different places in different manuscripts (after chapter 14, 15 or 16), which has led to discussion of the letter's early circulation. Its content is fully Pauline.

1.ctx: Peter writes, probably from Rome ('Babylon', 5:13) in the early 60s, to Christians scattered across five provinces of what is now Turkey. Many were Gentiles facing hostility for their new faith.
1.mean: Peter greets them as elect exiles of the dispersion, chosen according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, in the sanctification of the Spirit, for obedience to Jesus Christ and sprinkling with his blood. Father, Spirit and Son are all named in the opening sentence.
1.big: Believers are exiles in this world but chosen by the Father, set apart by the Spirit and cleansed by the Son.
1.diff: Some scholars think a later follower wrote in Peter's name, pointing to the polished Greek; others note that Silvanus helped write it (5:12), which could explain the style. The traditional view of Petrine authorship remains widely held.

1.ctx: A great opening blessing, one long sentence in the Greek, like Ephesians 1:3–14.
1.mean: Peter says God has caused them to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ, to an inheritance that is imperishable, kept in heaven for them, who by God's power are being guarded through faith. For a little while they may be grieved by various trials, so that the tested genuineness of their faith may result in praise at Christ's revelation. Though they have not seen him, they love him and rejoice with joy inexpressible. The prophets searched and enquired about this salvation.
1.big: Suffering believers have a living hope and an inheritance that God himself guards.
1.diff: Reformed interpreters see in verse 5 ('guarded through faith') both God's keeping power and the faith through which he keeps believers — part of the doctrine of perseverance.

1.ctx: The first practical instruction, grounded in the hope just described.
1.mean: Peter says to prepare their minds for action and set their hope fully on the grace coming at Christ's revelation. As obedient children, they must not be conformed to their former passions, but be holy in all their conduct, since it is written: you shall be holy, for I am holy. They were ransomed from their futile ways not with silver or gold but with the precious blood of Christ, like a lamb without blemish, foreknown before the foundation of the world.
1.big: Believers are to be holy because the holy God ransomed them at the cost of Christ's blood.

1.ctx: Continuing the call to holiness, now focused on love within the church.
1.mean: Peter says having purified their souls by obedience to the truth, they should love one another earnestly from a pure heart, since they have been born again of imperishable seed, through the living and abiding word of God. All flesh is like grass, but the word of the Lord remains for ever (Isaiah 40:6–8).
1.big: New birth through God's enduring word produces sincere love among believers.

2.ctx: Peter draws on Old Testament images of a temple and of Israel as God's people, applying them to a largely Gentile church.
2.mean: Peter says to long for pure spiritual milk. Coming to Christ, a living stone rejected by men but chosen by God, they too are being built as living stones into a spiritual house, a holy priesthood. They are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession, to proclaim the excellencies of him who called them out of darkness into his marvellous light.
2.big: The titles once given to Israel now belong to all who belong to Christ, the chosen cornerstone.
2.diff: The phrase 'royal priesthood' underlies the Reformation doctrine of the priesthood of all believers — every Christian has direct access to God through Christ.
2.h: The Living Stone and Chosen People

2.ctx: Instructions for living as exiles within a hostile society, beginning with civil authority.
2.mean: Peter says be subject for the Lord's sake to every human institution, whether the emperor or governors. Live as people who are free, not using freedom as a cover-up for evil, but as servants of God. Honour everyone, love the brotherhood, fear God, honour the emperor. Servants are to be subject to their masters, even the unjust.
2.big: Believers show their freedom by honourable conduct that silences critics.
2.diff: As at Romans 13, the limits of submission are discussed; Peter himself told the Sanhedrin 'we must obey God rather than men' (Acts 5:29). Instructions to slaves regulate an existing institution rather than approve it.

2.ctx: The instruction to suffering servants leads into one of the richest passages about Christ's death.
2.mean: Peter says Christ suffered for them, leaving an example so they might follow in his steps. He committed no sin; when reviled, he did not revile in return. He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we might die to sin and live to righteousness. By his wounds you have been healed. You were straying like sheep, but have now returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls. Peter draws heavily on Isaiah 53.
2.big: Christ's suffering is both the pattern for believers to follow and the sacrifice that bore their sins.
2.diff: Reformed and evangelical theology reads verse 24 as a clear statement of substitution. 'By his wounds you have been healed' refers in context to spiritual healing from sin; whether it also promises physical healing now is debated, though Peter's own focus is on sin.

3.ctx: The household code continues with marriage. Many of these women had husbands who were not believers.
3.mean: Peter says wives should be subject to their husbands, so that even if some do not obey the word, they may be won without a word by their conduct. Their beauty should be the hidden person of the heart with the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit. Husbands should live with their wives in an understanding way, showing honour, since they are heirs together of the grace of life, so that their prayers may not be hindered.
3.big: Christian marriage is marked by respect and honour on both sides, and can itself be a witness.
3.diff: As with Ephesians 5, Christians differ over how the call for wives to submit applies today, and over the phrase 'weaker vessel'. Peter's command that husbands honour their wives as fellow heirs of grace was striking in its setting.

3.ctx: A summary of the whole ethical section from 2:11, addressed now to everyone. Peter's readers were suffering insults and mistreatment from neighbours for their faith.
3.mean: Peter says all of them should have unity of mind, sympathy, brotherly love, a tender heart and a humble mind. Do not repay evil for evil or reviling for reviling, but bless. He quotes Psalm 34: whoever desires to love life must keep his tongue from evil and seek peace.
3.big: Believers are called to bless even those who treat them badly.

3.ctx: Addressed to believers suffering unjustly. Christians were suspected of disloyalty and immorality because they withdrew from pagan festivals and emperor worship.
3.mean: Peter says even if they suffer for righteousness' sake, they will be blessed. In their hearts they should honour Christ the Lord as holy, always being prepared to make a defence to anyone who asks for a reason for the hope in them — yet with gentleness and respect. Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring us to God. He went and proclaimed to the spirits in prison. Baptism now saves, not as removing dirt, but as an appeal to God for a good conscience, through the resurrection of Jesus Christ.
3.big: Believers can answer for their hope with gentleness because Christ suffered once to bring them to God.
3.diff: Verse 15 is the verse apologetics takes its name from. Verses 18–22 are among the hardest in the New Testament. The 'spirits in prison' have been read as fallen angels, as the dead to whom Christ announced his victory, or as people of Noah's day to whom Christ preached through Noah. Verse 21 on baptism is read by some traditions as baptism conveying salvation, and by most Protestants as baptism signifying the salvation received by faith, as Peter's own clarification suggests.

4.ctx: Peter returns to the example of Christ's suffering from 3:18. Converts from paganism had left behind a social life of feasts, drinking and idol worship, and faced mockery for it.
4.mean: Peter says since Christ suffered in the flesh, arm yourselves with the same way of thinking, living no longer for human passions but for the will of God. Former companions are surprised they no longer join in the same flood of debauchery. The end of all things is at hand, so be self-controlled for prayer, love one another earnestly, show hospitality without grumbling, and use every gift to serve one another, so that in everything God may be glorified through Jesus Christ.
4.big: Living for God's will instead of old passions shows itself in prayer, love, hospitality and service.

4.ctx: Persecution was either happening or expected. Peter writes as it grew under Nero.
4.mean: Peter says do not be surprised at the fiery trial as though something strange were happening, but rejoice insofar as you share Christ's sufferings. If insulted for the name of Christ, you are blessed. Let no one suffer as a murderer or thief, but if as a Christian, let him not be ashamed. Judgement begins at the household of God. Let those who suffer according to God's will entrust their souls to a faithful Creator while doing good.
4.big: Suffering for Christ is not a sign that something has gone wrong, but a share in his sufferings.

5.ctx: Peter addresses church leaders. Elders, also called overseers, led the local churches.
5.mean: Peter writes as a fellow elder and witness of Christ's sufferings. He tells elders to shepherd the flock of God, exercising oversight not under compulsion but willingly, not for shameful gain but eagerly, not domineering but being examples. When the chief Shepherd appears, they will receive the unfading crown of glory.
5.big: Church leaders are under-shepherds who serve willingly and lead by example, answerable to Christ.

5.ctx: Instruction to the younger members, and then to everyone. Verse 5 quotes Proverbs 3:34, the same verse James quotes (James 4:6).
5.mean: Peter says the younger should be subject to the elders, and all should clothe themselves with humility, for God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble. Humble yourselves under God's mighty hand, casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you. Be sober-minded; your adversary the devil prowls like a roaring lion. Resist him, firm in your faith.
5.big: Humble dependence on God, who cares, is the way to face both anxiety and the devil.

5.ctx: The closing blessing and greetings. 'Babylon' is widely understood as a coded name for Rome.
5.mean: Peter says after they have suffered a little while, the God of all grace, who called them to his eternal glory in Christ, will restore, confirm, strengthen and establish them. He wrote through Silvanus, and sends greetings from the church in Babylon and from Mark, his son.
5.big: The God who called them will himself restore and establish them after their suffering.
5.diff: The mention of Mark supports the early tradition that Mark's Gospel draws on Peter's preaching.

1.ctx: Peter writes what he presents as his final letter, knowing his death is near (1:14). Its authorship has been more widely questioned than any other New Testament book.
1.mean: Peter greets those who have obtained a faith of equal standing by the righteousness of our God and Saviour Jesus Christ.
1.big: Peter's greeting calls Jesus Christ both God and Saviour.
1.diff: Many scholars doubt Peter wrote this letter, citing its style and its apparent knowledge of Paul's letters as Scripture (3:16). Others, including many evangelical scholars, defend Petrine authorship, possibly with a different secretary. The church accepted it as Scripture after some hesitation. In verse 1 the Greek construction most naturally reads as one person, 'our God and Saviour', a direct statement of Christ's deity.

1.ctx: The letter's main positive teaching, against false teachers who treated grace as permission to sin.
1.mean: Peter says God's divine power has granted all things for life and godliness, and through his promises believers become partakers of the divine nature. So they must make every effort to add to their faith virtue, knowledge, self-control, steadfastness, godliness, brotherly affection and love. Be all the more diligent to confirm your calling and election.
1.big: Having been given everything by God, believers must make every effort to grow in godliness.
1.diff: 'Partakers of the divine nature' has been understood very differently: Eastern Orthodox theology builds on it a doctrine of theosis (becoming like God by grace); Reformed and evangelical theology understands it as sharing God's moral character through union with Christ, not becoming divine in essence.

1.ctx: Peter defends the reliability of the apostolic message about Christ's return.
1.mean: Peter says they did not follow cleverly devised myths, but were eyewitnesses of his majesty when he received honour and glory from the Father on the holy mountain. And they have the prophetic word more fully confirmed. No prophecy of Scripture comes from someone's own interpretation; men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit.
1.big: The apostles' message rests on eyewitness testimony and on Scripture inspired by the Holy Spirit.
1.diff: Verses 20–21 are a foundational text for the doctrine of the inspiration of Scripture, alongside 2 Timothy 3:16.

2.ctx: A long warning closely parallel to Jude, from which it probably draws. The false teachers claimed Christian freedom meant freedom from moral restraint.
2.mean: Peter says false teachers will arise among them, even denying the Master who bought them. He cites God's judgement on angels who sinned, on the ancient world in the flood, and on Sodom and Gomorrah, while rescuing Noah and Lot. So the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials and keep the unrighteous under punishment. The false teachers are bold, greedy and sensual, promising freedom while slaves of corruption. It would have been better for them never to have known the way of righteousness.
2.big: God will judge false teachers who exploit the church, and will rescue those who belong to him.
2.diff: Verse 1 ('denying the Master who bought them') is discussed in debates about the extent of the atonement, and verses 20–22 in debates about whether true believers can fall away. Reformed interpreters generally read them as describing those who professed faith without genuine conversion.

3.ctx: The false teachers mocked the promise of Christ's return because it had not yet happened.
3.mean: Peter says scoffers will come saying 'Where is the promise of his coming? All things continue as they were.' They deliberately overlook that the world was created by God's word and was once destroyed by water. By the same word the present heavens and earth are stored up for fire, kept until the day of judgement.
3.big: The God who created and once judged the world will certainly judge it again.

3.ctx: Peter answers the scoffers' question about delay. Decades had passed since Jesus' promise to return, and some were concluding it would never happen.
3.mean: Peter says with the Lord one day is as a thousand years. The Lord is not slow to fulfil his promise, but patient, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance. The day of the Lord will come like a thief; the heavens will pass away and the earth be exposed. Since all these things are to be dissolved, what sort of people ought they to be? They wait for new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells.
3.big: The apparent delay in Christ's return is God's patience, giving time for repentance.
3.diff: Verse 9 ('not wishing that any should perish') is often discussed alongside election. Reformed interpreters read it variously as God's genuine desire for all, distinct from his decree, or as referring to his elect ('you'); others see it as showing salvation is open to all. All agree it reveals God's patience and mercy.

3.ctx: The closing exhortations of what Peter presents as his last letter, drawing together the letter's themes of holy living, patience and guarding against error.
3.mean: Peter says to be diligent to be found without spot, at peace. Count the Lord's patience as salvation, as Paul also wrote, whose letters contain some things hard to understand, which the ignorant twist to their destruction, as they do the other Scriptures. Beware of being carried away; grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ.
3.big: Believers must hold fast against error and keep growing in grace and knowledge of Christ.
3.diff: Verse 16 is notable for placing Paul's letters alongside 'the other Scriptures', showing an early recognition of their authority.

1.ctx: Jude, brother of James and so a brother of Jesus, writes a short urgent letter, probably to Jewish Christians.
1.mean: Jude greets those who are called, beloved in God the Father and kept for Jesus Christ, with mercy, peace and love.
1.big: Believers are called, loved and kept by God.
1.diff: Jude calls himself a servant of Jesus Christ rather than his brother — a mark of humility and of his recognition of who Jesus was.

1.ctx: Jude had intended to write about salvation, but felt compelled to warn instead.
1.mean: Jude urges them to contend for the faith once for all delivered to the saints, because ungodly people have crept in, perverting grace into sensuality and denying Jesus Christ. He cites God's judgement on Israel in the wilderness, on angels who sinned, and on Sodom. He quotes a tradition about Michael disputing with the devil over Moses' body, and a prophecy from the book of Enoch.
1.big: The faith has been delivered once for all, and must be defended against those who twist grace into licence.
1.diff: Jude quotes the book of 1 Enoch and alludes to a tradition in the Assumption of Moses, neither of which is in the Bible. Most interpreters conclude that quoting a true statement from a non-canonical book does not make the whole book Scripture, as Paul quoted pagan poets.

1.ctx: Having exposed the false teachers, Jude turns to the faithful. The apostles had warned that scoffers would come, as 2 Peter 3:3 also records.
1.mean: Jude says to remember the apostles' predictions that there would be scoffers in the last time. Build yourselves up in your most holy faith, pray in the Holy Spirit, keep yourselves in the love of God, and wait for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ. Have mercy on those who doubt; save others by snatching them out of the fire.
1.big: Believers keep themselves in God's love, and reach out with mercy to those who are wavering.

1.ctx: One of the great doxologies of the New Testament, often used as a benediction at the close of church services. It balances the letter's stern warnings.
1.mean: Jude gives glory to him who is able to keep them from stumbling and to present them blameless before his glory with great joy — to the only God, our Saviour, through Jesus Christ our Lord.
1.big: The God who warns his people is the same God able to keep them from falling.

1.ctx: A short letter from 'the elder', traditionally John the apostle, to 'the elect lady and her children' — probably a church and its members.
1.mean: The elder writes to those he loves in the truth, because of the truth that abides in them and will be with them for ever.
1.big: Truth and love belong together in the Christian community.
1.diff: Whether 'the elect lady' is an individual woman or a church is debated; most scholars favour a church.

1.ctx: The elder has heard news of the church, perhaps from travelling believers, and finds that some — though apparently not all — are walking in the truth.
1.mean: The elder rejoices to find some walking in the truth, and asks that they love one another — which means walking according to God's commandments.
1.big: Love and obedience to God's commandments are inseparable.

1.ctx: The same false teachers as 1 John, travelling between churches and relying on their hospitality.
1.mean: The elder says many deceivers have gone out who do not confess the coming of Jesus Christ in the flesh. Anyone who goes on ahead and does not abide in the teaching of Christ does not have God. Do not receive such a person into your house or give him any greeting, for that would share in his wicked works.
1.big: Love for the truth means refusing to support those who deny Christ's coming in the flesh.
1.diff: The instruction not to receive false teachers concerns giving them a platform and support in house churches, not general courtesy to unbelievers. How to apply it today is worth discussing.

1.ctx: The closing. Letters in the ancient world were costly and slow, and a visit was the preferred way to settle important matters.
1.mean: The elder has much to write but would rather speak face to face, so that their joy may be complete. The children of their elect sister send greetings.
1.big: Written words serve, but do not replace, face-to-face fellowship.

1.ctx: A short personal letter from the elder to Gaius, a faithful church member.
1.mean: The elder prays that all may go well with Gaius and that he may be in good health, as it goes well with his soul.
1.big: The elder cares for his friend's whole wellbeing, body and soul.
1.diff: Verse 2 is sometimes used to teach that God promises believers prosperity and health. In context it is simply a customary greeting wishing a friend well.

1.ctx: Travelling missionaries relied on the hospitality of local believers.
1.mean: The elder commends Gaius for his faithful hospitality to brothers who were strangers, and asks him to send them on their way in a manner worthy of God. We ought to support such people, that we may be fellow workers for the truth.
1.big: Supporting those who carry the gospel makes believers partners in their work.

1.ctx: A church power struggle. Diotrephes apparently led a house church and had refused to receive the elder's letter or the travelling teachers the elder sent.
1.mean: The elder says Diotrephes, who likes to put himself first, does not acknowledge the elder's authority, spreads malicious talk, refuses to welcome the brothers, and puts out of the church those who do. Do not imitate evil but good. Demetrius has received a good testimony from everyone.
1.big: Love of pre-eminence damages the church; faithful service earns a good name.
1.diff: Whether Diotrephes was a false teacher or simply ambitious and controlling is not stated.

1.ctx: The closing, very similar to 2 John. 'The friends' echoes Jesus' words calling his disciples friends (John 15:14–15).
1.mean: The elder hopes to see Gaius soon and speak face to face. Peace be to you. The friends greet you; greet the friends, each by name.
1.big: The church is a community of friends known to one another by name.

1.ctx: Paul writes from prison to Philemon, a wealthy believer in Colossae whose house hosted the church. The letter was carried with Colossians by Tychicus and Onesimus.
1.mean: Paul and Timothy greet Philemon, Apphia (probably his wife), Archippus, and the church in his house.
1.big: A private matter is set before the whole church.
1.diff: Paul addresses the church as well as Philemon, which means the request that follows would be heard publicly.

1.ctx: Paul's thanksgiving, as in his other letters. It carefully prepares for his request by praising the very love he will ask Philemon to show.
1.mean: Paul thanks God for Philemon's love and faith, and prays that the sharing of his faith may become effective. He says the hearts of the saints have been refreshed through Philemon.
1.big: Philemon's known love for the saints is the ground of Paul's appeal.

1.ctx: Onesimus was a slave who had run away from Philemon, possibly after stealing, and had met Paul and become a Christian. Runaway slaves faced severe punishment under Roman law.
1.mean: Paul says though he could command, he prefers to appeal on the basis of love, for his child Onesimus, whose name means 'useful' — formerly useless to Philemon but now useful to both. Paul is sending him back, no longer as a slave but more than a slave, as a beloved brother. If he owes anything, charge it to Paul's account; Paul will repay it. He is confident Philemon will do even more than he asks.
1.big: The gospel turns a runaway slave into a brother, and Paul offers to pay his debt himself.
1.diff: Paul does not directly demand Onesimus's freedom, which has troubled readers; many think 'even more than I say' hints at it. Martin Luther and many since have seen in Paul's 'charge it to my account' a picture of Christ taking our debt. The principle of 'no longer a slave but a brother' was one later Christians drew on in opposing slavery.

1.ctx: The closing greetings, overlapping closely with Colossians 4:10–14, which confirms the two letters were written and sent together.
1.mean: Epaphras, a fellow prisoner, sends greetings, as do Mark, Aristarchus, Demas and Luke. The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.
1.big: The same circle of co-workers stands behind this small, personal letter.

1.ctx: Paul writes to Titus, a Gentile co-worker he left on the island of Crete to organise the churches there. This is one of the three 'Pastoral Letters' with 1 and 2 Timothy.
1.mean: Paul writes as a servant of God and apostle, for the sake of the faith of God's elect and their knowledge of the truth, in hope of eternal life promised by God, who never lies, before the ages began.
1.big: Paul's ministry serves the faith and hope of God's chosen people, grounded in God's ancient promise.
1.diff: The authorship of the Pastoral Letters is debated more than most of Paul's letters, owing to differences in vocabulary and church organisation. Many scholars think a follower of Paul wrote them; many evangelical scholars defend Paul's authorship, perhaps using a secretary.

1.ctx: Crete had several scattered churches needing organised leadership.
1.mean: Paul tells Titus to appoint elders in every town. An elder, or overseer, must be above reproach, the husband of one wife, with faithful children, not arrogant, quick-tempered, a drunkard, violent or greedy, but hospitable, self-controlled, upright, holy and disciplined, holding firm to the trustworthy word so he can give instruction in sound doctrine and rebuke those who contradict it.
1.big: Church leaders are chosen above all for proven character and faithfulness to sound teaching.
1.diff: 'Husband of one wife' is read as requiring marital faithfulness, as excluding the divorced and remarried, as excluding polygamy, or as requiring that elders be married. The most common reading is faithfulness in marriage. The requirements assume male elders, which complementarian churches follow and egalitarian churches read differently.

1.ctx: False teachers, many associated with Jewish myths and circumcision, were upsetting households.
1.mean: Paul says many are insubordinate, empty talkers and deceivers, teaching for shameful gain. He quotes a Cretan poet: 'Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons', and says the testimony is true. Rebuke them sharply. To the pure all things are pure. They profess to know God but deny him by their works.
1.big: False teaching is exposed by the way its teachers live.
1.diff: Paul quotes the Cretan poet Epimenides. Some readers find the generalisation uncomfortable; Paul is using a well-known local saying to make a point about the false teachers' conduct.

2.ctx: Instruction for different groups within the church, linked throughout to how the gospel is seen by outsiders.
2.mean: Paul tells Titus to teach what accords with sound doctrine: older men to be sober and dignified, older women reverent and to teach what is good, training younger women; younger men to be self-controlled; Titus himself to be a model of good works. Slaves are to be trustworthy, so that in everything they may adorn the doctrine of God our Saviour.
2.big: Sound doctrine shows itself in ordinary godly living that makes the gospel attractive.
