2.ctx: The theological basis for the practical instructions of 2:1–10. 'Grace appeared' refers to Christ's first coming; the 'appearing' of verse 13 to his return.
2.mean: Paul says the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation for all people, training us to renounce ungodliness and to live self-controlled, upright and godly lives, waiting for the blessed hope, the appearing of the glory of our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ, who gave himself to redeem us from lawlessness and to purify a people for his own possession.
2.big: God's grace not only saves but trains believers to live godly lives as they wait for Christ's return.
2.diff: As at 2 Peter 1:1, the grammar of verse 13 most naturally reads 'our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ' as one person, a direct statement of Christ's deity. Some translations separate them.

3.ctx: Instruction for believers living among unbelieving neighbours and authorities.
3.mean: Paul says to be submissive to rulers, ready for every good work, speaking evil of no one, gentle and courteous to all. We ourselves were once foolish and disobedient. But when the goodness and loving kindness of God our Saviour appeared, he saved us, not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy, by the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out richly through Jesus Christ, so that being justified by his grace we might become heirs.
3.big: God saved us by his mercy alone, through the Spirit's renewal, which is why believers treat outsiders with gentleness.
3.diff: 'Washing of regeneration' is read by some traditions as baptism conveying new birth, and by most Protestant interpreters as the inner cleansing of new birth by the Spirit, which baptism signifies. The whole Trinity is named in verses 4–6.

3.ctx: Final practical warnings. The disputes over genealogies and the law seem to have been Jewish speculations the false teachers promoted (compare 1:14).
3.mean: Paul says avoid foolish controversies, genealogies and quarrels about the law, for they are unprofitable. As for a divisive person, after warning him once and then twice, have nothing more to do with him.
3.big: Pointless disputes damage the church, and persistently divisive people must be firmly dealt with.

3.ctx: Closing arrangements. Nicopolis was probably the city on the west coast of Greece, a natural place to spend winter when sea travel stopped.
3.mean: Paul says he will send Artemas or Tychicus, and asks Titus to join him at Nicopolis for the winter. Help Zenas and Apollos on their way. Our people must learn to devote themselves to good works. Grace be with you all.
3.big: The letter closes as it has run throughout: faith expressed in practical good works.

1.ctx: Thessalonica was the capital of Macedonia and a major port. Paul founded the church on his second journey, but was forced out after a few weeks by opposition (Acts 17:1–10). This is probably his earliest surviving letter, written from Corinth around AD 50.
1.mean: Paul, Silvanus and Timothy greet the church and give thanks for their work of faith, labour of love and steadfastness of hope. The gospel came to them not only in word but in power and in the Holy Spirit. They turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God, and to wait for his Son from heaven, whom he raised from the dead, Jesus who delivers us from the wrath to come.
1.big: The Thessalonians' conversion was real: they turned from idols to serve God and wait for his Son.
1.diff: Faith, love and hope appear together here, as in 1 Corinthians 13, and the whole letter is shaped by waiting for Christ's return.

2.ctx: Paul's opponents apparently accused him of being a travelling preacher in it for money and flattery, a common type in the Greek world.
2.mean: Paul reminds them how he came: not with flattery, greed or seeking glory, but gentle among them like a nursing mother, working night and day so as not to be a burden, and exhorting each one like a father with his children. When they received the word of God from him, they accepted it not as the word of men but as what it really is, the word of God. They suffered from their own countrymen as the Judean churches had.
2.big: Paul's conduct shows his message was genuine, and they received it rightly as God's own word.

2.ctx: Paul had been forced to leave Thessalonica suddenly and had been unable to return.
2.mean: Paul says he was torn away from them, but only in person, not in heart. He eagerly wanted to see them again, but Satan hindered him. They are his glory and joy.
2.big: Paul's affection for the church is deep, and separation has not diminished it.

3.ctx: Unable to go himself, Paul had sent Timothy from Athens to strengthen them.
3.mean: Paul says he sent Timothy to establish and exhort them in their faith, so that no one would be moved by these afflictions, for they had been told in advance that they were destined for them.
3.big: Suffering for the faith was expected, not a sign that something had gone wrong.

3.ctx: Timothy has just returned to Paul with news from Thessalonica.
3.mean: Paul says Timothy has brought good news of their faith and love, and that they long to see him. Now he really lives, since they are standing fast in the Lord. He prays night and day to see them, and that the Lord would make them increase and abound in love and establish their hearts blameless in holiness at the coming of Jesus.
3.big: The church's steadfastness brings Paul new life, and he prays they will grow in love until Christ comes.

4.ctx: Paul turns to instruction. Sexual morality in the Greco-Roman world was loose by Christian standards, and many of these converts had come from paganism.
4.mean: Paul says this is God's will, their sanctification: that they abstain from sexual immorality and each learn to control his own body in holiness and honour, not in the passion of lust like the Gentiles who do not know God. God has not called them to impurity but in holiness. They are to love one another more and more, live quietly, mind their own affairs and work with their hands.
4.big: God's will for his people is their holiness, shown in sexual purity, love and honest work.

4.ctx: Some believers had died, and the church was grieving, perhaps fearing the dead would miss out when Christ returned.
4.mean: Paul says he does not want them to grieve as others do who have no hope. Since Jesus died and rose again, God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep. The Lord himself will descend from heaven with a cry of command, the voice of an archangel and the trumpet of God. The dead in Christ will rise first. Then those who are alive will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so will always be with the Lord. Encourage one another with these words.
4.big: Christians grieve, but with hope, because believers who have died will rise and all will be with the Lord for ever.
4.diff: Verse 17 ('caught up') is the text behind the idea of a 'rapture'. Some Christians, especially dispensationalists, believe believers will be removed secretly before a period of tribulation. Most historic and Reformed interpreters read the passage as describing Christ's single, public return, with believers going out to meet him as citizens went out to welcome a visiting king — and the scene is anything but secret.

5.ctx: Continuing on Christ's return, now on its timing. 'Peace and security' was a slogan of Roman imperial propaganda, which may be what Paul has in mind.
5.mean: Paul says they know the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night. When people say 'peace and security', destruction will come suddenly. But they are children of light and of the day, so they should stay awake and sober, wearing faith and love as a breastplate and the hope of salvation as a helmet. God has not destined them for wrath but to obtain salvation through Jesus, who died for us.
5.big: Believers do not know when Christ will come, so they live ready, as people of the day.

5.ctx: A rapid series of instructions for church life. The church was only months old, with leaders newly appointed after Paul's hurried departure.
5.mean: Paul says respect those who labour among them and are over them in the Lord. Be at peace. Admonish the idle, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, be patient with all. Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in all circumstances, for this is God's will. Do not quench the Spirit; do not despise prophecies, but test everything; hold fast what is good.
5.big: Church life is marked by care for one another, constant prayer and thanksgiving, and discernment.
5.diff: Verses 19–21 bear on the debate about whether prophecy continues today; all agree Paul requires prophecy to be tested.

5.ctx: The closing blessing and instructions. Letters were read aloud in the gathered church, which is why Paul insists this one be read to everyone.
5.mean: Paul prays that the God of peace would sanctify them completely, and that their whole spirit, soul and body be kept blameless at the coming of the Lord Jesus Christ. He who calls them is faithful; he will surely do it. He asks for prayer, and charges them to have the letter read to all the brothers.
5.big: God, who is faithful, will complete the work of making his people holy.
5.diff: 'Spirit, soul and body' has been used to argue that humans have three parts. Most interpreters think Paul is simply emphasising the whole person, not giving a technical anatomy.

1.ctx: Written shortly after 1 Thessalonians, probably from Corinth. Persecution had grown, and confusion about Christ's return had increased.
1.mean: Paul, Silvanus and Timothy give thanks that the Thessalonians' faith is growing and their love increasing, and boast of their steadfastness in all their persecutions.
1.big: Faith that grows under persecution is itself a cause for thanksgiving.
1.diff: Some scholars question whether Paul wrote 2 Thessalonians, because its teaching on the end seems different from the first letter. Many others, including most evangelicals, accept it as Paul's, written to correct misunderstanding of the first.

1.ctx: Paul reassures a church suffering growing persecution. The Old Testament language of fire and angels (Isaiah 66:15) is applied here to Christ's return.
1.mean: Paul says their suffering is evidence of God's righteous judgement. God will repay with affliction those who afflict them, and grant relief when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven with his mighty angels in flaming fire. Those who do not obey the gospel will suffer the punishment of eternal destruction, away from the presence of the Lord.
1.big: God will set things right when Christ returns, bringing relief to his people and judgement on their persecutors.
1.diff: Verse 9 is one of the texts in the debate about the nature of final judgement. The historic view reads 'eternal destruction' as unending punishment; some evangelicals argue for final annihilation. Both take the reality of judgement seriously.

2.ctx: Someone had told the church, perhaps claiming a letter from Paul, that the day of the Lord had already come.
2.mean: Paul says not to be shaken. That day will not come unless the rebellion comes first and the man of lawlessness is revealed, who exalts himself against every so-called god and takes his seat in the temple of God. Something is now restraining him. The Lord Jesus will kill him with the breath of his mouth. His coming will be by the activity of Satan with false signs, and those perishing will believe what is false.
2.big: The end has not yet come, and Christ will certainly overthrow every power that sets itself against God.
2.diff: This is among the most obscure passages in Paul, and he says he had already explained it to them in person. The 'man of lawlessness' has been identified with a future antichrist figure, a Roman emperor, or a recurring pattern of opposition; the 'restrainer' with the Roman state, the preaching of the gospel, the Holy Spirit, or an angel. Honest humility is appropriate here.

2.ctx: In contrast to those deceived, Paul gives thanks for the believers.
2.mean: Paul says God chose them as firstfruits to be saved, through sanctification by the Spirit and belief in the truth, and called them through the gospel to obtain the glory of Christ. So stand firm and hold to the traditions they were taught, by spoken word or by letter.
2.big: God chose and called his people to share Christ's glory, so they must hold fast to the apostolic teaching.
2.diff: 'Chose you... to be saved' is read by Reformed theology as God's election of individuals. 'Traditions' here means the apostolic teaching; Protestants understand it as now preserved in Scripture, while Catholic and Orthodox churches see a wider apostolic tradition alongside Scripture.

3.ctx: The closing section. Paul was in Corinth facing opposition from those who rejected the gospel (Acts 18:5–17), which explains his request for deliverance.
3.mean: Paul asks for prayer that the word of the Lord may spread quickly and that he may be delivered from wicked men. The Lord is faithful; he will establish them and guard them against the evil one.
3.big: The gospel's progress depends on prayer and on the faithfulness of the Lord.

3.ctx: Some in the church had stopped working, perhaps because they thought Christ's return was imminent, and were living off others.
3.mean: Paul says to keep away from any brother walking in idleness. Paul himself worked night and day so as not to be a burden. If anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat. Do not grow weary of doing good. Do not regard the disobedient as an enemy, but warn him as a brother.
3.big: Expecting Christ's return is no excuse for idleness; believers must work and not burden others.
3.diff: Verse 10 addresses those unwilling to work, not those unable to; it is not a verdict on people who cannot find work or cannot work.

3.ctx: Paul adds his own signature, perhaps because of the forged letter mentioned in 2:2.
3.mean: Paul prays that the Lord of peace himself give them peace at all times. He writes the greeting with his own hand as the mark of every genuine letter. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all.
3.big: Paul's own signature guards the church against forged teaching.

1.ctx: Paul had left Timothy, a younger co-worker, in Ephesus to deal with false teachers in the church there. This is the first of the 'Pastoral Letters'.
1.mean: Paul, an apostle by command of God our Saviour and Christ Jesus our hope, greets Timothy, his true child in the faith, with grace, mercy and peace.
1.big: Paul writes to his trusted spiritual son as one sent by God.
1.diff: As with Titus, the authorship of the Pastoral Letters is debated; many scholars think a follower of Paul wrote them, while many evangelical scholars defend Paul's authorship.

1.ctx: False teachers in Ephesus were occupied with myths, genealogies and speculative use of the law.
1.mean: Paul tells Timothy to charge certain people not to teach different doctrine or devote themselves to myths and endless genealogies. The aim of the charge is love from a pure heart, a good conscience and sincere faith. The law is good if used lawfully, for the lawless and disobedient, in accordance with the gospel.
1.big: Sound teaching aims at love, not speculation.

1.ctx: Paul turns to his own conversion as an example of grace. Before becoming a Christian he had arrested believers and approved the execution of Stephen (Acts 7–9).
1.mean: Paul thanks Christ for appointing him, though he was formerly a blasphemer, persecutor and insolent opponent. The saying is trustworthy: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost. He received mercy so that Christ might display his perfect patience as an example to those who would believe.
1.big: If Christ could save Paul, the worst of sinners, he can save anyone.

2.ctx: Instructions for the church's public worship. The emperor at the time was Nero, which makes Paul's call to pray for 'kings and all in high positions' pointed.
2.mean: Paul urges prayers for all people, for kings and all in high positions, so that we may lead peaceful lives. This pleases God our Saviour, who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all.
2.big: The church prays for everyone because there is one God and one mediator, Christ Jesus, who gave himself for all.
2.diff: 'Desires all people to be saved' and 'ransom for all' feature in debates about election and the extent of the atonement. Reformed interpreters often read 'all' as all kinds of people, including the kings just mentioned; others read it as every individual. 'The man Christ Jesus' stresses his humanity as mediator (see Mark 4:35 on the two natures).

2.ctx: Instructions about women in public worship, one of the most debated passages in the New Testament.
2.mean: Paul says women should adorn themselves modestly, with good works rather than elaborate display. A woman should learn quietly with all submissiveness. He does not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man; she is to remain quiet. He gives reasons from creation — Adam was formed first — and from the fall. She will be saved through childbearing if they continue in faith, love and holiness.
2.big: Paul grounds instructions about men and women in worship in the order of creation.
2.diff: Complementarian churches, including most Reformed churches and this group, read verse 12 as restricting the church's authoritative teaching office to qualified men, since Paul grounds it in creation. Egalitarian scholars read it as addressing a specific situation in Ephesus, such as false teaching spreading among women. 'Saved through childbearing' is obscure, with readings including Christ's birth, women's ordinary calling, or safe delivery. Nothing here concerns women's worth or standing before God.

3.ctx: The church in Ephesus needed trustworthy leaders to replace or resist the false teachers.
3.mean: Paul says aspiring to be an overseer is a noble task. An overseer must be above reproach, the husband of one wife, sober-minded, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach, not a drunkard, not violent but gentle, not quarrelsome, not a lover of money. He must manage his own household well, not be a recent convert, and be well thought of by outsiders.
3.big: Church leaders must be men of proven character, able to teach, whose homes show how they would care for God's church.
3.diff: As at Titus 1, 'husband of one wife' is read variously; the most common reading is marital faithfulness. 'Overseer' and 'elder' appear to be the same office in the New Testament.

3.ctx: The second recognised office in the church, serving practical needs.
3.mean: Paul says deacons likewise must be dignified, not double-tongued, not addicted to wine or greedy, holding the mystery of the faith with a clear conscience, and tested first. The women likewise must be dignified and faithful. Deacons must manage their households well.
3.big: Those who serve the church practically must share the same godly character as its leaders.
3.diff: 'The women' in verse 11 may be deacons' wives or women deacons; the Greek allows either. Phoebe is called a deacon in Romans 16:1. Churches differ on whether women may be deacons.

3.ctx: Paul explains why he has written these instructions: he hopes to visit, but may be delayed. The temple of Artemis in Ephesus was renowned for its great pillars.
3.mean: Paul says he writes so that Timothy may know how to behave in the household of God, the church of the living God, a pillar and buttress of the truth. Great indeed is the mystery of godliness: he was manifested in the flesh, vindicated by the Spirit, seen by angels, proclaimed among the nations, believed on in the world, taken up in glory.
3.big: The church exists to uphold the truth about Christ, who came in the flesh and was taken up in glory.
3.diff: Verse 16 is probably an early hymn. 'Manifested in the flesh' affirms the incarnation; some later manuscripts read 'God was manifested', but the best manuscripts read 'He who'.

4.ctx: Paul returns to the false teachers, who taught a harsh asceticism.
4.mean: Paul says the Spirit says that in later times some will depart from the faith, devoting themselves to deceitful spirits and teachings of demons, forbidding marriage and requiring abstinence from foods that God created to be received with thanksgiving. Everything created by God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if received with thanksgiving.
4.big: Rejecting God's good gifts of marriage and food is false teaching, not superior holiness.

4.ctx: Paul instructs Timothy on his own conduct. Timothy was probably in his thirties, young for a leader in a culture that honoured age.
4.mean: Paul says a good servant of Christ Jesus is trained in the words of faith and good doctrine. Have nothing to do with silly myths; train yourself for godliness, which is of value in every way. Let no one despise you for your youth, but set an example in speech, conduct, love, faith and purity. Devote yourself to public reading of Scripture, exhortation and teaching. Keep a close watch on yourself and on the teaching.
4.big: A minister's first duty is to guard his own life and his teaching.
4.h: A Good Servant of Jesus Christ

5.ctx: Practical instruction for relating to different members of the church family.
5.mean: Paul says not to rebuke an older man but encourage him as a father, younger men as brothers, older women as mothers, younger women as sisters, in all purity.
5.big: The church is a family, and its members are to be treated as such.

5.ctx: Widows without family had no social support in the ancient world; the church had taken on their care, which had become complicated.
5.mean: Paul says honour widows who are truly widows. Children and grandchildren should care for their own relatives; anyone who does not provide for his household has denied the faith. The church should support widows over sixty with a record of good works, while younger widows should remarry. Believers should care for their own widows so the church is not burdened.
5.big: Families must care for their own, and the church for those who have no one else.

5.ctx: Instructions about how the church treats its elders, apparently needed because some elders in Ephesus had fallen into error or faced accusations.
5.mean: Paul says elders who rule well are worthy of double honour, especially those who labour in preaching and teaching; the worker deserves his wages. Do not admit a charge against an elder except on the evidence of two or three witnesses. Those who persist in sin should be rebuked publicly. Do not be hasty in laying on hands.
5.big: Faithful elders should be supported and protected from false accusation, and held accountable when they sin.
5.diff: Verse 17 has been read as distinguishing 'ruling elders' from 'teaching elders', a distinction in Presbyterian church order. Verse 18 quotes Luke 10:7 alongside Deuteronomy as 'Scripture'.

5.ctx: A solemn personal charge, with practical asides. Water in the ancient world was often unsafe, and wine was widely used medicinally.
5.mean: Paul charges Timothy before God, Christ Jesus and the elect angels to keep these rules without prejudice or partiality. He advises him to use a little wine for his stomach. The sins of some are obvious; others appear later. Good works too cannot remain hidden.
5.big: Leaders must act impartially, knowing that the truth about everyone will eventually come out.

6.ctx: Instruction to Christian slaves, including those with believing masters.
6.mean: Paul says slaves should regard their masters as worthy of honour, so that God's name and the teaching may not be reviled. Those with believing masters must not be disrespectful because they are brothers, but serve all the better.
6.big: Believers' conduct in every station of life should adorn the gospel.
6.diff: As elsewhere in the New Testament, the instruction regulates an existing institution rather than approving it.

6.ctx: Paul returns to the false teachers of chapter 1 and exposes their motives. Travelling teachers could make a good living from their followers.
6.mean: Paul says anyone who teaches a different doctrine is puffed up and understands nothing, with an unhealthy craving for controversy, imagining that godliness is a means of gain.
6.big: False teaching is often driven by pride and love of money.

6.ctx: Following directly from the warning against treating godliness as gain.
6.mean: Paul says godliness with contentment is great gain; we brought nothing into the world, and we cannot take anything out. Those who desire to be rich fall into temptation and harmful desires. The love of money is a root of all kinds of evils; some have wandered from the faith through it.
6.big: Contentment with God is true gain, and the love of money leads people away from faith.
6.diff: Verse 10 is often misquoted as 'money is the root of all evil'. Paul says the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil.

6.ctx: Paul turns directly to Timothy. 'Man of God' was a title used of Old Testament prophets such as Moses and Elijah.
6.mean: Paul says flee these things; pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, steadfastness, gentleness. Fight the good fight of the faith; take hold of eternal life. Keep the commandment until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ, whom God will display — the King of kings and Lord of lords, who alone has immortality and dwells in unapproachable light.
6.big: Timothy is to flee greed, pursue godliness and hold fast until Christ appears.

6.ctx: A charge to wealthy believers. Ephesus was one of the richest cities in the Roman world, and the church included people of means.
6.mean: Paul says to charge the rich not to be haughty or set their hopes on uncertain riches, but on God, who richly provides everything to enjoy. They are to do good, be rich in good works, be generous and ready to share, storing up treasure as a good foundation for the future.
6.big: Wealth is to be enjoyed as God's gift and used generously, not trusted.

6.ctx: The closing charge, returning to the letter's main concern. 'Knowledge' (gnosis) may point to early forms of the teaching later called Gnosticism.
6.mean: Paul says O Timothy, guard the deposit entrusted to you. Avoid irreverent babble and contradictions of what is falsely called knowledge, by which some have swerved from the faith. Grace be with you.
6.big: The apostolic faith is a trust to be guarded, not improved upon.

1.ctx: Paul writes from prison in Rome, expecting execution. This is probably the last letter of his we have, written to Timothy around AD 64–67.
1.mean: Paul, an apostle by the will of God according to the promise of life in Christ Jesus, greets Timothy, his beloved child.
1.big: Facing death, Paul writes of the promise of life in Christ.
1.diff: As with the other Pastoral Letters, authorship is debated; the letter's personal detail is often cited in support of Paul's authorship.

1.ctx: Paul remembers Timothy with deep affection, and Timothy's own family background of faith.
1.mean: Paul says he remembers Timothy's tears and longs to see him. He recalls the sincere faith that dwelt first in his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice. He tells him to fan into flame the gift of God, for God gave us a spirit not of fear but of power, love and self-control. Do not be ashamed of the testimony about our Lord, nor of me his prisoner, but share in suffering for the gospel, by the power of God, who saved us and called us, not because of our works but because of his own purpose and grace given us in Christ Jesus before the ages began.
1.big: Timothy must not be ashamed of the gospel, because God, who saved by his own grace, gives power to endure.
1.diff: Reformed theology draws on verse 9 for God's eternal purpose of grace in salvation, given in Christ before time began.

1.ctx: Paul contrasts those who have deserted him with one who stood by him.
1.mean: Paul says to follow the pattern of sound words and guard the good deposit by the Holy Spirit who dwells in us. All in Asia have turned away from him. But Onesiphorus often refreshed him, was not ashamed of his chains, and searched for him in Rome until he found him.
1.big: Faithfulness is shown in guarding the truth and in standing by those who suffer for it.

2.ctx: Paul prepares Timothy to carry on after his death, using several images of endurance.
2.mean: Paul says be strengthened by the grace in Christ Jesus. Entrust what you have heard to faithful men who will be able to teach others also. Share in suffering as a good soldier; an athlete competes by the rules; a farmer works hard. Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead. The saying is trustworthy: if we have died with him, we will also live with him; if we endure, we will reign with him; if we deny him, he will deny us; if we are faithless, he remains faithful, for he cannot deny himself.
2.big: The gospel is passed on through faithful endurance, grounded in Christ who remains faithful.
2.diff: Verse 2 describes four generations of teaching — Paul, Timothy, faithful men, others — and is often taken as a pattern for training leaders, which fits this group's approach to developing brothers to lead.

2.ctx: Instruction on Timothy's conduct as a teacher amid controversy.
2.mean: Paul says do your best to present yourself to God as one approved, a worker who has no need to be ashamed, rightly handling the word of truth. Avoid irreverent babble. The Lord knows those who are his. Flee youthful passions and pursue righteousness, faith, love and peace. The Lord's servant must not be quarrelsome but kind to everyone, able to teach, patiently enduring evil, correcting opponents with gentleness. God may perhaps grant them repentance.
2.big: A faithful teacher handles God's word rightly and corrects opponents gently, hoping God will bring them to repentance.
2.diff: Verse 25 ('God may perhaps grant them repentance') is one of the texts Reformed theology cites for repentance itself being God's gift.

3.ctx: Paul describes the character of 'the last days', which in the New Testament means the whole period between Christ's first and second comings.
3.mean: Paul says in the last days there will come times of difficulty. People will be lovers of self, lovers of money, proud, abusive, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, unholy, heartless, lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God, having the appearance of godliness but denying its power. Avoid such people.
3.big: Religion without real godliness is a mark of the age, and must be recognised and avoided.

3.ctx: A contrast between the false teachers and Timothy's own formation.
3.mean: Paul reminds Timothy that he has followed Paul's teaching, conduct, faith, patience, love and sufferings. All who desire to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted. Continue in what you have learned, knowing from whom you learned it, and that from childhood you have been acquainted with the sacred writings, which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus. All Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable for teaching, reproof, correction and training in righteousness, that the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work.
3.big: Scripture comes from God himself and fully equips his people for salvation and for every good work.
3.diff: Verse 16 is the foundational text for the doctrine of the inspiration of Scripture. 'Breathed out by God' means Scripture originates from God. Christians differ in how they express its reliability — terms such as 'inerrant' and 'infallible' are used with somewhat different meanings — but this group holds, with the historic evangelical position, that Scripture is fully God's word and our final authority.

4.ctx: Paul's final charge to Timothy, written as he faces death under Nero. The language is formal and solemn, like a legal charge before witnesses.
4.mean: Paul charges Timothy in the presence of God and Christ Jesus: preach the word; be ready in season and out of season; reprove, rebuke and exhort with complete patience and teaching. The time is coming when people will not endure sound teaching, but accumulate teachers to suit their passions. Do the work of an evangelist. As for Paul, he is already being poured out as a drink offering. He has fought the good fight, finished the race, kept the faith. There is laid up for him the crown of righteousness, and not only for him but for all who have loved Christ's appearing.
4.big: Facing death, Paul hands on the charge to preach the word faithfully, whatever the response.

4.ctx: Personal requests from a Roman prison, where prisoners depended on friends for food, clothing and company. Winter in a stone cell would have been cold.
4.mean: Paul asks Timothy to come soon. Demas has deserted him, in love with this present world. Only Luke is with him. Bring Mark, for he is very useful. Bring the cloak left at Troas, and the books, especially the parchments.
4.big: Even the great apostle needed friends, warmth and books in his last days.
4.diff: Paul's request for Mark, whom he once refused to take on a journey (Acts 15:37–39), shows reconciliation.

4.ctx: Paul reflects on his 'first defence', a preliminary hearing in his trial, at which none of his supporters appeared on his behalf.
4.mean: Paul says at his first defence no one came to stand by him; all deserted him — may it not be charged against them. But the Lord stood by him and strengthened him, so that the message might be fully proclaimed. The Lord will rescue him from every evil deed and bring him safely into his heavenly kingdom.
4.big: When everyone else deserted him, the Lord stood by him.

4.ctx: The final greetings of what is probably Paul's last letter. Prisca and Aquila had worked with Paul in Corinth, Ephesus and Rome.
4.mean: Paul greets Prisca and Aquila and the household of Onesiphorus. He asks Timothy to come before winter. The Lord be with your spirit. Grace be with you.
4.big: Paul's last recorded words are grace.

1.ctx: Hebrews was written to Jewish Christians, probably before the temple's destruction in AD 70, who were under pressure and tempted to drift back from Christ to the familiar forms of Judaism. The author is unnamed.
1.mean: The writer says God spoke long ago through the prophets in many ways, but in these last days has spoken by his Son, whom he appointed heir of all things and through whom he created the world. The Son is the radiance of God's glory and the exact imprint of his nature, upholding the universe by his word. After making purification for sins, he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high. He is superior to the angels: a chain of seven Old Testament quotations shows that God calls him Son, commands angels to worship him, addresses him as 'God' whose throne is for ever (Psalm 45), and speaks to him as the Lord who laid the foundation of the earth (Psalm 102).
1.big: God's final and fullest word is his Son, who shares God's very nature and is far above the angels.
1.diff: The author is unknown; suggestions have included Paul, Barnabas, Apollos and Priscilla. The early church father Origen concluded that only God knows. Verses 8 and 10–12 are among the clearest New Testament texts applying the title 'God' and Old Testament words about the LORD to the Son.

2.ctx: The first of several warning passages woven through the letter, each tied to the teaching just given.
2.mean: The writer says we must pay much closer attention to what we have heard, lest we drift away. If the message given through angels (the law) proved reliable and every transgression received just punishment, how shall we escape if we neglect such a great salvation, declared first by the Lord and confirmed by those who heard him, with God bearing witness by signs and gifts of the Holy Spirit?
2.big: If disobeying the law brought judgement, neglecting the salvation Christ brings is far more serious.

2.ctx: The writer turns from Christ's divine glory to his true humanity.
2.mean: The writer quotes Psalm 8: what is man, that you are mindful of him? You made him a little lower than the angels and put everything under his feet. We do not yet see everything subject to humanity, but we see Jesus, made for a little while lower than the angels, crowned with glory because of the suffering of death, so that by God's grace he might taste death for everyone. He is not ashamed to call them brothers. Since the children share in flesh and blood, he himself likewise partook of the same, that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, the devil. He had to be made like his brothers in every respect, so that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest to make propitiation for the sins of the people. Because he himself has suffered when tempted, he is able to help those who are being tempted.
2.big: The Son became fully human, like his brothers in every respect, so that he could die for them and help them.
2.diff: Chapters 1 and 2 together are one of the clearest biblical foundations for the church's teaching that Christ is fully God and fully man in one person (see Mark 4:35). His real humanity is not incidental: it is necessary for him to die, to be our priest and to sympathise with us.

3.ctx: Moses was the most honoured figure in Judaism, the one through whom the law came.
3.mean: The writer says to consider Jesus, the apostle and high priest of our confession. Moses was faithful in all God's house as a servant, but Christ is faithful over God's house as a Son. And we are his house, if we hold fast our confidence and boasting in our hope.
3.big: Jesus is greater than Moses as a son is greater than a servant in the household.
3.h: Jesus Our Apostle and High Priest

3.ctx: A long quotation of Psalm 95, which recalls Israel's rebellion in the wilderness.
3.mean: The writer introduces Psalm 95 with 'as the Holy Spirit says': today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts as in the rebellion, when your fathers put me to the test for forty years, so I swore in my wrath, they shall not enter my rest.
3.big: Scripture speaks with a present voice — 'today' — and warns against the hardness that kept Israel out of the promised land.
3.diff: The writer attributes the psalm directly to the Holy Spirit speaking now, one of several places in Hebrews that treat Scripture as the Spirit's own voice (compare 10:15).

3.ctx: The writer applies Psalm 95 directly to his readers, who were in danger of the same hardening that kept Israel's wilderness generation out of the promised land.
3.mean: The writer says take care that none of you has an evil, unbelieving heart, leading you to fall away from the living God. Exhort one another every day, as long as it is called 'today', that none may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin. We share in Christ if we hold our original confidence firm to the end. The wilderness generation could not enter because of unbelief.
3.big: Believers guard one another against hardening by daily encouragement.
3.diff: Verse 13's call to exhort one another daily sits close to the group's anchor text in chapter 10.

4.ctx: The argument about Israel's failure to enter the land continues, applied to the rest God offers now.
4.mean: The writer says the promise of entering God's rest still stands. Joshua did not give them rest, or God would not have spoken later of another day. So there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God. Whoever has entered God's rest has rested from his works as God did from his. Let us strive to enter that rest.
4.big: God's true rest, pictured by the Sabbath and the promised land, is still open to those who believe.
4.diff: Christians differ over whether 'Sabbath rest' here bears on Sunday observance, or refers wholly to the eternal rest of salvation. Most interpreters read it chiefly as salvation — rest begun now by faith and completed in the age to come.

4.ctx: A short, famous passage on God's word, followed by the introduction of Christ's priesthood.
4.mean: The writer says the word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword, discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart. No creature is hidden from his sight. Since we have a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus, the Son of God, let us hold fast our confession. We do not have a high priest unable to sympathise with our weaknesses, but one who in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin. Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need.
4.big: Because our high priest was tempted as we are yet without sin, believers can approach God's throne with confidence.
4.diff: Verse 15 — tempted in every way yet without sin — is central to the church's teaching on Christ's true humanity (see Mark 4:35). Whether Christ could have sinned is a question theologians have discussed; the text's point is that his temptation was real and his sympathy genuine.

5.ctx: The writer explains what a high priest is, in the terms of the Old Testament priesthood.
5.mean: The writer says every high priest is chosen from among men to act on their behalf before God, offering gifts and sacrifices. He can deal gently with the ignorant because he too is beset with weakness. No one takes this honour for himself. So Christ did not exalt himself but was appointed by God, a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek (Psalm 110:4). In the days of his flesh, Jesus offered prayers with loud cries and tears to him who was able to save him from death, and was heard. Although he was a son, he learned obedience through what he suffered.
5.big: Jesus is a true high priest, appointed by God and made perfect through suffering.
5.diff: 'Learned obedience' does not mean he was ever disobedient, but that he experienced the full cost of obedience as a man — part of his genuine humanity.

5.ctx: The writer breaks off from Melchizedek to rebuke his readers.
5.mean: The writer says there is much to say, but they have become dull of hearing. By now they ought to be teachers, but they need someone to teach them the basics again. They need milk, not solid food. Solid food is for the mature, who have trained their powers of discernment.
5.big: Believers are meant to grow up in understanding, not stay on spiritual milk.

6.ctx: One of the most difficult and discussed passages in the New Testament.
6.mean: The writer urges them to go on to maturity. For it is impossible, in the case of those who have once been enlightened, tasted the heavenly gift, shared in the Holy Spirit, tasted the goodness of God's word and the powers of the age to come, and then have fallen away, to restore them again to repentance, since they are crucifying the Son of God once again. Land that bears only thorns is near to being cursed. Yet the writer is sure of better things in their case, things that belong to salvation.
6.big: The warning is severe because turning away from Christ after knowing him is the most serious danger there is.
6.diff: Christians have read this passage in several ways. Reformed interpreters generally hold that it describes people who experienced much of the church's life without genuine regeneration, or that it is a real warning God uses to keep true believers persevering. Arminian interpreters read it as describing genuine believers who can finally fall away. A third view sees it as hypothetical. The writer's own conclusion in verse 9 — 'we are sure of better things in your case' — should be read with it.

6.ctx: The writer grounds hope in God's own promise and oath. In the ancient world an oath sworn by a greater authority settled a dispute; God, having none greater, swore by himself (Genesis 22:16).
6.mean: The writer says when God made a promise to Abraham, since he had no one greater to swear by, he swore by himself. By two unchangeable things — his promise and his oath — in which it is impossible for God to lie, we have strong encouragement to hold fast to the hope set before us. We have this as a sure and steadfast anchor of the soul, a hope that enters the inner place behind the curtain, where Jesus has gone as a forerunner on our behalf.
6.big: Believers' hope is anchored in God's unbreakable promise and in Jesus, who has gone before them into God's presence.
6.diff: Verse 19 is the verse behind the Community of Brothers' anchor emblem.

7.ctx: Melchizedek appears briefly in Genesis 14 as king of Salem and priest of God Most High, who blessed Abraham.
7.mean: The writer says Melchizedek, whose name means king of righteousness, received a tenth from Abraham and blessed him. He appears without father, mother or genealogy, resembling the Son of God, and continues a priest for ever. Even Levi, in a sense, paid tithes through Abraham, so Melchizedek is greater than the Levitical priests.
7.big: Melchizedek foreshadows a priesthood greater than Israel's.
7.diff: Some have thought Melchizedek was an appearance of Christ himself before the incarnation. Most interpreters read the writer as saying he resembles the Son because Scripture records no beginning or end for him, not that he literally had none.

7.ctx: The writer argues that a new priesthood means the old system was never final.
7.mean: The writer says if perfection had been attainable through the Levitical priesthood, there would have been no need for another priest after the order of Melchizedek. Jesus became a priest not by physical descent but by the power of an indestructible life. The former priests were many, because death prevented them from continuing; but he holds his priesthood permanently, and so he is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him, since he always lives to make intercession for them. He offered one sacrifice once for all when he offered up himself.
7.big: Jesus' priesthood is permanent and his sacrifice complete, so he saves completely those who come to God through him.

8.ctx: The writer summarises his main point so far. The tabernacle was built to a pattern Moses was shown on the mountain (Exodus 25:40), which Hebrews reads as a copy of the heavenly reality.
8.mean: The writer says we have such a high priest, seated at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in heaven, a minister in the true tent that the Lord set up, not man. The earthly priests serve a copy and shadow of the heavenly things.
8.big: Christ serves in the true sanctuary, of which the earthly one was only a copy.

8.ctx: The longest Old Testament quotation in the New Testament, from Jeremiah 31:31–34.
8.mean: The writer says Christ's ministry is as much more excellent as the covenant he mediates is better. If the first covenant had been faultless, there would have been no need for a second. God promised a new covenant: I will put my laws into their minds and write them on their hearts; they shall all know me; I will remember their sins no more. In speaking of a new covenant, he makes the first one obsolete.
8.big: Christ mediates the new covenant God promised, which writes his law on hearts and fully forgives sin.

9.ctx: The writer describes the tabernacle, the portable sanctuary of Israel's wilderness years, as laid out in Exodus.
9.mean: The writer describes the Holy Place and the Most Holy Place, into which only the high priest went, once a year, not without blood, for his own sins and the people's. The Holy Spirit indicates by this that the way into the holy places was not yet opened. The sacrifices could not perfect the conscience.
9.big: The old system, by its very design, showed that the way to God was not yet open.

9.ctx: The heart of the letter's argument about Christ's sacrifice.
9.mean: The writer says Christ entered once for all into the holy places, not by the blood of goats and calves but by his own blood, securing an eternal redemption. How much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, purify our conscience to serve the living God. Without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness of sins. He appeared once for all at the end of the ages to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself. Just as it is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgement, so Christ, having been offered once to bear the sins of many, will appear a second time to save those eagerly waiting for him.
9.big: Christ's one sacrifice of himself accomplishes what all the old sacrifices could only picture: eternal redemption.
9.diff: Verse 14 names the Father, the Son and the eternal Spirit together in the one act of Christ's self-offering.

10.ctx: The conclusion of the argument about sacrifice begun in chapter 7. If the temple was still standing, sacrifices were still being offered daily as the writer wrote.
10.mean: The writer says the law is only a shadow of good things to come; its repeated sacrifices could never make perfect those who draw near, for it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins. So Christ said, quoting Psalm 40: 'a body you have prepared for me; I have come to do your will.' By that will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all. Every priest stands daily offering the same sacrifices; but Christ offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins and sat down at God's right hand. By a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified. The Holy Spirit bears witness in Jeremiah's words: I will remember their sins no more.
10.big: Christ's single sacrifice, once for all, has done what endlessly repeated sacrifices never could.
10.diff: The phrase 'a body you have prepared for me' makes the incarnation essential to the atonement. The contrast between priests who stand and Christ who sits expresses a finished work. Protestants have drawn on this passage in disagreeing with the Catholic understanding of the Mass as a sacrifice; Catholic theology holds that the Mass re-presents rather than repeats Christ's one sacrifice.

10.ctx: The practical application of everything since 4:14, and the passage from which the Community of Brothers takes its name and shape (verses 23–25).
10.mean: The writer says since we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way he opened through the curtain — his flesh — and since we have a great priest, let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith. Let us hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering, for he who promised is faithful. Let us consider how to stir up one another to love and good works, not neglecting to meet together, as is the habit of some, but encouraging one another, and all the more as you see the Day drawing near. Then comes another warning: if we go on sinning deliberately after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins. The writer recalls their earlier endurance under persecution and says: do not throw away your confidence; we are not of those who shrink back and are destroyed, but of those who have faith.
10.big: Because Christ has opened the way to God, believers must draw near, hold fast and meet together to encourage one another.
10.diff: Verses 26–31 raise the same questions as chapter 6. Reformed interpreters generally read them as describing deliberate, final rejection of Christ by those who never truly belonged, or as a warning God uses to preserve his people; others see a real possibility of falling away. The writer again ends with confidence (verse 39).

11.ctx: The famous chapter on faith, often called the 'hall of faith', listing Old Testament examples.
11.mean: The writer says faith is the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen. By faith we understand that the universe was created by the word of God, so that what is seen was not made out of things that are visible.
11.big: Faith is confident trust in what God has promised but cannot yet be seen.
11.diff: Verse 1 is less a full definition than a description of faith's character as the chapter will illustrate it.

11.ctx: The first examples come from Genesis 4–6, before the flood: Abel, Enoch and Noah, figures from the very beginning of the biblical story.
11.mean: The writer says by faith Abel offered a more acceptable sacrifice than Cain. By faith Enoch was taken up and did not see death, for he pleased God. Without faith it is impossible to please him, for whoever would draw near to God must believe that he exists and that he rewards those who seek him. By faith Noah built an ark.
11.big: From the beginning, people have pleased God by trusting him.
11.h: The Faith of Abel, Enoch, Noah

11.ctx: The longest single example is Abraham, whom Jewish readers honoured as the father of their nation, and whom Paul also presents as the father of faith (Romans 4).
11.mean: The writer says by faith Abraham obeyed when called to go out, not knowing where he was going. He lived as a stranger in the land of promise, looking forward to the city whose designer and builder is God. By faith Sarah received power to conceive. These all died in faith, not having received the things promised, but seeing them from afar, and acknowledging that they were strangers and exiles on the earth, desiring a better country, a heavenly one. By faith Abraham offered up Isaac, considering that God was able even to raise him from the dead.
11.big: Faith obeys God's call and lives as a stranger on earth, looking for the city God is building.
11.h: The Faith of Abraham and Sarah

11.ctx: The patriarchs at the end of their lives, from Genesis 27–50. Each blessing or instruction looked forward to promises none of them lived to see fulfilled.
11.mean: The writer says by faith Isaac blessed Jacob and Esau, by faith Jacob blessed the sons of Joseph, and by faith Joseph, at the end of his life, gave directions about his bones, confident Israel would leave Egypt.
11.big: Faith looks beyond death to God's future promises.
11.h: The Faith of Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph

11.ctx: Moses, the central figure of the old covenant, raised in Pharaoh's court with every advantage Egypt could give (Exodus 2; Acts 7:22).
11.mean: The writer says by faith Moses' parents hid him. By faith Moses refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter, choosing to be mistreated with the people of God rather than enjoy the fleeting pleasures of sin. He considered the reproach of Christ greater wealth than the treasures of Egypt. By faith he kept the Passover and crossed the Red Sea.
11.big: Faith chooses suffering with God's people over the passing pleasures of sin.

11.ctx: The chapter accelerates, moving from Joshua and the conquest through the judges, the kings, the prophets and the martyrs of the period between the Testaments.
11.mean: The writer says by faith the walls of Jericho fell, and Rahab the prostitute did not perish. Time would fail to tell of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel and the prophets, who conquered kingdoms, shut the mouths of lions and escaped the sword. Others were tortured, mocked, flogged, stoned, sawn in two, went about destitute — of whom the world was not worthy. All these, though commended through their faith, did not receive what was promised, since God had provided something better for us, that apart from us they should not be made perfect.
11.big: Faith sometimes brings deliverance and sometimes brings suffering, and both are commended by God.
11.diff: The list includes deeply flawed figures such as Samson and Jephthah, which shows the chapter commends their faith, not everything they did.

12.ctx: The 'cloud of witnesses' refers back to the heroes of chapter 11. The image is of a race run in a crowded stadium.
12.mean: The writer says since we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight and sin which clings so closely, and run with endurance the race set before us, looking to Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith, who for the joy set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is seated at the right hand of the throne of God. Consider him, so that you may not grow weary.
12.big: Believers run the race of faith by keeping their eyes on Jesus, who ran it first.

12.ctx: The readers had faced public insult, imprisonment and confiscation of property (10:32–34), but not yet martyrdom. The Roman persecution under Nero may have been approaching.
12.mean: The writer says in their struggle against sin they have not yet resisted to the point of shedding blood. They have forgotten the exhortation: do not regard lightly the discipline of the Lord, for the Lord disciplines the one he loves (Proverbs 3). God is treating them as sons. For the moment all discipline seems painful, but later it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those trained by it.
12.big: Hardship, received rightly, is the loving training of a Father, not a sign of his absence.
12.diff: Not all suffering in Scripture is discipline for particular sin; the writer presents hardship as training that God uses for his children's good.

12.ctx: Practical warnings drawn from the argument. The story of Esau selling his birthright for a meal comes from Genesis 25:29–34.
12.mean: The writer says strive for peace with everyone, and for the holiness without which no one will see the Lord. See that no one fails to obtain the grace of God, that no root of bitterness springs up, that no one is like Esau, who sold his birthright for a single meal and later found no chance to repent, though he sought it with tears.
12.big: Holiness and perseverance in grace matter, as Esau's example shows.
12.diff: Esau's tears are read by most interpreters as regret over lost blessing rather than genuine repentance toward God.

12.ctx: A contrast between Mount Sinai and Mount Zion, between the old covenant and the new.
12.mean: The writer says you have not come to a mountain that may be touched, a blazing fire and darkness, where even Moses trembled. You have come to Mount Zion, the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, to innumerable angels, to the assembly of the firstborn, to God the judge of all, and to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant, whose sprinkled blood speaks a better word than the blood of Abel. See that you do not refuse him who is speaking. Since we are receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken, let us offer acceptable worship with reverence and awe, for our God is a consuming fire.
12.big: Believers have come not to the terror of Sinai but to the joyful assembly of heaven, which calls for grateful, reverent worship.

13.ctx: Practical instructions for the community's life together. Travelling believers relied on hospitality, and imprisoned Christians depended on others for food and support.
13.mean: The writer says let brotherly love continue. Do not neglect hospitality to strangers, for some have entertained angels unawares. Remember those in prison and those mistreated. Let marriage be held in honour among all, and the marriage bed undefiled.
13.big: Brotherly love shows itself in hospitality, care for sufferers and faithfulness in marriage.

13.ctx: The instructions ground themselves in Christ's unchanging faithfulness.
13.mean: The writer says keep your life free from love of money, and be content, for he has said, 'I will never leave you nor forsake you.' Remember your leaders who spoke to you the word of God, and imitate their faith. Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and for ever. Do not be led away by diverse and strange teachings. We have an altar from which those who serve the tent have no right to eat. Jesus suffered outside the gate; let us go to him outside the camp and bear the reproach he endured. For here we have no lasting city, but we seek the city that is to come.
13.big: Because Christ never changes and never leaves, believers can be content and bear reproach for him.

13.ctx: The sacrifices believers now offer. With Christ's once-for-all sacrifice complete, the writer names the offerings that remain for God's people.
13.mean: The writer says through him let us continually offer a sacrifice of praise to God, the fruit of lips that acknowledge his name. Do not neglect to do good and to share what you have, for such sacrifices are pleasing to God. Obey your leaders, for they keep watch over your souls, as those who will have to give an account. Pray for us.
13.big: The old sacrifices are replaced by praise, generosity and faithful submission to godly leaders.

13.ctx: One of the most loved benedictions in Scripture, and the letter's closing.
13.mean: The writer prays that the God of peace, who brought again from the dead our Lord Jesus, the great shepherd of the sheep, by the blood of the eternal covenant, would equip them with everything good to do his will, working in us what is pleasing in his sight. He mentions Timothy's release and sends greetings from those from Italy.
13.big: The God who raised the great shepherd will equip his people to do his will.
13.diff: The mention of Timothy and 'those from Italy' has led many to link the letter with Paul's circle and possibly with Rome.

1.ctx: Corinth was a wealthy, cosmopolitan port city in Greece, notorious for immorality. Paul founded the church around AD 50 and wrote this letter from Ephesus about AD 54, answering reports and a letter from the church.
1.mean: Paul and Sosthenes greet the church of God in Corinth, those sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints, together with all who call on the name of the Lord Jesus Christ in every place.
1.big: A church full of problems is still addressed as God's holy people.
1.diff: Calling on 'the name of the Lord' was Old Testament language for worshipping God (Joel 2:32); Paul applies it to Jesus.

1.ctx: Paul's thanksgiving, even for a troubled church, prepares for the issues he will raise.
1.mean: Paul thanks God for the grace given them in Christ, enriched in all speech and knowledge, lacking no gift as they wait for Christ's revealing. God will sustain them to the end, guiltless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ. God is faithful, by whom they were called into the fellowship of his Son.
1.big: God's faithfulness, not the church's performance, guarantees that he will finish what he began.

1.ctx: The first problem Paul addresses: factions formed around favourite leaders, as Greek philosophers attracted rival followings.
1.mean: Paul appeals for unity and no divisions. Some say 'I follow Paul', others 'Apollos', 'Cephas' or 'Christ'. Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? He is thankful he baptised few of them, for Christ sent him not to baptise but to preach the gospel, not with words of eloquent wisdom, lest the cross be emptied of its power.
1.big: Loyalty to human leaders divides the church, which belongs to Christ alone.

1.ctx: Corinthian believers apparently prized rhetoric and philosophical wisdom, and some felt embarrassed by a crucified Messiah.
1.mean: Paul says the word of the cross is folly to those perishing, but to those being saved it is the power of God. Jews demand signs and Greeks seek wisdom, but we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles, but to those who are called, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God. The foolishness of God is wiser than men.
1.big: The cross looks like weakness and foolishness, but it is God's power and wisdom for salvation.

1.ctx: Paul points to the church's own membership as evidence. Corinth's church included a few wealthy people, but most were ordinary workers, freedmen and slaves.
1.mean: Paul says not many of them were wise, powerful or of noble birth. God chose what is foolish, weak, low and despised to shame the wise and strong, so that no one may boast before him. Because of him they are in Christ Jesus, who became to us wisdom from God, righteousness, sanctification and redemption. Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord.
1.big: God chooses the unimpressive so that all glory goes to him and all boasting is in Christ.
1.diff: Reformed theology draws on verses 26–30 for God's sovereign, gracious choice — the church's very existence is 'because of him'.

2.ctx: Paul contrasts his own preaching in Corinth with the polished speakers the Corinthians admired.
2.mean: Paul says he did not come with lofty speech or wisdom, but decided to know nothing among them except Jesus Christ and him crucified. He came in weakness and fear, and his message was in demonstration of the Spirit and of power, so that their faith might rest not in human wisdom but in the power of God.
2.big: Faith that rests on God's power, not on persuasive technique, is the kind that lasts.
2.h: Paul's Message by the Spirit's Power

2.ctx: Paul turns to the true wisdom God gives through the Spirit, in contrast to the Greek wisdom the Corinthians prized. 'Mature' may echo the language of mystery religions, reclaimed for the gospel.
2.mean: Paul says there is a wisdom he imparts to the mature, a secret and hidden wisdom of God, which none of the rulers of this age understood, or they would not have crucified the Lord of glory. What no eye has seen, God has revealed through the Spirit, for the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God. The natural person does not accept the things of the Spirit, for they are folly to him and spiritually discerned. We have the mind of Christ.
2.big: God's wisdom is understood only by the Spirit's revealing work.
2.diff: Verse 14 is cited in Reformed theology for the need of the Spirit's work before anyone can receive the gospel. 'The Lord of glory' in verse 8 is a divine title applied to the crucified Jesus.

3.ctx: Paul returns to the factions of chapter 1. Apollos was an eloquent Jewish preacher from Alexandria who had ministered in Corinth after Paul (Acts 18:24–28).
3.mean: Paul says he could not address them as spiritual people but as infants in Christ, since there is jealousy and strife among them. What is Apollos? What is Paul? Servants. Paul planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. They are God's field, God's building.
3.big: Leaders are only servants; God alone gives growth.

3.ctx: Paul develops the building image, with a warning for those who build on the foundation.
3.mean: Paul says like a skilled master builder he laid a foundation, and someone else builds on it. No one can lay any other foundation than Jesus Christ. Each one's work will be tested by fire on the Day; if it survives, he will receive a reward; if it is burned up, he will suffer loss, though he himself will be saved, but only as through fire.
3.big: Everything must be built on Christ, and each person's work will be tested by God.
3.diff: Roman Catholic theology has cited verse 15 in connection with purgatory; Protestants read it as testing the quality of ministers' work at the final judgement, not purifying believers' souls. The passage concerns leaders' work first of all.

3.ctx: Paul warns that damaging the church is a serious matter. Corinth had many pagan temples, and destroying a temple was regarded as a grave crime.
3.mean: Paul says do you not know that you (plural) are God's temple and God's Spirit dwells in you? If anyone destroys God's temple, God will destroy him. The wisdom of this world is folly with God. So let no one boast in men. All things are yours — Paul, Apollos, Cephas, the world, life, death, the present, the future — and you are Christ's, and Christ is God's.
3.big: The church is God's temple, and those who divide it answer to God.
3.diff: Here 'you' is plural and refers to the church as a whole; in 6:19 Paul applies the temple image to the individual believer's body.

4.ctx: Paul addresses the Corinthians' tendency to judge and rank their teachers.
4.mean: Paul says to regard apostles as servants of Christ and stewards of God's mysteries, and stewards must be found faithful. It is a small thing to be judged by them; he does not even judge himself. The Lord judges; do not pronounce judgement before the time. What do you have that you did not receive? Already you are rich, already kings! — while the apostles are like men condemned to death, fools for Christ's sake, the scum of the world.
4.big: Christian leaders answer to the Lord, and the apostles' suffering exposes the Corinthians' pride.

4.ctx: A change of tone, from the sharp irony of 4:8–13 to fatherly appeal. A 'guide' (paidagogos) was a household slave who supervised children, unlike a father who had begotten them.
4.mean: Paul says he writes not to shame them but to admonish them as beloved children. They may have countless guides but not many fathers; he became their father in Christ through the gospel. So be imitators of me. He is sending Timothy to remind them of his ways in Christ, and will come soon.
4.big: Paul corrects the church as a father who brought them to faith.

5.ctx: A case of sexual sin the church was tolerating, perhaps even boasting about as an expression of freedom.
5.mean: Paul says there is sexual immorality among them of a kind not tolerated even among pagans: a man has his father's wife. They are arrogant instead of mourning. When they are assembled, with the power of the Lord Jesus, they are to deliver this man to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord. A little leaven leavens the whole lump. Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.
5.big: Tolerating open sin damages the whole church; discipline is meant to lead the sinner to salvation.
5.diff: 'Deliver to Satan' is generally understood as putting the man out of the church's fellowship into the world, with the aim of his repentance. 2 Corinthians 2:5–11 may describe a later restoration. Church discipline is a serious and sensitive matter best handled by a church's own leaders.

5.ctx: Paul clarifies a misunderstanding of an earlier letter he had written, now lost.
5.mean: Paul says he did not mean they should not associate with immoral people of this world, since then they would need to leave the world. He meant not to associate with anyone who bears the name of brother if he is guilty of sexual immorality, greed, idolatry, reviling, drunkenness or swindling. God judges those outside; purge the evil person from among you.
5.big: The church is to hold its own members to account, not withdraw from unbelievers.

6.ctx: Corinthians were taking fellow believers to pagan courts, where wealthier people had the advantage.
6.mean: Paul asks how any of them dares take a grievance before the unrighteous instead of the saints. The saints will judge the world and even angels. To have lawsuits at all is already a defeat. Why not rather suffer wrong? Why not rather be defrauded? Instead they wrong and defraud their own brothers.
6.big: Believers should settle disputes within the church, even at personal cost, rather than shame Christ publicly.

6.ctx: A warning about the lifestyle some Corinthians thought their freedom permitted.
6.mean: Paul says the unrighteous will not inherit the kingdom of God: neither the sexually immoral, idolaters, adulterers, men who practise homosexuality, thieves, the greedy, drunkards, revilers or swindlers. And such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.
6.big: The gospel names sin plainly and transforms sinners: 'such were some of you, but you were washed'.
6.diff: The translation of the two Greek words in verse 9 behind 'men who practise homosexuality' is debated; most scholars understand them to refer to both partners in male same-sex sexual acts, which the historic church has consistently taught are outside God's design. Verse 11 makes clear the passage is addressed to a church full of forgiven people.

6.ctx: Some Corinthians argued that what they did with their bodies did not matter spiritually.
6.mean: Paul says flee from sexual immorality. Every other sin a person commits is outside the body, but the sexually immoral person sins against his own body. Your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God. You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body.
6.big: The body matters to God, is the Spirit's temple, and belongs to Christ who bought it.
6.h: The Temple of the Holy Spirit

7.ctx: Paul begins answering questions the Corinthians had written to him about. Some apparently taught that sex, even in marriage, was spiritually inferior.
7.mean: Paul says each man should have his own wife and each woman her own husband. Husband and wife should give each other their conjugal rights, since each has authority over the other's body. He wishes all were single as he is, but each has his own gift. To the married he says, from the Lord, a wife should not separate from her husband. If a believer has an unbelieving spouse who is willing to stay, they should not divorce; if the unbeliever leaves, the believer is not enslaved.
7.big: Marriage is good and mutual, and should be preserved wherever possible.
7.diff: Verse 15 is read by many Protestants as permitting divorce and remarriage when an unbelieving spouse deserts. Churches differ on grounds for remarriage, and this is best worked through with a church's own leadership.

7.ctx: A principle Paul applies to circumcision, slavery and marriage alike.
7.mean: Paul says each person should lead the life the Lord has assigned, and remain in the condition in which he was called. Circumcision and uncircumcision count for nothing, but keeping God's commandments. A slave who can gain freedom should take it. You were bought with a price; do not become slaves of men.
7.big: Christians need not change their outward station to serve God, because their calling in Christ matters more.

7.ctx: Paul turns to the unmarried and the widowed, in light of a 'present distress'.
7.mean: Paul says, as his judgement rather than a command, that it is good to remain as one is, because of the present distress and because the form of this world is passing away. The unmarried person can be anxious about the things of the Lord, the married about how to please their spouse. Marriage is not sin, but singleness allows undivided devotion. A widow may remarry, only in the Lord.
7.big: Both singleness and marriage are good, and singleness has particular freedoms for serving the Lord.
7.diff: The 'present distress' may have been a famine or persecution in Corinth. Paul distinguishes his own advice from the Lord's command, which is worth noticing.

8.ctx: Meat sold in Corinth's markets had often been offered to pagan gods, and social meals were held in temple dining rooms.
8.mean: Paul says knowledge puffs up, but love builds up. We know an idol has no real existence and there is no God but one. For us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things. But not everyone has this knowledge; some eat as if it were really offered to an idol, and their weak conscience is defiled. Take care that your freedom does not become a stumbling block to the weak.
8.big: Love for a weaker brother matters more than the freedom that knowledge gives.
8.diff: Verse 6 takes the Shema of Deuteronomy 6:4 ('the LORD our God, the LORD is one') and divides its words between the Father ('God') and Jesus ('Lord'), placing Jesus within the identity of the one God.

9.ctx: Paul uses himself as an example of giving up rights for others, while defending his apostleship.
9.mean: Paul says he is an apostle who has seen the Lord. He has the right to be supported financially, like other apostles, and quotes the law: do not muzzle an ox while it treads the grain. But he has made no use of this right, rather enduring anything than put an obstacle in the way of the gospel. Necessity is laid on him; woe to him if he does not preach the gospel.
9.big: Paul gave up his own rights so that nothing would hinder the gospel.

9.ctx: The famous statement of Paul's missionary principle, set within a chapter about giving up his rights for the sake of others.
9.mean: Paul says though he is free from all, he has made himself a servant to all, that he might win more. To the Jews he became as a Jew, to those outside the law as one outside the law (not being outside the law of God but under the law of Christ), to the weak weak. He has become all things to all people, that by all means he might save some.
9.big: Paul adapts everything except the gospel itself in order to reach people.
9.diff: 'All things to all people' concerns cultural adaptation, not compromise of truth or morality — Paul immediately notes he remains under the law of Christ.

9.ctx: Corinth hosted the Isthmian Games, second only to the Olympics.
9.mean: Paul says in a race all run, but only one receives the prize; so run that you may obtain it. Athletes exercise self-control for a perishable wreath, we for an imperishable one. He disciplines his body and keeps it under control, lest after preaching to others he himself should be disqualified.
9.big: The Christian life demands disciplined, purposeful effort toward a lasting prize.
9.diff: Some read 'disqualified' as losing salvation, others as losing reward or approval for ministry. Reformed interpreters generally take it as the real warning that accompanies genuine perseverance.

10.ctx: Paul returns to the question of idol food, warning against overconfidence.
10.mean: Paul says Israel's fathers were all under the cloud, all passed through the sea, all ate the same spiritual food and drank from the spiritual Rock, and the Rock was Christ. Yet with most of them God was not pleased. These things were written as examples for us. Let anyone who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall. No temptation has overtaken you that is not common to man. God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but with the temptation will provide the way of escape.
10.big: Privileges do not guarantee faithfulness, but God is faithful to provide a way through every temptation.
10.diff: Verse 13 is often quoted out of context as 'God won't give you more than you can handle'. Its subject is temptation to sin, not suffering in general.

10.ctx: Paul now forbids participating in meals within pagan temples.
10.mean: Paul says flee from idolatry. The cup of blessing is a participation in the blood of Christ, the bread a participation in his body. Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body. What pagans sacrifice they offer to demons. You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons.
10.big: Believers cannot share both in Christ's table and in pagan worship.
10.diff: Verses 16–17 are central to understanding the Lord's Supper as 'participation' (koinonia). Christian traditions understand this participation differently; all agree it is a real sharing in Christ and makes the church one body.

10.ctx: Paul sums up his principles for disputed matters. 'All things are lawful' seems to have been a Corinthian slogan, which Paul quotes and then qualifies.
10.mean: Paul says all things are lawful, but not all things are helpful or build up. Let no one seek his own good but the good of his neighbour. Eat whatever is sold in the market without raising questions of conscience. But if someone says 'this has been offered in sacrifice', do not eat it, for his conscience's sake. Whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.
10.big: Christian freedom is used for others' good and God's glory.
