5.diff: Christians differ over how the law applies now. The historic Reformed approach distinguishes moral law (still binding), ceremonial law (fulfilled in Christ) and civil law (for Israel as a nation); other traditions frame it differently, but most agree on the conclusion.

5.ctx: The first of six sayings in which Jesus contrasts what was heard with what he says, going behind the command to the heart.
5.mean: Jesus says anyone angry with his brother is liable to judgement. Be reconciled before offering your gift at the altar; settle matters quickly with an accuser.
5.big: Murder begins with anger, and reconciliation matters more than religious ritual.

5.ctx: The second contrast, on adultery. Rabbinic teaching also discussed the look that leads to sin.
5.mean: Jesus says anyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery in his heart, and speaks of tearing out an eye or cutting off a hand rather than going to hell.
5.big: Purity is a matter of the heart, and sin must be dealt with decisively.
5.diff: The language is deliberate exaggeration urging radical action, not a call to literal self-harm.

5.ctx: Rabbis debated the grounds for divorce in Deuteronomy 24, some allowing almost any reason.
5.mean: Jesus says whoever divorces his wife, except on the ground of sexual immorality, makes her commit adultery, and whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery.
5.big: Jesus treats marriage as binding, against a culture of easy divorce.
5.diff: Churches differ over the scope of the exception and over remarriage. Paul adds desertion by an unbelieving spouse (1 Corinthians 7:15). This is best worked through with your own church leadership.

5.ctx: Oaths were widely used and elaborate rules had developed about which ones were binding.
5.mean: Jesus says do not take an oath at all, neither by heaven nor earth nor Jerusalem nor your own head. Let what you say be simply yes or no; anything more comes from evil.
5.big: Truthfulness should make oaths unnecessary.
5.diff: Some Christians, including Quakers and Anabaptists, refuse all oaths on this basis; most hold that Jesus condemns evasive oath-taking, noting that God swears oaths and Paul calls God as witness.

5.ctx: 'Eye for eye' in the law limited revenge to proportionate justice administered by courts; it had come to be used to justify personal retaliation.
5.mean: Jesus says do not resist the one who is evil: turn the other cheek, give your cloak as well, go the second mile. Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, so that you may be sons of your Father, who sends rain on the just and the unjust. You therefore must be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect.
5.big: God's children are to reflect his indiscriminate kindness, even toward enemies.
5.diff: How far this applies to self-defence, policing and war has been debated throughout church history; pacifist and just-war traditions both appeal to Scripture.

6.ctx: Almsgiving, prayer and fasting were the three great acts of Jewish piety, and Jesus addresses each in turn.
6.mean: Jesus says beware of practising righteousness before others to be seen by them. When you give to the needy, do not sound a trumpet; do it in secret, and your Father who sees in secret will reward you.
6.big: Religion performed for an audience has already received all the reward it will get.

6.ctx: The model prayer, given in contrast to showy public prayer and to pagan repetition.
6.mean: Jesus says pray in secret, not heaping up empty phrases. Then: Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name; your kingdom come, your will be done on earth as in heaven; give us this day our daily bread; forgive us our debts as we forgive our debtors; lead us not into temptation but deliver us from evil. He adds that if you forgive others, your Father will forgive you.
6.big: Prayer begins with God's name, kingdom and will, and only then turns to our needs.
6.diff: The closing doxology ('for yours is the kingdom...') is absent from the earliest manuscripts and is usually footnoted; it is an early and fitting addition used in worship. On 'lead us not into temptation', James 1:13 makes clear God tempts no one; the petition asks to be spared severe testing.

6.ctx: Fasting was practised weekly by the devout, and its outward signs could easily become display.
6.mean: Jesus says when you fast, do not look gloomy as the hypocrites do; anoint your head and wash your face, so that your fasting is seen by your Father who is in secret.
6.big: Fasting is between a person and God, not a performance.

6.ctx: Wealth in the ancient world was held in cloth, grain and metal — vulnerable to moths, rot and theft.
6.mean: Jesus says do not lay up treasures on earth, but in heaven, for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.
6.big: What you treasure shapes what you love.

6.ctx: A short saying using the eye as a lamp, probably about generosity: a 'bad eye' was an idiom for stinginess.
6.mean: Jesus says the eye is the lamp of the body; if it is healthy the whole body is full of light. No one can serve two masters: you cannot serve God and money.
6.big: Money is not a neutral possession but a rival master.

6.ctx: Addressed to people for whom food and clothing were genuinely uncertain, not to the comfortable.
6.mean: Jesus says do not be anxious about your life. Look at the birds and the lilies: your heavenly Father feeds and clothes them, and you are of more value. Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you. Do not be anxious about tomorrow.
6.big: Anxiety is answered by knowing the Father who provides, and by seeking his kingdom first.
6.diff: This is not a promise of prosperity but of provision, given by one who himself had nowhere to lay his head.

7.ctx: A saying frequently quoted alone, though Jesus goes on to assume that discernment will still be needed (verses 5–6, 15–20).
7.mean: Jesus says judge not, that you be not judged; with the measure you use it will be measured to you. Take the log out of your own eye first, and then you will see clearly to take the speck out of your brother's eye. Do not give what is holy to dogs.
7.big: Self-examination must come before correcting anyone else, but correction is not forbidden.

7.ctx: Jesus turns to prayer, using an argument from the lesser to the greater that was common in Jewish teaching.
7.mean: Jesus says ask and it will be given, seek and you will find, knock and it will be opened. If you who are evil know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father give good things to those who ask him. So whatever you wish others would do to you, do also to them.
7.big: God is a Father who gives good gifts, so his children may ask with confidence.

7.ctx: Two gates, two roads, two destinations — the first of several contrasting pairs that close the sermon.
7.mean: Jesus says enter by the narrow gate, for the gate is wide and the way easy that leads to destruction, and many enter it; the gate is narrow and the way hard that leads to life, and those who find it are few.
7.big: The way of Christ is narrow and costly, and most will not take it.

7.ctx: False prophets were a live danger in Israel's history and in the early church.
7.mean: Jesus says beware of false prophets in sheep's clothing. You will recognise them by their fruits; a healthy tree cannot bear bad fruit. Not everyone who says 'Lord, Lord' will enter the kingdom, but the one who does the will of my Father. Many will say they prophesied and cast out demons in his name, and he will declare: I never knew you.
7.big: Profession and even religious activity mean nothing without genuine obedience.
7.diff: 'I never knew you' indicates these were never truly his, rather than that they lost salvation — a text Reformed theology cites in discussing false profession.

7.ctx: The closing parable, in a land where dry riverbeds flooded suddenly in the rainy season.
7.mean: Jesus says everyone who hears these words and does them is like a wise man who built his house on the rock; the one who hears and does not do them is like a foolish man who built on sand, and great was its fall.
7.big: Hearing Jesus' words without obeying them leaves a life with no foundation.

7.ctx: Matthew closes each of his five teaching blocks with a similar formula.
7.mean: The crowds are astonished at his teaching, for he taught them as one who had authority, and not as their scribes.
7.big: Jesus teaches on his own authority, unlike scribes who cited earlier teachers.

8.ctx: Leprosy covered several skin conditions; under Leviticus 13–14 it brought ritual uncleanness and exclusion from the community.
8.mean: A leper kneels and says: Lord, if you will, you can make me clean. Jesus stretches out his hand and touches him, saying: I will; be clean. He tells him to show himself to the priest as Moses commanded.
8.big: Jesus touches the untouchable, and cleanness passes from him to the man.

8.ctx: A centurion commanded around a hundred soldiers; this one was a Gentile in Capernaum, evidently respected locally.
8.mean: The centurion asks healing for his servant, and says Jesus need only say the word, since he himself understands authority. Jesus marvels and says he has not found such faith in Israel, and that many will come from east and west to sit with Abraham, while the sons of the kingdom are cast out.
8.big: A Gentile soldier understands Jesus' authority better than Israel does.

8.ctx: Peter's house in Capernaum, which archaeologists believe they have identified beneath a later church.
8.mean: Jesus heals Peter's mother-in-law of a fever and she rises and serves him. That evening many are brought, and he casts out spirits and heals all the sick, fulfilling Isaiah 53:4: he took our illnesses and bore our diseases.
8.big: Jesus' healings are part of his bearing the effects of sin foretold in Isaiah.

8.ctx: Two would-be followers approach as Jesus prepares to cross the lake.
8.mean: A scribe offers to follow him anywhere; Jesus says foxes have holes and birds nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head. Another asks first to bury his father; Jesus says: follow me, and leave the dead to bury their own dead.
8.big: Following Jesus takes priority over comfort and even over sacred duty.
8.diff: The second saying is deliberately shocking. Many think the man meant waiting until his father died, perhaps years away.

8.ctx: The Sea of Galilee lies in a basin surrounded by hills and is prone to sudden violent squalls.
8.mean: A great storm arises while Jesus sleeps. The disciples wake him crying 'save us, we are perishing'. He rebukes them for little faith, then rebukes the winds and sea, and there is a great calm. They marvel: what sort of man is this, that even winds and sea obey him?
8.big: Jesus sleeps like an exhausted man and commands the sea as only God does (see Mark 4:35 on the two natures).

8.ctx: Gentile territory east of the lake, hence the pigs, which Jews would not keep.
8.mean: Two demon-possessed men, so fierce no one could pass, cry out: what have you to do with us, Son of God? Have you come to torment us before the time? Jesus sends the demons into a herd of pigs, which rush into the sea. The townspeople beg him to leave.
8.big: The demons recognise Jesus and his authority, while the townspeople prefer their livelihood to his presence.
8.diff: Mark and Luke mention one man; Matthew often mentions two where they mention one. Explanations include Matthew recording both while the others focus on the more prominent.

9.ctx: Back in Capernaum, which Matthew calls 'his own city'. Mark and Luke add the detail of the men lowering the paralysed man through the roof.
9.mean: A paralysed man is brought and Jesus says: take heart, my son, your sins are forgiven. Scribes say he is blaspheming. Jesus asks which is easier to say, then tells the man to rise and go home — that they may know the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins. The crowds glorify God for giving such authority to men.
9.big: Jesus proves an invisible claim — authority to forgive sins — by a visible healing.

9.ctx: Tax collectors bought the right to collect for Rome and profited from the excess, making them collaborators and extortioners in popular view.
9.mean: Jesus calls Matthew from the tax booth, and he rises and follows. Jesus eats with tax collectors and sinners; asked why, he says those who are well have no need of a physician, and quotes Hosea: I desire mercy, not sacrifice. I came not to call the righteous but sinners.
9.big: Jesus deliberately seeks those the religious had written off.
9.diff: Matthew names himself as the tax collector, while Mark and Luke call him Levi — most likely the same man with two names.

9.ctx: John's disciples fasted, as did the Pharisees twice weekly; Jesus' disciples did not.
9.mean: Jesus asks whether wedding guests can mourn while the bridegroom is with them; the days will come when he is taken away, and then they will fast.
9.big: Jesus' presence is a wedding, and his first hearers are told he will be taken away.

9.ctx: Two short images continuing the answer about fasting, drawn from everyday life: cloth shrank when washed, and wineskins grew brittle with age.
9.mean: Jesus says no one puts a patch of unshrunk cloth on an old garment, or new wine into old wineskins. New wine is put into fresh wineskins.
9.big: What Jesus brings cannot be contained within the old religious forms.

9.ctx: Matthew interweaves two healings, as Mark does: a synagogue official's daughter and a woman with a haemorrhage.
9.mean: A ruler asks Jesus to raise his dead daughter. On the way a woman who had suffered a discharge of blood for twelve years touches his garment, and he says: take heart, daughter, your faith has made you well. At the ruler's house he puts out the flute players, takes the girl's hand, and she rises.
9.big: Jesus' power reaches ritual uncleanness and death itself.

9.ctx: Two more healings that show Jesus fulfilling Isaiah's signs of the coming kingdom.
9.mean: Two blind men call him Son of David, and he heals them according to their faith, sternly charging them to tell no one — but they spread his fame. A mute demon-possessed man is healed, and the crowds marvel, while Pharisees say he casts out demons by the prince of demons.
9.big: The same works produce faith in some and hostile explanations in others.
9.h: Jesus Heals the Blind and Mute

9.ctx: A summary passage that introduces the mission of the Twelve in chapter 10.
9.mean: Jesus goes through all the towns teaching, proclaiming the gospel of the kingdom and healing. Seeing the crowds, he has compassion, because they are harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd. He tells the disciples the harvest is plentiful but the labourers few; pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest to send out labourers.
9.big: Jesus' compassion for the crowds leads to a call to pray for workers.

10.ctx: The second teaching block. The Twelve correspond to Israel's twelve tribes, marking the formation of a renewed people.
10.mean: Jesus gives the twelve authority over unclean spirits and to heal. Matthew lists them, ending with Judas Iscariot, who betrayed him.
10.big: Jesus shares his own authority with the men he has chosen.

10.ctx: A limited mission, restricted for now to Israel, before the wider commission of 28:19.
10.mean: Jesus sends them only to the lost sheep of Israel, to preach that the kingdom is at hand, heal the sick and raise the dead. Freely you received, freely give. They are to take no money, and to stay with worthy households; where they are not received, shake off the dust.
10.big: The messengers travel light and depend on hospitality, carrying the kingdom's authority.

10.ctx: Jesus turns from the immediate mission to the longer experience of the church.
10.mean: Jesus says: I send you out as sheep among wolves; be wise as serpents and innocent as doves. They will be delivered to councils and flogged, and dragged before governors and kings. When arrested, do not be anxious how to speak, for the Spirit of your Father will speak through you. Brother will deliver brother to death; the one who endures to the end will be saved.
10.big: Persecution is promised, and so is the Spirit's help in it.

10.ctx: Three reasons not to fear, given to men Jesus has just told will be flogged and dragged before governors.
10.mean: Jesus says have no fear of them; nothing is covered that will not be revealed. Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather fear him who can destroy both in hell. Two sparrows sell for a penny, yet not one falls apart from your Father; even the hairs of your head are numbered.
10.big: Fear of God displaces fear of people, because the Father's care reaches the smallest detail.

10.ctx: A solemn word about public allegiance, spoken to men who would face real pressure to keep quiet about Jesus.
10.mean: Jesus says everyone who acknowledges him before others, he will acknowledge before his Father; whoever denies him, he will deny.
10.big: Public loyalty to Jesus now is matched by his acknowledgement of us before the Father.

10.ctx: One of Jesus' hardest sayings, easily misused. In a society where family and religion were inseparable, following Jesus could split a household.
10.mean: Jesus says he came not to bring peace but a sword, setting family members against one another. Whoever loves father or mother more than him is not worthy of him. Whoever does not take his cross and follow is not worthy of him. Whoever finds his life will lose it, and whoever loses his life for his sake will find it.
10.big: Allegiance to Jesus comes before every other loyalty, and will divide households.
10.diff: This describes the effect of following Christ, not an endorsement of conflict; Jesus elsewhere blesses peacemakers.

10.ctx: The closing of the mission discourse, about how people who receive Christ's messengers are treated by God.
10.mean: Jesus says whoever receives you receives me, and whoever receives me receives him who sent me. Even a cup of cold water given to a little one will not lose its reward.
10.big: Receiving Christ's messengers is receiving Christ himself.

11.ctx: John is in Herod's prison, and what he hears of Jesus does not match his expectation of a Messiah who would bring judgement.
11.mean: John sends to ask: are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another? Jesus tells them to report what they see — the blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the dead are raised and the poor have good news preached to them — words drawn from Isaiah. And blessed is the one not offended by me.
11.big: Jesus answers doubt not with rebuke but with evidence from Scripture.
11.diff: That the greatest prophet could doubt, and be answered gently, has comforted many believers.

11.ctx: Jesus speaks about John after his messengers leave, to a crowd who had gone out into the wilderness to hear him.
11.mean: Jesus says John is more than a prophet, the messenger of Malachi 3:1, and that among those born of women none is greater — yet the least in the kingdom is greater than he. He compares the generation to children who will not play: John came fasting and they called him demon-possessed; the Son of Man came eating and they called him a glutton.
11.big: John is the greatest of the old era, and the kingdom he announced is greater still.

11.ctx: Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum were the towns where most of Jesus' miracles were performed.
11.mean: Jesus denounces the cities that did not repent, saying it will be more bearable for Tyre, Sidon and even Sodom on the day of judgement than for them.
11.big: Greater exposure to Christ brings greater accountability.

11.ctx: One of the most striking sayings about Jesus' relationship to the Father, followed by the best known invitation in the Gospels.
11.mean: Jesus thanks the Father for hiding these things from the wise and revealing them to little children; such was his gracious will. All things have been handed over to him by his Father, and no one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him. Then: come to me, all who labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls.
11.big: The Son alone reveals the Father, and he calls the weary to himself for rest.
11.diff: Verse 27 is one of the strongest statements of Jesus' unique relationship with the Father outside John. Verses 25–27 speak of God's sovereign revealing, and verse 28 of a free invitation to all — Scripture holds both together.

12.ctx: Plucking grain while passing was permitted (Deuteronomy 23:25), but the Pharisees classed it as reaping, forbidden on the Sabbath.
12.mean: Jesus cites David eating the consecrated bread and priests working on the Sabbath, then says something greater than the temple is here. He quotes Hosea — I desire mercy, not sacrifice — and says the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath.
12.big: Jesus claims authority over the Sabbath and calls himself greater than the temple.

12.ctx: A second Sabbath confrontation, in the synagogue, with opponents looking for grounds to accuse him.
12.mean: Asked whether it is lawful to heal on the Sabbath, Jesus points to a sheep fallen into a pit, says a man is of more value, and heals the withered hand. The Pharisees go out and conspire to destroy him.
12.big: Doing good on the Sabbath is lawful, and saying so hardens his opponents into a plot.

12.ctx: Matthew pauses the narrative to quote the longest Old Testament passage in his Gospel.
12.mean: Jesus withdraws, heals many and orders them not to make him known, fulfilling Isaiah 42: behold my servant whom I have chosen; he will not quarrel or cry aloud; a bruised reed he will not break, and a smouldering wick he will not quench, until he brings justice to victory. In his name the Gentiles will hope.
12.big: Jesus is the gentle Servant of Isaiah, who will not crush the weak.

12.ctx: Jesus heals a blind and mute demon-possessed man, and the crowds begin asking whether he could be the Son of David.
12.mean: The Pharisees say he casts out demons by Beelzebul. Jesus answers that a kingdom divided against itself cannot stand, and that if he casts out demons by the Spirit of God, the kingdom of God has come upon them. No one plunders a strong man's house without first binding the strong man.
12.big: Jesus' power over demons shows God's kingdom has arrived and Satan is being bound.

12.ctx: One of the most feared passages in Scripture, spoken directly to those who had just attributed the Spirit's work to Satan.
12.mean: Jesus says every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven, but blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or the age to come.
12.big: Deliberately calling the Spirit's evident work satanic is a rejection that shuts the door from the inside.
12.diff: The consistent pastoral reading across traditions is that this describes a settled, hardened rejection, not a moment of doubt or an intrusive thought — and that anyone anxious about having committed it has shown by that anxiety that they have not.

12.ctx: Jesus continues to answer the Pharisees who had just attributed his works to Satan, turning to what their words reveal.
12.mean: Jesus says either make the tree good and its fruit good, or the tree bad and its fruit bad. Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. On the day of judgement people will give account for every careless word.
12.big: Words reveal the heart, and God takes them seriously.

12.ctx: Scribes and Pharisees ask for a sign, having just attributed his works to Satan.
12.mean: Jesus says an evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, but none will be given except the sign of Jonah: as Jonah was three days in the belly of the great fish, so will the Son of Man be three days in the heart of the earth. The men of Nineveh and the queen of the South will rise at the judgement and condemn this generation.
12.big: The only sign Jesus offers is his own death and resurrection.
12.diff: Jesus speaks of Jonah and the queen of Sheba as real people. 'Three days and three nights' is generally understood as a Jewish idiom for parts of three days.

12.ctx: A short, unsettling parable about reformation without genuine change.
12.mean: Jesus describes an unclean spirit that leaves a person, finds the house empty, swept and put in order, and returns with seven others, so that the last state is worse than the first.
12.big: Moral tidying without Christ leaves a person more vulnerable, not less.

12.ctx: Jesus' mother and brothers arrive while he is teaching; Mark says his family had set out because people were saying he was out of his mind.
12.mean: Told his mother and brothers are outside, Jesus stretches out his hand toward his disciples and says: here are my mother and my brothers. Whoever does the will of my Father in heaven is my brother and sister and mother.
12.big: The deepest family bond is obedience to the Father, not blood.

13.ctx: The third teaching block: seven parables of the kingdom, taught from a boat to crowds on the shore.
13.mean: Jesus tells of seed falling on the path, rocky ground, thorns and good soil, which produces a hundred, sixty or thirtyfold.
13.big: The word of the kingdom meets different responses, but will certainly produce a great harvest.

13.ctx: The disciples ask why he speaks in parables, and Jesus answers with Isaiah 6.
13.mean: Jesus says it has been given to them to know the secrets of the kingdom, but not to others. To the one who has, more will be given. He quotes Isaiah: they will indeed hear but never understand, for this people's heart has grown dull. But blessed are your eyes, for they see.
13.big: Parables reveal the kingdom to those given understanding and conceal it from those who have already closed their eyes.
13.diff: This is among the hardest sayings in the Gospels. Some read the concealment as God's purpose, others as the result of prior rejection; Matthew's 'because' leans toward the second while Mark's 'so that' leans toward the first. Reformed theology stresses that understanding is God's gift.

13.ctx: Private explanation to the disciples. Matthew's readers, facing pressure and the pull of wealth, would recognise the rocky ground and the thorns.
13.mean: The seed on the path is the word snatched by the evil one; rocky ground is one who receives it with joy but falls away under tribulation; thorns are the cares of the world and the deceitfulness of riches; good soil is the one who hears and understands and bears fruit.
13.big: Pressure and distraction are the two great threats to a fruitful hearing of God's word.
13.h: The Parable of the Sower Explained

13.ctx: A parable found only in Matthew, about a field sown with weeds by an enemy.
13.mean: The servants ask whether to pull up the weeds; the owner says no, lest they uproot the wheat with them, but to let both grow until the harvest.
13.big: Good and evil grow together until the final judgement, and God alone separates them.
13.diff: The parable has often been used in debates about church discipline and about how far a church can be a pure society; Jesus' own explanation (13:36–43) makes the field the world rather than the church.

13.ctx: A tiny seed producing a large plant, and a familiar image of unstoppable growth.
13.mean: Jesus says the kingdom is like a mustard seed, the smallest of seeds, which becomes a tree so that the birds come and nest in its branches.
13.big: The kingdom's unimpressive beginning is no measure of its final size.
13.h: The Parable of the Mustard Seed

13.ctx: A domestic image, in a culture where leaven was usually a symbol of corruption.
13.mean: Jesus says the kingdom is like leaven that a woman hid in three measures of flour until it was all leavened.
13.big: The kingdom works invisibly through everything until the whole is changed.

13.ctx: Matthew's own comment on Jesus' method of teaching, citing Psalm 78, a psalm that retells Israel's history as instruction.
13.mean: Matthew says Jesus said nothing to the crowds without a parable, fulfilling the words: I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter what has been hidden since the foundation of the world.
13.big: Jesus' parables fulfil Scripture's pattern of revealing hidden things through story.
13.h: I Will Open My Mouth in Parables

13.ctx: Jesus leaves the crowds and goes into the house, where the disciples ask him to explain the parable of the weeds.
13.mean: Jesus says the sower is the Son of Man, the field is the world, the good seed the sons of the kingdom, the weeds the sons of the evil one, the enemy the devil, the harvest the end of the age, and the reapers angels. The weeds will be gathered and burned, and the righteous will shine like the sun.
13.big: History ends in a separation carried out by God, not by his people.
13.h: The Parable of the Weeds Explained

13.ctx: Two very short parables about the worth of the kingdom, set among the longer ones. Burying valuables in a field was a normal way of protecting them.
13.mean: The kingdom is like treasure hidden in a field, which a man finds and covers up, and in his joy sells all he has to buy that field; and like a merchant who, finding one pearl of great value, sells everything to buy it.
13.big: The kingdom is worth everything, and those who see it give up all they have with joy.
13.h: The Parables of the Treasure and the Pearl

13.ctx: The last of the seven parables, using the fishing trade familiar to his disciples.
13.mean: The kingdom is like a net thrown into the sea gathering fish of every kind; when full, the good are sorted into containers and the bad thrown away. So it will be at the close of the age.
13.big: The gathering is wide, but a sorting is coming.

13.ctx: Nazareth, a small village where everyone knew Jesus' family.
13.mean: The townspeople are astonished and ask: is not this the carpenter's son? Is not his mother called Mary, and his brothers James, Joseph, Simon and Judas? They take offence at him, and Jesus says a prophet is not without honour except in his home town. He did not do many mighty works there because of their unbelief.
13.big: Familiarity with Jesus' ordinary humanity becomes, for his own town, a reason not to believe.

14.ctx: Herod Antipas, tetrarch of Galilee, not the Herod of the nativity. Josephus independently records John's imprisonment and execution at the fortress of Machaerus.
14.mean: Herod thinks Jesus is John raised from the dead. Matthew recounts how Herod had arrested John for condemning his marriage to Herodias, his brother's wife, and how a rash oath at a birthday feast led to John's beheading. His disciples bury him and tell Jesus.
14.big: Speaking God's word to people in power can cost a prophet his life.

14.ctx: Jesus withdraws after hearing of John's death, but the crowds follow on foot.
14.mean: Jesus has compassion and heals the sick. In the evening the disciples want the crowds sent away, but Jesus says: you give them something to eat. With five loaves and two fish he feeds about five thousand men besides women and children, with twelve baskets left over.
14.big: Jesus provides abundantly for his people in a deserted place, as God did in the wilderness.
14.h: The Feeding of the Five Thousand

14.ctx: Between three and six in the morning, on a lake prone to sudden squalls.
14.mean: Jesus comes to them walking on the sea, saying: take heart, it is I; do not be afraid. Peter asks to come, walks on the water, then sees the wind and begins to sink, crying: Lord, save me. Jesus catches him and says: you of little faith, why did you doubt? Those in the boat worship him, saying: truly you are the Son of God.
14.big: Jesus does what only God does, and lifts a sinking disciple whose faith failed mid-step.
14.diff: Matthew alone records Peter's attempt. The disciples' worship and confession here anticipate Peter's fuller confession in chapter 16.

14.ctx: A summary of healing at Gennesaret, the fertile plain on the north-west shore.
14.mean: People recognise him, send word through the whole region, and beg that the sick might touch even the fringe of his garment; as many as touched it were made well.
14.big: Jesus' willingness to heal outruns even the crowds' expectations.

15.ctx: Scribes and Pharisees come from Jerusalem, the religious centre, to examine a Galilean teacher.
15.mean: They object that his disciples break the tradition of the elders by not washing their hands. Jesus answers by exposing 'Corban': declaring property dedicated to God to avoid supporting ageing parents. He quotes Isaiah: this people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me.
15.big: Human tradition was being used to cancel a plain command of God.

15.ctx: Jesus calls the crowd to hear what he has just said to the leaders.
15.mean: Jesus says it is not what goes into the mouth that defiles but what comes out, for out of the heart come evil thoughts, murder, adultery, sexual immorality, theft, false witness and slander.
15.big: Defilement is a matter of the heart, not of ritual.
15.diff: Mark adds the editorial comment that Jesus thus declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19); Matthew, writing for Jewish readers, records the teaching without that conclusion.

15.ctx: Tyre and Sidon, Gentile cities on the coast of what is now Lebanon.
15.mean: A Canaanite woman begs mercy for her demon-possessed daughter. Jesus says he was sent only to the lost sheep of Israel, and that it is not right to take the children's bread and throw it to the dogs. She says: yet even the dogs eat the crumbs. Jesus says: O woman, great is your faith. Her daughter is healed instantly.
15.big: Persistent faith from an outsider receives what Israel's leaders were refusing.
15.diff: Jesus' words are deliberately hard, and attempts to soften them usually weaken the passage. Readers differ over whether it is a test of her faith or Jesus voicing a prevailing attitude in order to overturn it.
15.h: The Faith of the Canaanite Woman

15.ctx: Still in largely Gentile territory near the Sea of Galilee, after the encounter with the Canaanite woman.
15.mean: Great crowds bring the lame, blind, crippled and mute, and Jesus heals them, so that they glorify the God of Israel. Unwilling to send them away hungry, he feeds four thousand men besides women and children from seven loaves and a few fish, with seven baskets left over.
15.big: Jesus provides for Gentile crowds as he did for Jewish ones.
15.h: The Feeding of the Four Thousand

16.ctx: Pharisees and Sadducees, normally opposed to each other, unite to test Jesus.
16.mean: They ask for a sign from heaven. Jesus says they can read the sky but not the signs of the times; no sign will be given except the sign of Jonah.
16.big: Those who will not read the evidence already given will not be convinced by more.

16.ctx: Crossing the lake after the demand for a sign, the disciples realise they have forgotten to bring bread.
16.mean: Jesus warns them of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees, and they think he is talking about loaves. He reminds them of the two feedings and asks: how is it you fail to understand? Then they perceive he meant their teaching.
16.big: False teaching spreads quietly, like leaven, and the disciples are slow to grasp it.
16.h: The Leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees

16.ctx: Caesarea Philippi, near a centre of pagan worship and a temple to Caesar, at the northern edge of Israel.
16.mean: Jesus asks who people say the Son of Man is, then who they say he is. Peter answers: you are the Christ, the Son of the living God. Jesus says flesh and blood did not reveal this but his Father in heaven, and that on this rock he will build his church, and the gates of hell will not prevail against it, giving Peter the keys of the kingdom.
16.big: The turning point of the Gospel: Jesus is confessed as Messiah and promises to build his church.
16.diff: Catholic teaching sees here the foundation of the papacy. Protestant interpreters have variously identified the rock as Peter's confession, Christ himself, or Peter as the first of the apostles on whom the church was built (Ephesians 2:20). What is not in doubt is that the church is Christ's and that he builds it.

16.ctx: Immediately after the confession. Popular expectation was of a Messiah who would defeat Rome.
16.mean: Jesus begins to show that he must go to Jerusalem, suffer, be killed and on the third day be raised. Peter rebukes him: this shall never happen to you. Jesus answers: get behind me, Satan; you are a hindrance to me, for you are not setting your mind on the things of God.
16.big: The same man who confessed Jesus rightly misunderstands what kind of Messiah he is.

16.ctx: Jesus turns from his own path to the path of anyone who follows him.
16.mean: Jesus says if anyone would come after him, let him deny himself, take up his cross and follow. Whoever would save his life will lose it. What will it profit a man to gain the whole world and forfeit his soul? The Son of Man will repay each according to what he has done.
16.big: Following Jesus means the cross, and the only life worth keeping is the one given away.

17.ctx: Six days after Peter's confession, on a high mountain, with Peter, James and John.
17.mean: Jesus is transfigured, his face shining like the sun. Moses and Elijah appear. Peter offers to build three tents; a bright cloud overshadows them and a voice says: this is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased; listen to him. The disciples fall on their faces, terrified, and Jesus touches them: rise, have no fear. He tells them to say nothing until he is raised.
17.big: The glory of the one who must suffer is briefly revealed, and the Father commands them to listen to him.
17.diff: Moses and Elijah represent the law and the prophets, and their disappearance leaving Jesus alone is the point. 'Listen to him' echoes Deuteronomy 18:15.

17.ctx: Coming down from the mountain, they find the other disciples have failed to heal a boy.
17.mean: A father kneels for his epileptic son. Jesus rebukes the demon and the boy is healed instantly. Asked why they could not cast it out, he says: because of your little faith; if you have faith like a grain of mustard seed you will say to this mountain 'move' and it will move.
17.big: Small genuine faith in a great God accomplishes what self-reliance cannot.
17.diff: Verse 21 ('this kind does not go out except by prayer and fasting') is absent from the earliest manuscripts and footnoted in modern translations.

17.ctx: The disciples ask privately why they could not cast out the demon, having been given authority to do so in chapter 10.
17.mean: Jesus speaks of faith like a mustard seed and says nothing will be impossible for them.
17.big: The issue is not the size of faith but the greatness of the God it rests on.

17.ctx: The second passion prediction, given as they gather in Galilee.
17.mean: Jesus says the Son of Man is about to be delivered into the hands of men, and they will kill him, and he will be raised on the third day. They are greatly distressed.
17.big: Jesus keeps telling them plainly where the road leads.
17.h: The Second Prediction of the Passion

17.ctx: The temple tax was a half-shekel paid annually by Jewish males for the temple's upkeep.
17.mean: Collectors ask whether Jesus pays the tax. Jesus asks Peter whether kings tax their sons or others; sons are free. But so as not to give offence, he tells Peter to catch a fish, in whose mouth he will find a coin to pay for them both.
17.big: Jesus is free from the tax as the Son, yet pays it rather than cause needless offence.
17.diff: Found only in Matthew. The principle of surrendering a right to avoid giving offence runs through the New Testament.

18.ctx: The fourth teaching block, on life together in the church — a word Matthew alone among the Gospels uses.
18.mean: Asked who is greatest, Jesus puts a child among them and says unless you turn and become like children you will never enter the kingdom. Whoever humbles himself like this child is the greatest.
18.big: Greatness in the kingdom means the lowliness of a child.

18.ctx: A severe warning about causing others to stumble, following directly from Jesus setting a child among the disciples.
18.mean: Jesus says whoever causes one of these little ones to sin would be better off drowned with a millstone round his neck. Temptations are sure to come, but woe to the one through whom they come. Better to enter life crippled than be thrown into the eternal fire.
18.big: Causing another believer to fall is among the gravest sins Jesus names.
18.diff: The language about hand, foot and eye is deliberate exaggeration urging decisive action, not literal self-harm.

18.ctx: A parable Luke tells in a different setting; here it is about pastoral care within the church.
18.mean: Jesus says their angels always see the Father's face. If a man has a hundred sheep and one goes astray, he leaves the ninety-nine and seeks the one, rejoicing more over it. So it is not the will of your Father that one of these little ones should perish.
18.big: God's care pursues the individual straying believer.
18.h: The Parable of the Lost Sheep

18.ctx: The clearest process for handling sin in the church given anywhere in Scripture.
18.mean: Jesus says if your brother sins against you, go and tell him his fault between you alone; if he listens you have gained your brother. If not, take one or two others; if he refuses them, tell it to the church; if he refuses the church, let him be to you as a Gentile and a tax collector.
18.big: Correction begins privately and aims at winning the brother, not exposing him.
18.diff: Churches apply this differently, and it is a matter for a church's own leadership rather than individuals acting alone.

18.ctx: Two famous verses, best read within the discipline passage they belong to.
18.mean: Jesus says whatever they bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, that if two agree about anything they ask it will be done, and that where two or three are gathered in his name, he is among them.
18.big: Christ is present with his gathered people, including when they take difficult decisions together.
18.diff: Verse 20 is often quoted about small prayer meetings; its immediate context is the church acting together in discipline, though the promise of Christ's presence is not thereby narrowed to that.

18.ctx: Peter's question follows naturally from the teaching on forgiving a sinning brother. Rabbis commonly taught forgiving three times.
18.mean: Peter asks whether seven times is enough; Jesus says seventy-seven times. He tells of a servant forgiven a debt of ten thousand talents who then seizes a fellow servant owing a hundred denarii. The master delivers him to the jailers. So also my heavenly Father will do to every one of you, if you do not forgive your brother from your heart.
18.big: The debt God has forgiven is beyond calculation, which makes refusing to forgive unthinkable.
18.diff: Ten thousand talents was an astronomical sum, perhaps 200,000 years' wages; a hundred denarii about a hundred days'. The closing warning is severe and has been discussed in relation to assurance; most read it as showing that unforgiving hearts reveal hearts that have not received grace.

19.ctx: Jesus leaves Galilee for Judea. Pharisees test him on a question rabbis disputed sharply.
19.mean: Asked whether it is lawful to divorce for any cause, Jesus goes back to Genesis: from the beginning God made them male and female, and what God has joined together let no one separate. Moses allowed divorce because of hardness of heart, but from the beginning it was not so. Whoever divorces except for sexual immorality and marries another commits adultery. The disciples say it is better not to marry; Jesus speaks of those who are eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom.
19.big: Jesus grounds marriage in God's creation design rather than in the law's concessions.
19.diff: Churches differ over the scope of the exception and over remarriage, and Paul adds desertion (1 Corinthians 7:15). This is best worked through with your own church leadership.

19.ctx: Children had no social standing; the disciples see them as an interruption.
19.mean: People bring children for Jesus to lay hands on them and pray. The disciples rebuke them, but Jesus says: let the little children come to me, for to such belongs the kingdom of heaven.
19.big: The kingdom belongs to those who come with nothing but need.

19.ctx: A wealthy young man, in a culture where wealth was widely seen as a sign of God's favour.
19.mean: He asks what good deed he must do to have eternal life. Jesus lists commandments; the man says he has kept them all. Jesus says: if you would be perfect, go, sell what you possess and give to the poor, and come, follow me. He goes away sorrowful, for he had great possessions. Jesus says it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom. With man this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.
19.big: Salvation is humanly impossible and possible only as God's gift.
19.diff: The command to sell everything targets this man's particular idol rather than setting a universal price. 'The eye of a needle' is a literal needle; the popular explanation about a gate in Jerusalem has no ancient evidence.

20.ctx: A parable found only in Matthew, using the day-labour market familiar to his readers.
20.mean: A master hires workers at different hours and pays them all the same. Those hired first grumble. He replies: did you not agree with me for a denarius? Am I not allowed to do what I choose with what belongs to me? Or do you begrudge my generosity? So the last will be first, and the first last.
20.big: Grace is not wages, and it cannot be audited as though it were.

20.ctx: The third and most detailed passion prediction, given on the road up to Jerusalem.
20.mean: Jesus says the Son of Man will be delivered to the chief priests, condemned to death, delivered to the Gentiles to be mocked, flogged and crucified, and raised on the third day.
20.big: Jesus goes to his death knowingly and by choice.
20.h: The Third Prediction of the Passion

20.ctx: Immediately after the prediction, the mother of James and John makes a request.
20.mean: She asks that her sons sit at his right and left in his kingdom. Jesus speaks of drinking his cup, and says such places are the Father's to give. The ten are indignant. Jesus says rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, but it shall not be so among you: whoever would be great must be your servant, for the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.
20.big: Greatness is service, and Jesus' death is a ransom given in the place of many.
20.diff: 'Ransom' was the price paid to free a slave or captive; 'for many' echoes Isaiah 53. The verse is central to the New Testament's understanding of why Jesus died.

20.ctx: Jericho, the last town before the climb to Jerusalem, crowded with Passover pilgrims.
20.mean: Two blind men cry out: Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David. The crowd rebukes them, but they cry out more. Jesus stops, asks what they want, and in pity touches their eyes; immediately they recover sight and follow him.
20.big: Two blind beggars see who Jesus is when the crowd does not.
20.h: The Blind Men by the Road

21.ctx: Passover week begins. Jesus approaches Jerusalem from the Mount of Olives, arranging the entry deliberately.
21.mean: Jesus sends for a donkey and a colt, which Matthew says fulfils Zechariah 9:9: behold, your king is coming to you, humble and mounted on a donkey. The crowds spread cloaks and branches, crying Hosanna to the Son of David. The city is stirred up, asking who this is.
21.big: Jesus enters Jerusalem openly as the humble king the prophets promised.

21.ctx: The outer court of the temple, the only area Gentiles could enter, was used for trade in sacrificial animals and currency exchange.
21.mean: Jesus drives out those buying and selling, overturns the tables, and quotes Isaiah and Jeremiah: my house shall be called a house of prayer, but you make it a den of robbers. The blind and lame come to him and he heals them, and children cry Hosanna, which angers the chief priests.
21.big: Jesus acts with authority over the temple itself, and the marginalised are welcomed where trade had been.

21.ctx: The next morning, returning from Bethany. Matthew places the fig tree after the temple cleansing, where Mark splits it around.
21.mean: Jesus, hungry, finds a fig tree with leaves but no fruit and says: may no fruit ever come from you again. It withers at once. The disciples marvel, and Jesus speaks of faith that can move mountains.
21.big: The fruitless tree is an acted parable of a temple full of activity and empty of fruit.

21.ctx: In the temple courts, confronted by the chief priests and elders.
21.mean: They demand to know his authority. Jesus asks whether John's baptism was from heaven or from men. They refuse to answer, fearing the crowd, so he declines to tell them.
21.big: Those who will not face the truth about God's messenger forfeit the right to an answer.

21.ctx: The first of three parables of judgement told to the leaders.
21.mean: A father tells two sons to work in the vineyard; one refuses then goes, the other agrees then does not. Which did his father's will? Jesus says tax collectors and prostitutes go into the kingdom before them, because they believed John.
21.big: Doing God's will matters more than saying the right thing.
21.h: The Parable of the Two Sons

21.ctx: The vineyard image comes from Isaiah 5, and the leaders recognise it.
21.mean: Tenants beat and kill the owner's servants, then kill his son to seize the inheritance. Jesus asks what the owner will do, and they answer that he will destroy them and let out the vineyard to others. He quotes Psalm 118 on the rejected stone becoming the cornerstone, and says the kingdom will be taken from them and given to a people producing its fruits.
21.big: Jesus is the beloved son whose rejection brings judgement and vindication.
21.h: The Parable of the Wicked Tenants

22.ctx: The third parable of judgement, about a wedding feast for a king's son.
22.mean: The invited guests refuse to come, some killing the servants; the king destroys them and sends his servants to the roads to gather all they find, good and bad. But a man without a wedding garment is cast out. Many are called, but few are chosen.
22.big: The invitation goes out to all, but coming on one's own terms is no coming at all.
22.diff: The wedding garment has been read as the righteousness Christ provides. The closing line is much discussed in relation to calling and election.

22.ctx: Pharisees and Herodians together set a trap over the Roman poll tax, hated by many Jews.
22.mean: They ask whether it is lawful to pay taxes to Caesar. Jesus asks whose image is on the coin, and says: render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's. They marvel and leave.
22.big: The coin bears Caesar's image and people bear God's — so the question of what is owed to God answers itself.

22.ctx: The Sadducees accepted only the five books of Moses and denied the resurrection.
22.mean: They pose a case of a woman married to seven brothers. Jesus says they know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God; in the resurrection people neither marry nor are given in marriage but are like angels. And he argues from Exodus 3 that God is not God of the dead but of the living.
22.big: Jesus proves the resurrection from the very books his opponents accepted.

22.ctx: A lawyer asks which is the great commandment, a question rabbis debated among the 613 commands.
22.mean: Jesus joins Deuteronomy 6:5 — love the Lord your God with all your heart, soul and mind — with Leviticus 19:18 — love your neighbour as yourself — and says on these two depend all the Law and the Prophets.
22.big: The whole law is summed up in love for God and for neighbour.

22.ctx: With his opponents silenced, Jesus takes the initiative and asks a question of his own, using Psalm 110.
22.mean: Jesus asks whose son the Christ is. They say David's. He asks how David, in the Spirit, calls him Lord: the Lord said to my Lord, sit at my right hand. No one can answer him a word, and from that day no one dares ask him any more questions.
22.big: The Messiah is David's descendant and also David's Lord — a puzzle answered by the incarnation.
22.diff: Psalm 110:1 is the most quoted Old Testament verse in the New Testament.

23.ctx: A sustained denunciation of the religious leadership, delivered publicly in the temple during Jesus' final week.
23.mean: Jesus tells the crowds to do what the scribes and Pharisees teach but not what they do, for they tie up heavy burdens and love places of honour and titles. He pronounces seven woes: shutting the kingdom in people's faces, making converts twice as much sons of hell, blind guides who tithe herbs while neglecting justice, mercy and faithfulness, cleaning the outside of the cup, whitewashed tombs, and building the tombs of the prophets their fathers killed.
23.big: Religion that is all display and no justice draws Jesus' sharpest words.
23.diff: These verses have been misused to justify hostility toward Jewish people. Jesus speaks as a Jew to Jewish leaders, in the tradition of Israel's own prophets, and the next passage shows his grief rather than hatred.

23.ctx: The lament that closes the denunciation, and shows what lies behind it.
23.mean: Jesus says: O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, killing the prophets and stoning those sent to you! How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing! See, your house is left to you desolate.
23.big: The anger of the woes is the grief of a rejected saviour.

24.ctx: The fifth and final teaching block. A disciple admires the temple's stones, some of which weighed many tonnes.
24.mean: Jesus says not one stone will be left on another. On the Mount of Olives the disciples ask when this will be, and what will be the sign of his coming and of the end of the age. Jesus warns of false messiahs, wars, famines and earthquakes: these are the beginning of birth pains.
24.big: Jesus prepares his followers both for the fall of Jerusalem and for a long wait before his return.
24.diff: The disciples ask two questions at once, which is why the discourse moves between AD 70 and the final coming. Interpreters divide over where the line falls: many read verses 4–35 as chiefly about Jerusalem and 36–51 as the return; others see a double reference throughout. All agree on the repeated command to stay alert.

24.ctx: Warnings of persecution and false teaching within the church.
24.mean: Jesus says they will be delivered up, hated by all nations, and many will fall away and betray one another. Lawlessness will increase and love grow cold, but the one who endures to the end will be saved. And this gospel of the kingdom will be proclaimed throughout the whole world as a testimony to all nations, and then the end will come.
24.big: Endurance under pressure marks genuine faith, and the gospel will reach all nations first.

24.ctx: The 'abomination of desolation' comes from Daniel, first applied to Antiochus IV desecrating the temple in 167 BC.
24.mean: When they see it standing in the holy place, those in Judea must flee to the mountains without going back for anything. Pray that flight not be in winter or on a Sabbath, for there will be tribulation such as has not been from the beginning. If those days had not been cut short, no human being would be saved; but for the elect's sake they will be cut short.
24.big: Jesus gives practical warning to escape a coming catastrophe in Judea.
24.diff: Proposed identifications include Roman standards in the temple and the Zealot occupation before the siege; the Judea-specific instructions fit AD 70 closely. Eusebius records that Jerusalem's Christians fled before the city fell.

24.ctx: The coming of the Son of Man, described with prophetic imagery from Isaiah and Daniel.
24.mean: Jesus says do not believe reports that he is in the wilderness or inner rooms, for as lightning flashes from east to west, so will the coming of the Son of Man be. The sun will be darkened, and they will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds with power and great glory, and he will gather his elect from the four winds.
24.big: Christ's return will be unmistakable and universal, needing no announcement.
24.diff: Interpreters differ over whether these verses describe the second coming or use prophetic imagery for God's judgement in AD 70; most evangelical and Reformed interpreters take the first.
24.h: The Return of the Son of Man

24.ctx: Still on the Mount of Olives. Fig trees in Judea lose their leaves in winter, so new leaves were a reliable sign that summer was near.
24.mean: When the fig tree's branch becomes tender and puts out leaves, summer is near. So when they see all these things, they know he is near. This generation will not pass away until all these things take place. Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.
24.big: The generation that heard Jesus saw the temple fall, exactly as he said.
24.diff: 'This generation' is most naturally the generation alive at the time, which saw AD 70; some take it as the Jewish people or the generation alive at the end.
24.h: The Lesson of the Fig Tree

24.ctx: The hinge of the discourse, turning from signs to the unknown timing of the end.
24.mean: Jesus says concerning that day and hour no one knows, not even the angels, nor the Son, but the Father only. As in the days of Noah they were eating and drinking until the flood came and swept them away, so will be the coming of the Son of Man. Two will be in a field; one is taken and one left. Stay awake, for you do not know on what day your Lord is coming.
24.big: Because no one knows the day, the only right response is constant readiness.
24.diff: That the Son does not know is understood in historic Christian teaching as spoken according to his human nature, having genuinely taken on human limitation (see Mark 4:35). 'One taken, one left' is read by some as the rapture and by others as judgement sweeping people away, as in Noah's flood.

25.ctx: Three parables about readiness, given as the final teaching block closes.
25.mean: Ten virgins take lamps to meet the bridegroom; five bring oil and five do not. While he is delayed all sleep, but at midnight the cry comes. The foolish ask for oil and are sent to buy it, and while they are away the door is shut. Watch therefore, for you know neither the day nor the hour.
25.big: Readiness cannot be borrowed at the last moment.
25.h: The Parable of the Ten Virgins

25.ctx: A parable about faithfulness during the master's absence. A talent was an enormous sum, around twenty years' wages.
25.mean: A man entrusts five, two and one talents to three servants. The first two trade and double them and are commended: well done, good and faithful servant. The third hides his in the ground, saying he knew the master was hard, and is condemned as wicked and slothful.
25.big: Those who belong to Christ are trusted with something and expected to use it.

25.ctx: The final judgement scene, unique to Matthew, closing the whole teaching block.
25.mean: The Son of Man sits on his throne and separates all nations as a shepherd separates sheep from goats. To those on his right: I was hungry and you gave me food, thirsty and you gave me drink, a stranger and you welcomed me, naked and you clothed me, sick and in prison and you visited me — as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me. Those on his left are sent away to eternal punishment, the righteous into eternal life.
25.big: Christ identifies himself with the hungry and imprisoned, and judges by how people treated them.
25.diff: Whether 'the least of these my brothers' means all the poor, or Christ's persecuted messengers, is debated. Either way the passage rules out a professed faith indifferent to need. The parallel of 'eternal punishment' with 'eternal life' is central to discussions of the nature of final judgement.

26.ctx: Two days before Passover, when Jerusalem was crowded with pilgrims.
26.mean: Jesus tells the disciples he will be delivered up to be crucified. The chief priests and elders plot to arrest him by stealth, but not during the feast, lest there be an uproar.
26.big: Jesus announces his death before his enemies have even settled their plan.

26.ctx: Bethany, at the house of Simon the leper, two miles from Jerusalem.
26.mean: A woman pours very expensive ointment on his head. The disciples are indignant at the waste, but Jesus says she has done a beautiful thing, preparing him for burial, and that wherever the gospel is proclaimed, what she has done will be told.
26.big: Extravagant devotion to Jesus is honoured, and his burial is acknowledged in advance.

26.ctx: Immediately after the anointing at Bethany, in deliberate contrast to the woman who had just poured out a year's wages.
26.mean: Judas goes to the chief priests and asks what they will give him; they pay him thirty pieces of silver — the price of a slave in Exodus 21:32.
26.big: One person pours out a year's wages; another sells him for the price of a slave.

26.ctx: The first day of Unleavened Bread, when Passover lambs were sacrificed.
26.mean: Jesus sends disciples into the city to a certain man, saying: my time is at hand; I will keep the Passover at your house.
26.big: Jesus directs the arrangements rather than being overtaken by events.

26.ctx: The Passover meal, which recalled the exodus through a set order of food and cups.
26.mean: Jesus says one of them will betray him, and each asks: is it I, Lord? Then he takes bread, blesses and breaks it: take, eat; this is my body. And the cup: this is my blood of the covenant, poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins. He will not drink of the fruit of the vine again until he drinks it new with them in his Father's kingdom.
26.big: Jesus interprets his own death in advance as the covenant sacrifice for the forgiveness of sins.
26.diff: Christian traditions differ over what happens at the Lord's Supper. All accept that Jesus himself gave this meaning to his death and commanded the meal. Matthew alone adds 'for the forgiveness of sins'.

26.ctx: On the way to the Mount of Olives, after singing the Passover psalms.
26.mean: Jesus quotes Zechariah 13:7 — I will strike the shepherd and the sheep will be scattered — and promises to go before them to Galilee after he is raised. Peter insists he will never fall away, and Jesus tells him that this night, before the rooster crows, he will deny him three times.
26.big: Jesus foresees his followers' failure and promises to meet them beyond it.

26.ctx: Gethsemane, meaning oil press, an olive grove on the Mount of Olives.
26.mean: Jesus becomes sorrowful and troubled, saying his soul is very sorrowful, even to death. He falls on his face and prays: my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will. Three times he prays, and three times finds the disciples sleeping: the spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak.
26.big: Jesus' human will genuinely recoils and genuinely submits to the Father.
26.diff: This is one of the clearest windows in the Gospels onto Christ's full humanity (see Mark 4:35). That he asked and was not spared says something important about unanswered prayer.

26.ctx: Judas arrives with a crowd from the chief priests and elders.
26.mean: Judas identifies Jesus with a kiss. A disciple draws a sword and cuts off the ear of the high priest's servant; Jesus says: put your sword back, for all who take the sword will perish by the sword. Do you think I cannot appeal to my Father, and he will send more than twelve legions of angels? But how then should the Scriptures be fulfilled? All the disciples forsake him and flee.
26.big: Jesus goes to his death by choice, refusing the force available to him.
26.diff: Matthew alone records the saying about the sword and the twelve legions, and it has featured in Christian discussion of violence ever since.

26.ctx: A night hearing before Caiaphas and the council, irregular under later Jewish law.
26.mean: False witnesses come forward but do not agree. Jesus is silent until the high priest puts him under oath: tell us if you are the Christ, the Son of God. Jesus says: you have said so. But I tell you, from now on you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds of heaven. The high priest tears his robes and charges blasphemy, and they judge him deserving death.
26.big: Jesus claims the place beside God from Psalm 110 and Daniel 7, and is condemned for it.

26.ctx: In the courtyard, while the trial goes on inside. Matthew interweaves the two scenes.
26.mean: A servant girl says Peter was with Jesus; he denies it. Another accuses him; he denies with an oath. Bystanders say his accent betrays him; he begins to invoke a curse and swear that he does not know the man. Immediately the rooster crows, and Peter goes out and weeps bitterly.
26.big: While Jesus confesses who he is, his leading disciple denies knowing him.

27.ctx: Early morning, after the night hearing before Caiaphas. Under Roman rule the Sanhedrin could not carry out a death sentence, so they take him to the governor.
27.mean: Matthew says that when morning came, all the chief priests and elders of the people took counsel against Jesus to put him to death, and they bound him, led him away and delivered him over to Pilate the governor.
27.big: A religious verdict must be turned into a political charge to be carried out.

27.ctx: Matthew alone records Judas's end here, placing it between the council's verdict and Jesus' appearance before Pilate.
27.mean: Judas, seeing Jesus condemned, returns the thirty pieces of silver saying he has sinned in betraying innocent blood. They refuse it, and he throws it down, departs and hangs himself. The priests buy the potter's field with it, which Matthew links to a prophecy associated with Jeremiah.
27.big: Remorse without repentance ends in despair.
27.diff: Acts 1:18 describes Judas's death differently; common explanations combine hanging with a subsequent fall. Matthew's citation blends Zechariah 11 with Jeremiah 19 and 32, a known difficulty.

27.ctx: Pilate's questioning, with the charge now framed as claiming kingship.
27.mean: Pilate asks: are you the King of the Jews? Jesus says: you have said so. To the accusations of the chief priests he gives no answer, so that the governor is greatly amazed.
27.big: Jesus is silent before his accusers, fulfilling Isaiah 53:7.

27.ctx: A Passover custom of releasing a prisoner, not attested outside the Gospels.
27.mean: Pilate offers Barabbas or Jesus. His wife sends word about a dream, warning him to have nothing to do with this righteous man. The chief priests persuade the crowd to ask for Barabbas, and they cry: let him be crucified.
27.big: The guilty man goes free and the innocent one is condemned in his place.

27.ctx: Pilate's attempt to clear himself, in a province he governed badly enough to be recalled to Rome a few years later.
27.mean: Seeing a riot beginning, Pilate washes his hands, saying he is innocent of this man's blood. The people answer: his blood be on us and on our children. He releases Barabbas and delivers Jesus to be crucified.
27.big: Pilate performs innocence while doing the thing he knows is unjust.
27.diff: Verse 25 has been terribly misused through history to justify violence against Jewish people. Matthew records the crowd in Jerusalem on one day, not a verdict on a whole people for all time; the New Testament lays responsibility for Jesus' death on human sin generally and on God's purpose (Acts 2:23).

27.ctx: Inside the governor's headquarters, before the whole battalion.
27.mean: The soldiers strip him, put a scarlet robe on him, twist a crown of thorns, put a reed in his right hand, kneel and mock him as King of the Jews, spit on him and strike him.
27.big: The soldiers' mockery states the truth they cannot see.

27.ctx: Golgotha, outside the city walls. Simon of Cyrene, in North Africa, is compelled to carry the cross.
27.mean: Jesus refuses wine mixed with gall. They crucify him and divide his garments by lot, and put the charge above his head: this is Jesus, the King of the Jews. Two robbers are crucified with him. Passers-by, chief priests and the robbers mock him: he saved others; he cannot save himself.
27.big: The mockers speak more truly than they know: to save others, he would not save himself.

27.ctx: From noon to three in the afternoon, near the end of some six hours on the cross.
27.mean: Darkness covers the land. Jesus cries: Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani — my God, my God, why have you forsaken me — the opening of Psalm 22. He cries out again and yields up his spirit. The temple curtain is torn from top to bottom, the earth shakes, tombs are opened, and the centurion and those with him say: truly this was the Son of God.
27.big: At the moment of his death a Roman officer confesses what the leaders denied.
27.diff: Matthew alone records the opened tombs, a passage much discussed. How to understand Jesus' forsakenness is a theological question Christians answer differently: Reformed and much evangelical theology holds that he bore the judgement due to sinners in his human nature, without division in the Trinity. Psalm 22 ends in vindication, not despair.

27.ctx: Late Friday afternoon. Jewish law required burial before nightfall, and the Sabbath began at sunset, which made haste necessary.
27.mean: Joseph of Arimathea, a rich man and a disciple, asks Pilate for the body, wraps it in a clean linen shroud and lays it in his own new tomb, rolling a great stone to the entrance. Mary Magdalene and the other Mary sit opposite the tomb.
27.big: The burial is witnessed, and the tomb is known.

27.ctx: Matthew alone records the guard at the tomb, which matters for the accusation in 28:11–15.
27.mean: The chief priests ask Pilate for a guard, recalling that Jesus said he would rise after three days, lest the disciples steal the body. Pilate grants it, and they seal the stone and set a guard.
27.big: Jesus' enemies remember his prediction better than his disciples do.

28.ctx: Early on the first day of the week. Women's testimony carried little legal weight, which makes them unlikely invented witnesses.
28.mean: There is a great earthquake, and an angel rolls back the stone and sits on it. The guards tremble and become like dead men. The angel tells the women: he is not here, for he has risen, as he said. Come, see the place, then go quickly and tell his disciples. As they run, Jesus meets them and says: greetings. They take hold of his feet and worship him.
28.big: The tomb is empty, and the risen Jesus is worshipped by the first witnesses.

28.ctx: The counter-story, which Matthew says was still circulating when he wrote.
28.mean: Some of the guard report to the chief priests, who give the soldiers a sum of money to say the disciples stole the body while they slept. This story has been spread among the Jews to this day.
28.big: The earliest explanation offered against the resurrection still conceded that the tomb was empty.

28.ctx: The closing scene, on a mountain in Galilee where Jesus had directed them.
28.mean: They see him and worship, but some doubt. Jesus says: all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptising them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you. And behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age.
28.big: The risen Christ sends his people to all nations with all authority and his abiding presence.
28.diff: The singular 'name' shared by Father, Son and Spirit is a key text for the doctrine of the Trinity. The promise 'I am with you' answers the name Immanuel in 1:23, closing the Gospel where it began.

1.ctx: Luke, a doctor and Paul's travelling companion, is the only Gentile author in the New Testament. He writes to Theophilus, probably a patron, and his Gospel is the first of two volumes with Acts.
1.mean: Luke says many have undertaken to compile a narrative, and that he too, having followed all things closely from the beginning, decided to write an orderly account, so that Theophilus may have certainty concerning the things he has been taught.
1.big: Luke states his method openly: careful investigation of eyewitness testimony, written so the reader can be sure.
1.diff: This is the only Gospel that begins by explaining how it was researched, and it is often cited in discussions of the Gospels' historical reliability.

1.ctx: Zechariah, a priest of the division of Abijah (1 Chronicles 24:10), serves in the temple; burning incense was a once-in-a-lifetime privilege chosen by lot.
1.mean: Gabriel appears and says Elizabeth will bear a son named John, who will be great, filled with the Holy Spirit from birth, and go before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah. Zechariah doubts because of their age and is struck mute until the birth.
1.big: God begins his great work with an elderly childless couple and a priest who struggles to believe.

1.ctx: Nazareth, an obscure Galilean village. Mary is betrothed, a legally binding arrangement before the couple lived together.
1.mean: Gabriel tells Mary she will conceive and bear a son, Jesus, who will be great, called the Son of the Most High, and given the throne of his father David, reigning for ever. She asks how, since she is a virgin. The angel says the Holy Spirit will come upon her, and the child will be called holy, the Son of God. Nothing will be impossible with God. Mary says: behold, I am the servant of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word.
1.big: The eternal Son enters the world through the willing obedience of an ordinary young woman.
1.diff: Mary's question is about means rather than doubt, and she is not rebuked as Zechariah was. The virgin conception is affirmed in the historic creeds and underlies Christ being truly God and truly man (see Mark 4:35).

1.ctx: Mary travels to the Judean hill country, a journey of several days, to visit her relative Elizabeth.
1.mean: When Mary greets her, the baby leaps in Elizabeth's womb, and Elizabeth, filled with the Holy Spirit, cries: blessed are you among women, and why is this granted to me that the mother of my Lord should come to me? Blessed is she who believed.
1.big: Elizabeth recognises Mary's unborn child as her Lord.

1.ctx: Mary's song, traditionally called the Magnificat, draws heavily on Hannah's song in 1 Samuel 2.
1.mean: Mary says her soul magnifies the Lord and her spirit rejoices in God her Saviour, for he has looked on the humble estate of his servant. He has scattered the proud, brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted the humble, filled the hungry with good things and sent the rich away empty, in remembrance of his mercy to Abraham and his offspring.
1.big: God's salvation overturns the world's order, lifting the lowly and humbling the powerful.
1.diff: Mary calls God 'my Saviour', which Christians have long noted as her own acknowledgement of need.

1.ctx: The birth of John, and the naming ceremony on the eighth day at his circumcision.
1.mean: Neighbours assume he will be named after his father, but Elizabeth insists on John. Zechariah writes: his name is John. Immediately his mouth is opened and he blesses God, and fear comes on all their neighbours.
1.big: Obedience to God's word restores the voice doubt had silenced.
1.h: The Birth of John the Baptist

1.ctx: Zechariah's song, traditionally called the Benedictus, the first prophecy after centuries of silence.
1.mean: Zechariah, filled with the Holy Spirit, blesses God for visiting and redeeming his people, raising a horn of salvation in the house of David, remembering his holy covenant and the oath to Abraham, so that they might serve him without fear. His child will be called the prophet of the Most High, going before the Lord to give knowledge of salvation in the forgiveness of sins, because of the tender mercy of our God, the sunrise visiting us from on high.
1.big: God is keeping promises made to Abraham and David, and the dawn is breaking.

2.ctx: Luke anchors the birth in datable imperial history. The census under Quirinius has been much discussed by historians.
2.mean: Joseph goes from Nazareth to Bethlehem, the city of David, with Mary. While they are there she gives birth to her firstborn son, wraps him in swaddling cloths and lays him in a manger, because there was no place for them in the inn.
2.big: The Saviour of the world is born in the town of David and laid in a feeding trough.
2.diff: Josephus dates a census under Quirinius to AD 6, later than Herod's death, which is a recognised difficulty. Proposed solutions include an earlier registration, a different translation of 'first', or an earlier term of office for Quirinius. The word rendered 'inn' more probably means the guest room of a family house.

2.ctx: Shepherds were a disreputable trade, often unable to keep ceremonial law and not accepted as witnesses in court.
2.mean: An angel announces good news of great joy for all the people: a Saviour, Christ the Lord, born in the city of David. A multitude of the heavenly host praises God: glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace among those with whom he is pleased. The shepherds go and find it as they were told, and make it known.
2.big: The first people told are shepherds, and the first evangelists are men whose word no court would take.

2.ctx: Jewish law required circumcision on the eighth day and presentation of the firstborn, with a sacrifice.
2.mean: He is circumcised and named Jesus, and they bring him to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord, offering a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons.
2.big: Jesus is born under the law, and his family's offering is the one allowed for the poor.
2.diff: Leviticus 12:8 permits birds instead of a lamb for those who cannot afford one — quiet evidence that the family was poor.

2.ctx: Simeon, a righteous and devout man, had been told he would not die before seeing the Lord's Christ.
2.mean: Simeon takes the child in his arms and blesses God: Lord, now you are letting your servant depart in peace, for my eyes have seen your salvation, a light for revelation to the Gentiles and for glory to your people Israel. He tells Mary the child is appointed for the fall and rising of many, and a sword will pierce her own soul.
2.big: An old man sees in an infant the salvation prepared for Gentiles as well as Israel.

2.ctx: Anna, a prophetess of great age, had worshipped in the temple with fasting and prayer night and day.
2.mean: Anna comes up at that very hour, gives thanks to God, and speaks of the child to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem.
2.big: A widow of eighty-four is among the first to proclaim the Messiah.

2.ctx: The family returns to Galilee after fulfilling the law's requirements.
2.mean: Luke says the child grew and became strong, filled with wisdom, and the favour of God was upon him.
2.big: Jesus grew as a real child, in wisdom as well as body (see Mark 4:35 on his full humanity).

2.ctx: The only glimpse of Jesus between infancy and adulthood. Families travelled to Passover in large groups, which explains how he was missed.
